chapters.title: Introduction to Human Anatomy and Physiology
chapters.intro: Connect structure with function, explain homeostasis, and describe the body with precise anatomical language.

sections.title: Structure, function, and levels of organization
focus: Connect a specific structural feature to its functional advantage.
Trace the hierarchy in order; an organ contains multiple tissue types.
sections.text:
Anatomy examines structure; physiology explains function. Thin lung exchange surfaces are an anatomical feature that permits rapid gas diffusion, a physiological process. A structural change can therefore alter performance.

The course's expanded hierarchy is: subatomic particles → atoms → molecules → macromolecules → organelles → cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism. An atom retains an element's identity; a molecule contains joined atoms. Macromolecules such as proteins build cellular structures. Organelles perform specialized tasks inside cells. The cell is the basic living structural and functional unit. A tissue combines similar cells and extracellular material; an organ combines at least two tissue types; an organ system coordinates organs.

For example, contractile proteins form cellular machinery; cardiac muscle cells form cardiac muscle tissue; the heart combines muscle, nervous, connective, and epithelial tissues; the cardiovascular system includes the heart and vessels. Histology studies tissues, whereas cytology studies cells. Do not confuse an organelle such as a mitochondrion with an organ such as a kidney.

🖼 Figure — Levels of Org in Body (image)
Description: Version 8.25 from the Textbook OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology Published May 18, 2016

sections.title: Life processes and survival requirements
focus: Distinguish digestion, absorption, assimilation, and excretion.
Match nutrients, oxygen, water, heat, and pressure to their contributions.
sections.text:
The ten course life processes describe different aspects of a living system. Movement changes position; responsiveness detects and responds to change; growth increases size or cell number; reproduction produces cells or a new organism. Respiration includes processes that make oxygen available and use it in cellular energy metabolism. Digestion breaks food into smaller components; absorption moves substances across a boundary into body fluids; circulation transports materials; assimilation incorporates absorbed substances into body structures; excretion removes metabolic wastes.

Metabolism is the total of chemical reactions, including synthesis and breakdown. Digestion, absorption, and assimilation are sequential but distinct: a protein is broken into amino acids, the amino acids cross the intestine, and cells use them to construct new proteins.

The five course requirements are nutrients, oxygen, water, suitable heat, and pressure. Nutrients supply energy and building materials. Oxygen accepts electrons during aerobic energy production. Water supports reactions and transport. Temperature affects enzymes; pressure gradients drive ventilation and filtration. Heat and pressure are physical conditions rather than chemical nutrients. Vital signs include body temperature, pulse, respiratory rate, and blood pressure; their interpretation depends on context.

sections.title: Feedback and homeostasis
focus: Negative feedback opposes a deviation; positive feedback amplifies a process.
Trace temperature regulation through receptor, control center, and effectors.
sections.text:
Homeostasis maintains internal conditions within a useful range despite ongoing disturbances. It is a dynamic balance, not an absence of change. A variable such as temperature fluctuates around a regulated range; normal values vary with activity, time, and measurement site.

A receptor detects change, a control center integrates information relative to a reference range, and an effector produces a response. In negative feedback, the response opposes the initial deviation. When core temperature rises, hypothalamic circuits promote sweating and increased skin blood flow; evaporating sweat and heat transfer reduce temperature. Cooling can reduce sweating, constrict skin vessels, and trigger shivering, which generates heat. Name the stimulus, receptor, controller, effectors, and response when explaining a feedback loop.

Positive feedback amplifies an initiating process until a separate stopping event occurs. Platelet activation recruits additional platelets during clot formation; sealing the injury and regulatory mechanisms limit the process. Positive feedback is not synonymous with beneficial, nor negative feedback with harmful. Failure of homeostatic regulation can contribute to disease. Studying a feedback loop means explaining what the response does to the original stimulus, rather than merely memorizing the response's name.

🖼 Figure — Negative Feedback Loops (image)
Description: Caption: In a negative feedback loop, a stimulus—a deviation from a set point—is resisted through a physiological process that returns the body to homeostasis. (a) A negative feedback loop has four basic parts. (b) Body temperature is regulated by negative feedback. Speficic URL: https://cnx.org/contents/FPtK1zmh@8.108:8Q_5pQQo@4/Homeostasis

sections.title: Body cavities and serous membranes
focus: Distinguish organ location from the potential space between serous layers.
Visceral covers an organ; parietal lines a wall.
sections.text:
The axial body comprises the head, neck, and trunk; the appendicular portion comprises limbs. Dorsal cavities include the cranial cavity containing the brain and the vertebral canal containing the spinal cord. The diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity. The thorax includes two pleural compartments and the mediastinum; the heart lies within its pericardial sac in the mediastinum.

The abdominal portion contains much of the digestive tract, liver, gallbladder, and spleen; the pelvic portion includes the urinary bladder, rectum, and internal reproductive structures. No physical wall separates abdominal and pelvic portions. Kidneys, adrenal glands, and much of the pancreas are retroperitoneal, posterior to the peritoneal lining rather than suspended within the peritoneal cavity.

A parietal serous layer lines a cavity wall; a visceral layer covers an organ. Pleura relates to lungs, pericardium to the heart, and peritoneum to abdominopelvic organs. The thin fluid-filled potential space between layers permits low-friction movement. The lung itself is not located inside the thin pleural fluid space. Additional head spaces include oral, nasal, orbital, middle-ear cavities, and paranasal sinuses.

🖼 Figure — Body cavities and thoracic landmarks (image)
Figure key: 1 cranial; 2 thoracic; 3 abdominal; 4 pelvic; 5 ventral; 6 abdominopelvic. Letters: a mediastinum, b vertebral canal, c pleural compartment, d pericardial compartment, e diaphragm.
Description: The head contains the cranial cavity and the vertebral canal continues inferiorly. The thorax contains right and left pleural compartments with the mediastinum between them and the pericardial compartment around the heart. The diaphragm separates thorax from the abdominal region; abdomen and pelvis together form the abdominopelvic cavity. The ventral cavity grouping includes thoracic and abdominopelvic compartments.

sections.title: Eleven organ systems working together
focus: Associate each system with organs and a specific function.
Bone marrow forms blood cells; kidneys regulate blood composition and produce urine.
sections.text:
| System | Representative organs | Main contributions |
|---|---|---|
| Integumentary | Skin, hair, nails, skin glands | Barrier, sensation, heat regulation, vitamin D precursor production |
| Skeletal | Bones, cartilage, ligaments | Support, protection, mineral storage, blood cell formation |
| Muscular | Skeletal muscles and tendons | Movement, posture, heat |
| Nervous | Brain, spinal cord, nerves | Rapid sensory processing and control |
| Endocrine | Hormone-secreting glands | Chemical regulation of growth, reproduction, and metabolism |
| Cardiovascular | Heart, blood vessels | Transport of gases, nutrients, hormones, and wastes |
| Lymphatic/immune | Lymph vessels, nodes, thymus, spleen | Fluid return, defense, transport of absorbed fats |
| Respiratory | Airways and lungs | Oxygen/carbon dioxide exchange and acid-base contribution |
| Digestive | Digestive tract, liver, pancreas, gallbladder | Food breakdown and nutrient absorption |
| Urinary | Kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra | Waste excretion, fluid/electrolyte and acid-base regulation |
| Reproductive | Testes and ducts; ovaries, uterine tubes, uterus and associated structures | Gametes, sex hormones, reproduction |

Systems overlap functionally: skeletal marrow produces blood cells, while blood transports oxygen used by muscles. The kidneys form urine; the bladder stores it. Male and female reproductive structures belong to one system category in the eleven-system count. Organ function can depend on cooperation among multiple systems.

sections.title: Anatomical position and directional terms
focus: Apply directional terms from the subject’s anatomical position.
Proximal/distal refer to attachment, whereas medial/lateral refer to the midline.
sections.text:
In anatomical position, the person stands upright, faces forward, holds upper limbs at the sides, and turns palms anteriorly with forearms supinated. Right and left always refer to the subject's perspective. Directional descriptions retain this reference even if a person lies down.

| Pair | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Superior / inferior | Toward head / toward feet | The chest is superior to the pelvis. |
| Anterior / posterior | Toward front / toward back | The sternum is anterior to the heart. |
| Medial / lateral | Toward / away from midline | The nose is medial to the eyes. |
| Proximal / distal | Nearer / farther from attachment | The elbow is proximal to the wrist. |
| Superficial / deep | Nearer / farther from the surface | Skin is superficial to muscle. |
| Ipsilateral / contralateral | Same side / opposite sides | Right arm and right leg are ipsilateral. |

Ventral generally corresponds to anterior and dorsal to posterior for the human trunk. The thumb is lateral to the little finger in anatomical position. The subject's right may appear on the viewer's left. Use a comparison structure when applying a relational term rather than saying an isolated structure is simply proximal.

Description: Caption: Paired directional terms are shown as applied to the human body. URL:https://cnx.org/contents/FPtK1zmh@8.108:F-TuqKAF@5/Anatomical-Terminology

sections.title: Body planes and surface landmarks
focus: Sagittal: right/left; coronal: front/back; transverse: upper/lower.
Distinguish patellar from popliteal and brachial from antebrachial.
sections.text:
A sagittal plane divides right and left portions; midsagittal divides equal halves, whereas parasagittal divides unequal portions. A frontal or coronal plane divides anterior and posterior portions. A transverse or horizontal plane divides superior and inferior portions. Oblique sections cross at an angle. A cross-section is perpendicular to an object's long axis; a longitudinal section follows it.

Surface landmarks communicate location precisely. Cephalic means head; cranial skull; frontal forehead; orbital eye; otic ear; nasal nose; buccal cheek; oral mouth; mental chin; cervical neck; acromial shoulder; axillary armpit; brachial upper arm; antecubital anterior elbow; antebrachial forearm; carpal wrist; metacarpal hand; digital fingers or toes. Mammary refers to breast, umbilical navel, lumbar lower back, coxal hip, inguinal groin, pubic anterior pelvic region, gluteal buttock, femoral thigh, patellar front of knee, popliteal back of knee, crural leg, sural calf, tarsal ankle, pedal foot, plantar sole, and calcaneal heel.

The anatomical leg is the segment between knee and ankle, not the entire lower limb. Match a plane with the portions it produces rather than the direction in which a drawing is displayed.

sections.title: Abdominal regions and quadrants
focus: Locate all nine regions and four quadrants using the subject’s right/left.
Epigastric is superior to umbilical; hypogastric is inferior to it.
sections.text:
Two crossing reference lines create right upper, left upper, right lower, and left lower quadrants. The liver and gallbladder occupy much of the right upper quadrant; the stomach and spleen relate to the left upper quadrant. The appendix is typically in the right lower quadrant; sigmoid colon is associated with the left lower quadrant. Organs may extend across more than one region.

The nine-region arrangement uses two vertical and two horizontal reference lines. From the subject's right to left:

| Subject's right | Middle | Subject's left |
|---|---|---|
| Right hypochondriac: liver/gallbladder region | Epigastric: stomach and part of liver | Left hypochondriac: spleen/stomach |
| Right lumbar: ascending colon | Umbilical: small intestine/transverse colon | Left lumbar: descending colon |
| Right iliac/inguinal: cecum/appendix | Hypogastric/pubic: bladder and small intestine | Left iliac/inguinal: sigmoid colon |

The table follows the subject's right-to-left orientation; rows proceed from superior to inferior. Epigastric is upper middle; hypogastric is lower middle. A distended bladder rises from the pelvis toward the hypogastric region. Regional descriptions help locate findings but do not identify a diagnosis by themselves.

Figure key: 1 right hypochondriac; 2 epigastric; 3 left hypochondriac; 4 right lumbar; 5 umbilical; 6 left lumbar; 7 right iliac; 8 hypogastric; 9 left iliac. Right and left are the subject’s.
Description: The grid is viewed from the front. Across its upper row, numbers 1–3 identify right hypochondriac, epigastric, and left hypochondriac regions. Across the middle row, 4–6 identify right lumbar, umbilical, and left lumbar. Across the lower row, 7–9 identify right iliac, hypogastric, and left iliac. The subject’s right appears on the viewer’s left.

chapters.title: Chemical Basis of Life
chapters.intro: Use atomic structure, bonding, water, pH, and biological molecules to explain cellular behavior.

sections.title: Elements, atoms, isotopes, and electrons
focus: Calculate protons, neutrons, and electrons separately.
Distinguish isotope, ion, mass number, and average atomic mass.
sections.text:
Matter occupies space and has mass. An element consists of atoms with the same proton number. A proton is positively charged and a neutron uncharged; both occupy the nucleus and contribute approximately one atomic mass unit. Electrons have negative charge, occupy an electron cloud, and have much less mass, not zero mass.

Atomic number equals proton number. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons. Mass number counts protons plus neutrons for one isotope; periodic-table atomic mass is an abundance-weighted average of isotopes. Isotopes share proton numbers but differ in neutron numbers. Changing electrons makes an ion; changing neutrons makes another isotope of the same element.

In the simplified shell model used here, the first shell holds up to two electrons and the next holds up to eight for the common light elements. Nitrogen has seven electrons in a neutral atom: two inner and five outer electrons. Outer valence electrons strongly influence bonding. Oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, calcium, and phosphorus are major body elements. Other important symbols include Na sodium, K potassium, Cl chlorine, Mg magnesium, S sulfur, and Fe iron. Do not confuse the sodium symbol Na with nitrogen N.

🖼 Figure — Elements of the Human Body (image)
Description: The main elements that compose the human body, by mass percent, are shown from most abundant to least abundant element. The atomic fractions (fractions of atoms) are different due to differing atomic weights. As in water, oxygen contributes the most mass, but hydrogen is the most common atom.

Description: Study the labeled structures in Two Models of Atomic Structure. The accompanying section explains their relationships: Calculate protons, neutrons, and electrons separately. Distinguish isotope, ion, mass number, and average atomic mass.

Description: Study the labeled structures in Isotopes of Hydrogen. The accompanying section explains their relationships: Calculate protons, neutrons, and electrons separately. Distinguish isotope, ion, mass number, and average atomic mass.

sections.title: Ionic, covalent, and hydrogen bonding
focus: Electron transfer produces ions; sharing produces covalent bonds.
Distinguish bonds within water from hydrogen bonds between water molecules.
sections.text:
Ionic bonding follows electron transfer and electrostatic attraction. When sodium loses an electron it becomes Na+, a cation; chlorine gains an electron and becomes Cl−, an anion. Neither changes its proton number. Opposite charges attract. Dissolving sodium chloride in water separates ions that can carry current.

Covalent bonds share electron pairs. Nonpolar bonds share relatively equally; polar covalent bonds share unequally. Water contains polar O–H covalent bonds, with partial negative charge near oxygen and partial positive charge near hydrogen. A molecule can contain polar bonds yet have no overall dipole if its geometry cancels the polarities.

Hydrogen bonds are attractions involving a partially positive hydrogen and an electronegative partner. They help organize liquid water, stabilize protein shapes, and connect complementary DNA bases. They are weaker individually than covalent bonds. The bonds within a water molecule are covalent; attractions between water molecules include hydrogen bonds. A compound contains atoms of at least two different elements; O2 is a molecule but not a compound. In aqueous biological conditions, compare bonds in context: dissolved ions behave differently from ions in an intact crystal.

🖼 Figure — Ionic Bonding (image)
Description: (a) Sodium readily donates the solitary electron in its valence shell to chlorine, which needs only one electron to have a full valence shell. (b) The opposite electrical charges of the resulting sodium cation and chloride anion result in the formation of a bond of attraction called an ionic bond. (c) The attraction of many sodium and chloride ions results in the formation of large groupings called crystals.

sections.title: Chemical reactions and energy
focus: Recognize synthesis, decomposition, exchange, and reversible equations.
Hydrolysis consumes water; dehydration synthesis releases water.
sections.text:
Synthesis combines smaller units: A + B → AB. Decomposition separates a larger compound: AB → A + B. Exchange rearranges partners: AB + CD → AD + CB. Reversible reactions proceed in either direction depending on conditions, represented with a double arrow. At equilibrium, forward and reverse rates balance; molecules still react.

Anabolism builds larger biological molecules and requires energy input overall. Catabolism breaks down molecules and often releases usable energy overall. Dehydration synthesis joins subunits while removing the components of water; hydrolysis uses water to break a linkage. Building a peptide from amino acids and digesting that peptide illustrate opposite directions.

Energy is needed to break chemical bonds, while bond formation releases energy. Whether the whole reaction releases or requires energy depends on the balance between reactants and products. A catalyst lowers activation energy and speeds a reaction without being consumed; it does not change the overall energy difference or equilibrium position. Temperature, concentration, surface area, and catalyst availability affect reaction rates. Enzymes catalyze particular biological steps rather than making every possible reaction happen indiscriminately.

Energy clarification: breaking a chemical bond requires energy. Net reaction energy depends on all bonds broken and formed and the full reactant/product balance; the word analogy is for reaction patterns.

sections.title: Water, salts, and inorganic substances
focus: Explain water’s solvent, transport, reaction, and thermal roles.
A dissolved substance conducts current only when mobile charged particles are available.
sections.text:
Water is the most abundant inorganic substance in many cells. Its polarity makes it an effective solvent for ions and many polar compounds. Water also provides a reaction medium, participates in hydrolysis, lubricates tissues, cushions structures, and transports dissolved materials. Its relatively high heat capacity limits rapid temperature change; evaporation removes substantial heat.

Hydrogen bonding contributes to water's cohesion and thermal properties. Oil does not mix well with water because most lipid regions are nonpolar. Hydrophilic substances interact with water; hydrophobic regions avoid favorable mixing with it. Water is not a universal solvent for every substance.

Inorganic substances important to physiology include water, oxygen, carbon dioxide, and salts. Oxygen participates in aerobic cellular respiration; carbon dioxide is a metabolic product and contributes to acid-base chemistry. Salts supply ions such as sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride, phosphate, and bicarbonate. These support electrical signaling, contraction, fluid balance, mineralized tissue, and buffering. Dissociation of an electrolyte produces ions in solution, whereas dissolving a nonelectrolyte such as glucose need not produce ions. Concentration of dissolved particles influences osmosis, but charge and membrane permeability also matter. Organic biological compounds generally have carbon frameworks and often carbon–hydrogen bonds. Carbon dioxide and bicarbonate are important carbon-containing compounds still classified as inorganic. The four major organic classes studied here are carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids.

sections.title: Acids, bases, pH, and buffers
focus: A one-unit pH decrease means roughly ten times more hydrogen ions.
Buffers resist change; they do not amplify pH disturbances.
sections.text:
An acid donates hydrogen ions; a base accepts hydrogen ions or increases hydroxide availability in a simple aqueous description. An acid and a base can react to form water and a salt. pH expresses hydrogen ion activity on a logarithmic scale: a decrease of one pH unit represents about a tenfold increase in hydrogen ion concentration.

At approximately room temperature, pure water has pH 7 and equal hydrogen and hydroxide concentrations. Below 7 is acidic; above 7 is alkaline. Acetic acid solutions are acidic, distilled water is approximately neutral before gas absorption, blood is mildly alkaline, and ammonia solutions are alkaline. Physiological arterial blood pH is normally about 7.35–7.45; other body compartments differ. Do not assume stomach contents have blood's pH.

A buffer limits a change in pH by reversibly binding or releasing hydrogen ions; it does not prevent every change. The carbonic acid/bicarbonate relationship is CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−. Added hydrogen can combine with bicarbonate; carbonic acid can dissociate when hydrogen is removed. Lungs regulate CO2, and kidneys regulate acid excretion and bicarbonate. Buffering, ventilation, and kidney function cooperate.

sections.title: Carbohydrates and their building blocks
focus: Distinguish monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides with examples.
Starch is plant storage; glycogen is animal storage.
sections.text:
Carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Monosaccharides are single sugars: glucose, fructose, and galactose are familiar examples. Ribose and deoxyribose are five-carbon sugars in nucleic acids. Disaccharides contain two sugar units: sucrose combines glucose and fructose, lactose glucose and galactose, and maltose two glucose units. Hydrolysis separates them into smaller sugars.

Polysaccharides contain many linked monosaccharides. Starch stores glucose in plants; glycogen stores glucose in animals, particularly liver and skeletal muscle. Liver glycogen helps maintain blood glucose, whereas muscle glycogen fuels muscle activity. Cellulose forms plant structural material; humans do not digest its main linkages with their own digestive enzymes, so it contributes dietary fiber.

Sugar identity and linkage matter: compounds containing the same elements can have different structures and functions. Glucose oxidation can supply energy for ATP production, but a sugar is not itself an enzyme or a nucleic acid. Glycoproteins and glycolipids contain carbohydrate components that contribute to cell recognition. Associate each carbohydrate with its number of units, source, and physiological role rather than memorizing only a formula.

sections.title: Lipids: stored fuel, membranes, and signaling
focus: Compare triglyceride, phospholipid, and steroid structure with function.
Unsaturation means carbon–carbon double bonds.
sections.text:
Triglycerides consist of glycerol joined to three fatty acids. They store concentrated energy, insulate, and cushion. Saturated fatty acids have no carbon–carbon double bonds in their hydrocarbon chains; unsaturated fatty acids have one or more. Cis double bonds commonly introduce bends, reducing close packing. Physical state depends on composition and temperature, so avoid an absolute rule that every animal fat is solid or every plant fat liquid.

Phospholipids have a polar head and nonpolar fatty acid tails. Their amphipathic structure promotes bilayers, with heads toward water and tails away from it. Steroids have fused carbon rings; cholesterol stabilizes animal membranes and is a precursor of steroid hormones, bile acids, and vitamin D-related molecules. Lipids are not all long repeating polymers in the same sense as proteins or nucleic acids.

Fats provide the body's largest concentrated reserve of metabolic fuel. Breaking down fatty acids feeds energy pathways, while storing triglycerides requires biosynthesis. A molecule's role follows its structure: a phospholipid forms a membrane boundary, while a triglyceride is suited for energy storage. Cholesterol has essential functions even though its transport and concentration have health implications.

sections.title: Proteins, conformation, and denaturation
focus: Explain primary through quaternary structure without assuming every protein has all four.
Denaturation changes conformation and can impair function.
sections.text:
Proteins contain amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Each amino acid has an amino group, carboxyl group, hydrogen, and variable side chain attached to a central carbon. Peptide formation links one amino acid's carboxyl region to another's amino region. Sequence determines the possibilities for folding and function.

Primary structure is amino acid sequence. Secondary structure includes alpha helices and beta sheets stabilized by backbone hydrogen bonding. Tertiary structure is a polypeptide's overall three-dimensional shape; quaternary structure combines multiple polypeptide subunits. Hemoglobin has several subunits, while not every protein has a quaternary level.

Functions include catalysis by enzymes, transport, structural support, movement, receptors, signaling, defense, and fluid balance. Examples are collagen, keratin, hemoglobin, antibodies, actin, and membrane channels. A changed shape can impair an active site or binding region. Denaturation disrupts normal conformation through heat, extreme pH, or other conditions; it usually does not mean hydrolyzing every peptide bond. Some changes are reversible and others are not. Protein function depends on both sequence and the environment in which folding occurs.

🖼 Figure — Levels of protein structure (image)
Description: Primary structure is an amino acid chain. Secondary structure includes alpha helices and beta sheets. Tertiary structure is the overall folded form of one chain. Quaternary structure combines multiple chains, illustrated by hemoglobin.

sections.title: Nucleotides, DNA, RNA, and ATP
focus: DNA: deoxyribose and thymine; RNA: ribose and uracil.
Hydrogen bonds connect complementary DNA bases; covalent bonds form the backbone.
sections.text:
A nucleotide contains a nitrogenous base, a five-carbon sugar, and phosphate. DNA uses deoxyribose and the bases adenine, thymine, cytosine, and guanine. RNA uses ribose and uracil instead of thymine. DNA commonly forms two antiparallel strands; RNA commonly occurs as a single strand that may fold into complex shapes.

In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine with guanine through hydrogen bonding. Covalent bonds hold each sugar-phosphate backbone together. DNA stores inherited instructions. Messenger RNA carries a transcribed message, ribosomal RNA contributes to ribosomes, and transfer RNA connects codons with amino acids during protein synthesis. DNA occurs mainly in the nucleus but also in mitochondria; RNA is present in nucleus and cytoplasm.

ATP, adenosine triphosphate, contains adenine, ribose, and three phosphates. Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and inorganic phosphate can be coupled to cellular work; adding phosphate to ADP requires energy. ATP is an immediate energy-transfer molecule, not the largest long-term fuel store. Distinguish nucleotide components from amino acids and distinguish genetic information storage from translation into a polypeptide.

Source label correction: the lower-right sugar should read “Ribose (in RNA).” DNA contains deoxyribose. The original artwork is retained, and this correction applies to that printed label.
Description: A nucleotide combines a phosphate group, a pentose sugar, and a nitrogenous base. The left panel separates pyrimidines from purines; the right shows a sugar-phosphate backbone with attached bases. The lower panel compares deoxyribose with ribose. The source misprints the ribose label as “in DNA”; the correct association is ribose in RNA and deoxyribose in DNA.

sections.markdown:
A nucleotide contains a nitrogenous base, a five-carbon sugar, and phosphate. DNA uses deoxyribose and the bases adenine, thymine, cytosine, and guanine. RNA uses ribose and uracil instead of thymine. DNA commonly forms two antiparallel strands; RNA commonly occurs as a single strand that may fold into complex shapes.

In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine with guanine through hydrogen bonding. Covalent bonds hold each sugar-phosphate backbone together. DNA stores inherited instructions. Messenger RNA carries a transcribed message, ribosomal RNA contributes to ribosomes, and transfer RNA connects codons with amino acids during protein synthesis. DNA occurs mainly in the nucleus but also in mitochondria; RNA is present in nucleus and cytoplasm.

ATP, adenosine triphosphate, contains adenine, ribose, and three phosphates. Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and inorganic phosphate can be coupled to cellular work; adding phosphate to ADP requires energy. ATP is an immediate energy-transfer molecule, not the largest long-term fuel store. Distinguish nucleotide components from amino acids and distinguish genetic information storage from translation into a polypeptide.

chapters.title: Cells
chapters.intro: Explain how membranes, organelles, transport, and cell division support cellular life.

sections.title: The fluid mosaic membrane and cell junctions
focus: Relate selective permeability to solute size, charge, polarity, and transport proteins.
Tight junctions seal, desmosomes anchor, gap junctions communicate.
sections.text:
The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer containing proteins, cholesterol, and surface carbohydrates. Polar heads contact extracellular fluid and cytosol; nonpolar tails face inward. Small nonpolar molecules such as oxygen cross the lipid region relatively readily. Ions and many polar solutes require channels or carriers. Selective permeability permits some substances more readily than others.

Integral proteins are embedded in the membrane and may span it; peripheral proteins associate with a surface. Functions include transport, enzymatic activity, adhesion, receptors, and recognition. Glycoprotein and glycolipid carbohydrate chains on the extracellular face contribute to the glycocalyx and recognition of cell identity. A receptor changes cell behavior when an appropriate signal binds.

Tight junctions restrict movement between neighboring epithelial cells. Desmosomes anchor adjacent cells to resist mechanical stress. Gap junctions connect cytoplasm through channels, allowing ions and small signaling molecules to pass. These structures serve different purposes: sealing, anchoring, and communication. A membrane is dynamic, but its components are organized rather than randomly interchangeable with cell wall materials; human cells do not have cellulose cell walls.

🖼 Figure — Phospholipid bilayer (image)
Description: Two phospholipid layers place their hydrophilic heads toward extracellular fluid and cytosol. Hydrophobic tails face one another within the membrane interior. This arrangement produces a boundary with water-facing surfaces and a nonpolar interior.

🖼 Figure — Fluid mosaic membrane components (image)
Description: Membrane proteins are embedded in or associated with a phospholipid bilayer. Some span it as channels. Cholesterol lies among lipid tails. Carbohydrate chains project from the extracellular surface on glycoproteins and glycolipids, supporting recognition and surface interactions.

Description: Study the labeled structures in Types of Cell Junctions new. The accompanying section explains their relationships: Relate selective permeability to solute size, charge, polarity, and transport proteins. Tight junctions seal, desmosomes anchor, gap junctions communicate.

sections.title: Organelles and the protein shipping pathway
focus: Trace a secreted protein from ribosome through ER, Golgi, and vesicles.
Distinguish lysosomal digestion, peroxisomal oxidation, and mitochondrial ATP production.
sections.text:
Ribosomes assemble amino acids into polypeptides. Free ribosomes commonly make cytosolic proteins; ribosomes attached to rough endoplasmic reticulum produce proteins entering the secretory or membrane pathway. Rough ER consists of membrane-bound sacs called cisternae. Smooth ER lacks attached ribosomes and contributes to lipid synthesis, detoxification, and calcium storage in specialized cells.

The Golgi apparatus receives transport vesicles, modifies and sorts proteins/lipids, and packages products into vesicles. A vesicle is a small membrane-bound transport compartment. A secreted protein generally travels ribosome → rough ER → transport vesicle → Golgi → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane. Cisternae occur in both ER and Golgi; cristae specifically describe inner mitochondrial membrane folds.

Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that digest engulfed material and worn components. Autophagy recycles cellular components; extensive self-digestion is associated with autolysis after severe damage. Peroxisomes participate in oxidation and detoxification and contain catalase to handle hydrogen peroxide; liver and kidney cells have prominent detoxification roles. Mitochondria support aerobic ATP production with a matrix and folded inner membrane. A large need for secretion predicts abundant rough ER/Golgi, whereas high energy demand predicts many mitochondria.

🖼 Figure — Golgi processing and vesicle traffic (image)
Description: A cis receiving face lies near endoplasmic reticulum, with transport vesicles arriving at stacked Golgi cisternae. Products move through the stack and leave from the trans face in vesicles toward selected destinations, including the plasma membrane. The accompanying micrograph shows stacked membrane profiles.

🖼 Figure — Mitochondrion new (image)
Description: Version 8.25 from the Textbook OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology Published May 18, 2016

sections.title: Nucleus, cytoskeleton, and surface extensions
focus: Nuclear pores regulate exchange; the nucleolus assembles ribosomal subunits.
Microvilli increase area, cilia move surface material, a sperm flagellum propels the cell.
sections.text:
The nucleus contains most cellular DNA within a double-membrane envelope. Nuclear pores regulate traffic such as RNA export and protein import. The nucleolus assembles ribosomal subunits using ribosomal RNA and proteins. Chromatin is DNA associated with proteins; a nucleosome is DNA wrapped around histone proteins. Before division, chromatin condenses into visibly distinct chromosomes.

The cytoskeleton supports shape, transport, and movement. Microfilaments include actin; intermediate filaments provide mechanical strength; microtubules form intracellular tracks, spindle elements, and the core of cilia/flagella. Centrosomal machinery helps organize microtubules during division. Mature cell specialization can alter organelle composition, as in red blood cells lacking a nucleus.

Microvilli are actin-supported projections that increase absorptive surface area, such as in intestinal cells. Cilia generally move material along a surface, such as mucus in respiratory passages or fluid near uterine tubes. A flagellum propels a sperm cell. Motile cilia and flagella have microtubule-based structures. Do not assign the function of surface-area amplification to every projection: a moving cilium and an absorptive microvillus have different internal structures and roles.

🖼 Figure — Cytoskeletal Components (image)
Description: Version 8.25 from the Textbook OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology Published May 18, 2016

🖼 Figure — Nuclear envelope, pores, chromatin, and nucleolus (image)
Description: A double-membrane envelope surrounds the nucleus and contains pores for regulated exchange. Chromatin occupies the interior, and a prominent nucleolus supports ribosomal-subunit assembly. The outer membrane is associated with endoplasmic reticulum.

sections.title: Passive transport: diffusion and filtration
focus: Diffusion follows a concentration gradient; filtration follows a pressure gradient.
Facilitated diffusion uses proteins but remains passive.
sections.text:
Simple diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient due to molecular motion. Oxygen and carbon dioxide can diffuse through cell membranes. The rate increases with a steeper gradient, higher temperature, larger surface area, and shorter distance; larger particles generally move more slowly. Diffusion does not require cellular ATP, and individual molecules continue moving at equilibrium even when net flux is zero.

Facilitated diffusion also moves down an electrochemical gradient without direct ATP input, but uses a channel or carrier. Carrier-mediated movement is selective and can saturate when transporters are occupied. Glucose enters many cells through glucose transporters; insulin increases transporter availability in selected tissues. Some other glucose transport is coupled to ion gradients, so not all glucose transport is the same mechanism.

Filtration moves water and small solutes under a pressure gradient across a barrier. Renal glomerular filtration is driven principally by blood pressure and limited by the filtration barrier; it is not a mechanism by which whole blood cells routinely pass into urine. Passive means no direct metabolic energy expenditure by the transport process. It does not mean that blood pressure, membrane proteins, or prior physiological activity have no role.

🖼 Figure — Facilitated Diffusion (image)
Description: Caption: (a) Facilitated diffusion of substances crossing the cell (plasma) membrane takes place with the help of proteins such as channel proteins and carrier proteins. Channel proteins are less selective than carrier proteins, and usually mildly discriminate between their cargo based on size and charge. (b) Carrier proteins are more selective, often only allowing one particular type of molecule to cross. sections.title: Osmosis, tonicity, and cell volume
focus: Hypertonic shrinks cells; hypotonic swells cells; isotonic preserves volume.
Tonicity depends on effective, relatively nonpenetrating solutes.
sections.text:
Osmosis is net water movement across a selectively permeable membrane in response to a difference in effective solute concentration. Water moves toward the side with more nonpenetrating solute when other forces do not balance it. Aquaporins facilitate water movement, but water transport remains passive.

An isotonic solution produces no sustained net change in cell volume. In a hypertonic solution, extracellular effective solute concentration is higher: water leaves and the cell shrinks, a red-cell change called crenation. In a hypotonic solution, water enters and the cell swells; excessive swelling can cause lysis. Red blood cell rupture is hemolysis.

Tonicity depends on solutes that do not freely cross the relevant membrane and therefore differs from total osmolarity. An iso-osmotic solution need not be isotonic if its solute enters cells rapidly. Predict direction first by comparing effective concentrations, then predict cell volume. Do not reverse the water direction by imagining that water is moving along the solute's concentration gradient. In an isotonic environment water still crosses in both directions; the average fluxes balance.

🖼 Figure — Osmosis across a selectively permeable barrier (image)
Description: Two compartments initially have different solute concentrations. Water crosses the separating membrane toward the side with more effective solute, raising its fluid level and lowering the other side’s level. Solute particles remain separated in this schematic; water movement changes the fluid heights.

🖼 Figure — Red blood cells in hypertonic, isotonic, and hypotonic solutions (image)
Description: Panel a shows shrunken, crenated cells as water leaves in a hypertonic environment. Panel b shows normal red-cell form in an isotonic environment with balanced water movement. Panel c shows swelling and possible rupture as water enters in a hypotonic environment.

sections.title: Active transport and vesicular transport
focus: The sodium–potassium pump uses ATP and maintains ion gradients.
Distinguish phagocytosis, pinocytosis, receptor-mediated uptake, exocytosis, and transcytosis.
sections.text:
Primary active transport uses ATP directly to move substances against electrochemical gradients. The sodium–potassium pump exports three sodium ions and imports two potassium ions per ATP cycle, supporting ion gradients. Secondary active transport couples one solute's downhill movement to another's uphill movement; the supporting gradient is ultimately energy-dependent.

Endocytosis brings material into membrane-bound vesicles. Phagocytosis engulfs large particles such as bacteria; pinocytosis samples extracellular fluid and dissolved substances; receptor-mediated endocytosis concentrates selected ligands through receptors. A phagosome can fuse with lysosomes for digestion. The plasma membrane supplies the initial engulfing boundary, not the nuclear membrane.

Exocytosis releases vesicle contents when the vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane, as during hormone or neurotransmitter secretion. Transcytosis combines uptake on one cell surface, vesicle movement, and release from another. Vesicular processes require energy and cytoskeletal/trafficking machinery, even though a concentration gradient alone does not describe the movement of a large particle. Distinguish secretion by exocytosis from passive leakage through a channel.

🖼 Figure — Phagocytosis, pinocytosis, and receptor-mediated uptake (image)
Description: The left example engulfs a large particle into a vesicle. The middle example internalizes a small sample of extracellular fluid. The right example concentrates selected ligands through matching surface receptors before vesicle formation. All involve membrane remodeling and cellular energy.

🖼 Figure — Exocytosis (image)
Description: An intracellular vesicle approaches and fuses with the plasma membrane. Its contents are released to extracellular fluid, while the vesicle membrane becomes continuous with the cell surface.

sections.title: Cell cycle, mitosis, and cytokinesis
focus: DNA replication occurs in S phase; sister chromatids separate in anaphase.
Mitosis divides nuclear material; cytokinesis divides cytoplasm.
sections.text:
Interphase occupies much of the cycle. In G1, cells grow and perform normal functions. S phase duplicates DNA. G2 prepares for division and checks replicated material. A duplicated chromosome has two sister chromatids joined at a centromere; DNA replication precedes mitosis rather than occurring during metaphase.

During prophase, chromosomes condense and spindle assembly begins; nuclear envelope breakdown follows in the prometaphase subdivision often included within prophase in a four-phase course scheme. Metaphase aligns chromosomes at the equator. Anaphase separates sister chromatids as centromeric cohesion is released. Telophase forms new nuclei as chromosomes decondense. Cytokinesis divides cytoplasm, usually through an actin-based cleavage furrow in animal cells.

Mitosis distributes duplicated chromosomes into daughter nuclei; cytokinesis physically partitions the cell. Normal mitotic division generally preserves chromosome number. Cells may leave the cycle into G0. Mature skeletal muscle fibers and most mature neurons have very limited division; mature red cells cannot divide because they lack nuclei. Some specialized tissues rely on stem or progenitor cells for replacement. Distinguish a nondividing mature cell from a tissue that still contains dividing replacement cells.

sections.title: Division control, stem cells, and cancer
focus: Different gene expression drives much cellular specialization.
Distinguish self-renewal, differentiation, benign growth, invasion, and metastasis.
sections.text:
Cell division supports growth, replacement, and repair. Checkpoints monitor DNA integrity, replication, and chromosome attachment. Cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases help coordinate progression. Growth factors, nutrient supply, contact with neighboring cells, and internal damage signals influence whether a cell divides. Apoptosis removes selected damaged or unnecessary cells through regulated death.

Stem cells can self-renew and produce differentiated descendants. Progenitor cells generally have more limited developmental potential. Differentiation largely reflects differences in gene expression: most nucleated somatic cells contain similar genetic information but activate different sets of genes. A nerve cell and a skin cell usually do not differ because each possesses entirely unrelated genomes.

Cancer involves loss of normal growth regulation and may include invasion and metastasis. A benign tumor remains localized and does not metastasize, although location can still make it harmful. A malignant tumor can invade nearby tissues and spread. DNA mutations can affect growth-regulating genes; chemical carcinogens, radiation, inherited variants, and some infections contribute in different contexts. An exposure is a risk factor, not proof that every exposed cell becomes cancerous. Normal healing requires regulated cell growth and differs from uncontrolled proliferation.

chapters.title: Cellular Metabolism

sections.title: Metabolism, enzymes, and pathway control
focus: Explain active site specificity, cofactors/coenzymes, and feedback inhibition.
Enzymes lower activation energy and are reused.
sections.text:
Metabolism includes anabolic synthesis and catabolic breakdown. Dehydration reactions build many macromolecules, while hydrolysis breaks many biological linkages. A reaction pathway links products of one step to substrates of the next. Each step needs an appropriate catalyst; an enzyme acting on a sugar does not automatically catalyze fatty acid breakdown.

Enzymes lower activation energy without being consumed or changing a reaction's equilibrium. The active site binds particular substrates; induced fit refines the simple lock-and-key model by allowing conformational adjustment. Names often end in -ase: lipase acts on lipid, sucrase on sucrose, and DNA polymerase synthesizes DNA. Cofactors include metal ions; coenzymes are organic helpers, often derived from vitamins. Not all enzymes require a vitamin, and a whole vitamin is not necessarily identical to its active coenzyme derivative.

Substrate and enzyme concentration, pH, temperature, and inhibitors influence rates. Extreme conditions can denature proteins. In feedback inhibition, a pathway's final product reduces an earlier reaction's activity, conserving resources. Distinguish inhibition of enzyme activity from destruction of the enzyme, and regulation of a pathway from a change in the genetic code.

🖼 Figure — Enzymes (image)
Description: Caption:Enzymes decrease the activation energy required for a given chemical reaction to occur. (a) Without an enzyme, the energy input needed for a reaction to begin is high. (b) With the help of an enzyme, less energy is needed for a reaction to begin. (b) Substrates bind to active sites, producing an enzyme–substrate complex. (c) Changes internal to the enzyme–substrate complex facilitate interaction of the substrates. (d) Products are released and the enzyme returns to its original form, ready to facilitate another enzymatic reaction. sections.title: ATP, phosphorylation, and redox
focus: Oxidation loses electrons; reduction gains electrons.
Contrast substrate-level and oxidative phosphorylation.
sections.text:
ATP contains adenine, ribose, and three phosphate groups. ATP + water → ADP + inorganic phosphate can release free energy overall and drive coupled work. ADP + phosphate → ATP requires energy. Phosphorylation transfers or adds a phosphate group to a molecule. The ATP pool turns over rapidly, linking fuel oxidation to transport, contraction, and synthesis.

Breaking a bond requires energy; the favorable overall hydrolysis reaction reflects the properties and interactions of all reactants and products. Avoid describing the act of bond breaking alone as an energy source. Substrate-level phosphorylation transfers phosphate directly to ADP. Oxidative phosphorylation links electron transfer and a proton gradient to ATP synthase.

Oxidation loses electrons; reduction gains electrons. NAD+ and FAD accept electrons during fuel processing, becoming NADH and FADH2. They later donate electrons, regenerating oxidized carriers. In aerobic respiration glucose is oxidized and oxygen reduced to water. Unlike uncontrolled combustion, cellular oxidation occurs through enzyme-controlled steps that permit energy capture. An enzyme changes rate, whereas an electron carrier transfers reducing equivalents; these are distinct roles.

sections.title: Glycolysis and lactate formation
focus: One glucose yields two pyruvate, two net ATP, and two NADH in glycolysis.
Lactate formation regenerates NAD+ without adding extra ATP.
sections.text:
Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol and converts one six-carbon glucose into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules. It invests two ATP and generates four, giving a net yield of two ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation. It also yields two NADH. Oxygen is not directly required by glycolysis, but oxidized NAD+ must remain available.

When oxidative metabolism cannot reoxidize NADH quickly enough, lactate dehydrogenase transfers electrons from NADH to pyruvate, producing lactate and regenerating NAD+. This regeneration permits glycolysis to continue. Lactate formation itself produces no additional ATP beyond glycolysis. Red blood cells rely on glycolysis because they lack mitochondria; working muscle can increase lactate production even when some oxygen remains available.

Lactate is a usable metabolic intermediate rather than simply a toxic waste. It can be oxidized elsewhere or contribute to glucose production. Delayed muscle soreness after unfamiliar exercise is not explained by lactate persisting for days. Yeast can regenerate NAD+ through ethanol fermentation; this is not the normal human pathway. Distinguish lack of direct oxygen use from complete independence of all other metabolic conditions.

sections.title: Pyruvate oxidation, Krebs cycle, and electron transport
focus: Locate each stage and account for carbon, electron carriers, and ATP.
Oxygen is the final acceptor; the proton gradient powers ATP synthase.
sections.text:
Pyruvate enters mitochondria and is converted to two-carbon acetyl-CoA. Per glucose, this conversion releases two CO2 and produces two NADH. The citric acid or Krebs cycle occurs in the matrix: each acetyl group joins oxaloacetate, which is regenerated. Per glucose, the cycle yields four CO2, six NADH, two FADH2, and two ATP/GTP equivalents.

The electron transport chain is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Electrons from reduced carriers move through protein complexes, and released energy pumps protons into the intermembrane space. Protons return to the matrix through ATP synthase, driving ATP synthesis. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and water forms. If electron transfer stops, carriers remain reduced and oxidative ATP production falls; the cycle depends indirectly on oxygen to regenerate oxidized carriers.

| Stage | Location | Key output per glucose |
|---|---|---|
| Glycolysis | Cytosol | 2 net ATP, 2 NADH, 2 pyruvate |
| Pyruvate oxidation | Mitochondrial matrix | 2 NADH, 2 CO2, 2 acetyl-CoA |
| Krebs cycle | Matrix | 2 ATP/GTP, 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, 4 CO2 |
| Oxidative phosphorylation | Inner membrane | Most aerobic ATP and water |

Modern estimates often total about 30–32 ATP per glucose, varying with shuttles and coupling. Older course accounting uses 36–38 and older carrier yields. Keep the accounting convention explicit; do not mix estimates or make a disputed total the answer to an unqualified practice question.

Further explanation: Molecular Biology of the Cell: mitochondrial energy conversion.

sections.title: Fuel storage and metabolic integration
focus: Compare glycogen storage with triglyceride reserve fuel.
Fatty acids and amino acid carbon skeletons enter shared energy pathways.
sections.text:
Glucose can be oxidized immediately or stored as glycogen, particularly in liver and skeletal muscle. With sustained surplus energy, carbon can also contribute to fat synthesis. Fats provide the largest concentrated reserve fuel. Lipolysis releases glycerol and fatty acids; beta-oxidation converts fatty acids into acetyl-CoA while producing electron carriers. Glycerol can enter carbohydrate pathways.

Proteins have structural and functional priorities but can contribute energy. Removing amino groups permits carbon skeletons to enter metabolic pathways; nitrogen must be handled and excreted. Humans cannot synthesize every amino acid, so converting excess carbohydrate into amino acids does not eliminate the need for dietary essential amino acids.

Pathways share intermediates, yet each step remains enzyme-specific. When energy demand rises, cells draw on available fuels and regulate flux. Oxygen availability, tissue type, hormonal signals, and nutrition influence which fuels are used. The ATP yield from a fatty acid depends on chain length and accounting assumptions; learn the pathway relationships rather than transferring one historical value to every lipid. Anabolism and catabolism occur together across the body, connected by energy transfer and common intermediates.

sections.title: DNA structure, genes, and replication
focus: Replication makes DNA from DNA and preserves one old strand per daughter helix.
Separate replication from transcription and mutation from an inevitable disease outcome.
sections.text:
A gene is a DNA region whose expression contributes to a functional RNA or protein product. Human protein-coding gene estimates are roughly twenty thousand, while gene counts depend on definitions and annotation. DNA's sugar-phosphate backbone is covalently bonded; complementary bases pair A–T and C–G between antiparallel strands.

DNA replication occurs during S phase before mitosis. Helicase separates strands; primase supplies primers; DNA polymerases extend new DNA in the 5′ to 3′ direction using complementary templates. The leading strand is synthesized continuously relative to fork movement, while the lagging strand uses fragments joined by ligase. Each daughter double helix retains one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand: semiconservative replication.

Replication copies a genome for cell division; transcription copies selected information into RNA. They differ in product, enzymes, and purpose. Polymerase proofreading and repair reduce copying errors, but some mutations persist. A mutation is a change in DNA sequence. Depending on location and sequence, it can have no detectable effect, alter a protein, change expression, or contribute to disease. Not every mutation changes one amino acid or causes cancer.

sections.title: Transcription, translation, and the genetic code
focus: Transcription makes RNA; translation builds a polypeptide.
Read mRNA codons in the correct direction and distinguish template from coding DNA.
sections.text:
During transcription, RNA polymerase uses a DNA template to synthesize RNA. In a typical nucleated human cell this occurs in the nucleus. Messenger RNA processing includes a cap, poly-A tail, and removal of introns by splicing. Mature mRNA passes through nuclear pores to the cytoplasm. RNA uses uracil in place of thymine.

Translation occurs at ribosomes. A codon is a three-base mRNA unit; a transfer RNA anticodon pairs with it and delivers an amino acid. Ribosomal RNA contributes both structure and catalytic function. Translation generally begins at AUG, establishes a reading frame, elongates through peptide bond formation, and ends at a stop codon. Stop codons do not normally code for an additional amino acid.

For a template DNA sequence written 3′-TAC GGA ATT-5′, the mRNA is 5′-AUG CCU UAA-3′: methionine, proline, stop. Always identify whether a supplied DNA sequence is template or coding and its direction before using a code chart. Protein synthesis is essential because enzymes, receptors, transporters, and structural proteins determine cellular capabilities. DNA remains a template; it does not travel to each ribosome to become protein.

chapters.title: Tissues
chapters.intro: Recognize how cell arrangement and extracellular matrix predict tissue function and location.

sections.title: Four tissue classes and epithelial organization
focus: Relate epithelial polarity, basement membrane, avascularity, and regeneration.
Classify stratified tissue by the shape of its apical cells.
sections.text:
Epithelial tissue covers surfaces, lines spaces, and forms glands. Connective tissue supports, binds, protects, stores, and transports through diverse extracellular matrices. Muscle generates force by contraction. Nervous tissue processes and transmits information. Ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm contribute different tissue lineages; epithelium can arise from all three, while most connective/muscle tissue derives from mesoderm and nervous tissue from ectoderm.

Epithelia contain closely packed cells with little extracellular matrix. An apical surface faces a lumen or exterior; the basal surface attaches to a basement membrane above connective tissue. Epithelia are avascular: nutrients diffuse from underlying vascular connective tissue. Many epithelial populations regenerate rapidly. Tight junctions limit leakage, desmosomes resist separation, and gap junctions allow communication.

Classify by layers and the shape of cells at the free surface. Simple means one layer; stratified means multiple layers. Squamous cells are flattened, cuboidal approximately as tall as wide, and columnar taller than wide. A stratified squamous tissue can have rounded basal cells because classification uses its surface cells. Microvilli increase absorptive area; cilia move surface material.

Classify by layers and the shape of cells at the free surface. Simple means one layer; stratified means multiple layers. Squamous cells are flattened, cuboidal approximately as tall as wide, and columnar taller than wide. A stratified squamous tissue can have rounded basal cells because classification uses its surface cells. Microvilli increase absorptive area; cilia move surface material.

sections.title: Simple and pseudostratified epithelia
focus: Link thin squamous layers to exchange and cuboidal/columnar layers to secretion or absorption.
Pseudostratified means every cell contacts the basement membrane.
sections.text:
| Tissue | Recognition | Representative location | Function |
|---|---|---|---|
| Simple squamous | One thin flattened layer | Alveoli, vessel endothelium, serous mesothelium | Diffusion, filtration, low-friction lining |
| Simple cuboidal | One layer with rounded central nuclei | Kidney tubules, thyroid follicles, small gland ducts | Absorption and secretion |
| Simple columnar | Tall cells, often basal nuclei | Intestine; ciliated type in uterine tubes | Absorption, secretion, or movement |
| Pseudostratified columnar | Uneven nuclei; all cells reach basement membrane | Ciliated respiratory lining in trachea | Mucus secretion and clearance |

Goblet cells secrete mucus, while cilia move mucus and trapped particles. Pseudostratified tissue looks multilayered because nuclei sit at different heights, but it remains a single layer; not every cell reaches the lumen. Do not confuse cilia with microvilli. A thin exchange barrier favors diffusion, whereas multiple layers provide abrasion resistance. Endothelium is the specialized simple squamous lining of blood and lymphatic vessels; mesothelium covers serous surfaces.

sections.title: Stratified and transitional epithelia
focus: Keratinized stratified squamous forms epidermis; nonkeratinized protects moist surfaces.
Transitional epithelium stretches while maintaining a urinary barrier.
sections.text:
Stratified squamous epithelium resists abrasion. Its keratinized form constitutes the epidermis, with dead superficial cells rich in keratin. Nonkeratinized forms line moist surfaces such as the mouth, esophagus, and vagina; surface cells retain nuclei. Basal cells replenish cells lost from the surface.

Stratified cuboidal epithelium occurs in portions of sweat gland and other larger ducts. Stratified columnar tissue is less common and appears in selected large ducts and portions of the male urethra. Tissue names describe layers and apical cell shape rather than indicating that all cells have identical shape.

Transitional epithelium, or urothelium, lines urinary structures such as the bladder and ureters. Its surface cells appear rounded or dome-shaped when relaxed and flatten as the wall stretches. Multiple layers maintain a protective barrier while allowing distension. Stretching changes shape without converting it into simple squamous epithelium. Compare a distensible bladder lining with an intestinal absorptive surface: different mechanical demands explain different epithelial arrangements.

sections.title: Glands, secretion, and epithelial cancer
focus: Exocrine uses ducts; endocrine releases hormones without ducts.
Holocrine loses the entire secretory cell.
sections.text:
Exocrine glands deliver products through ducts onto surfaces or into lumens. Endocrine glands lack ducts and release hormones into interstitial fluid for circulation. A goblet cell is a unicellular exocrine gland. Multicellular glands can be simple or compound according to duct branching and tubular or acinar/alveolar according to secretory unit shape.

Merocrine secretion releases products by exocytosis without losing a major part of the cell. Apocrine secretion releases apical cytoplasm with product in the classical mechanism. Holocrine secretion releases the contents of disintegrating whole cells, as in sebaceous glands. Gland names and secretion mechanisms are not always identical: human apocrine sweat glands largely release products through exocytosis despite their historical name. Mammary secretion includes different mechanisms for lipid and protein components.

Serous secretions are relatively watery and often enzyme-rich; mucous secretions contain mucins and become viscous mucus. Carcinoma is a malignant tumor arising from epithelial cells; the term does not mean every epithelial growth is malignant. Distinguish the gland's destination, duct structure, product, and release mechanism as separate classification dimensions.

sections.title: Connective tissue cells, fibers, and matrix
focus: Matrix equals ground substance plus fibers; cell types contribute different functions.
Collagen resists tension, elastic fibers recoil, reticular fibers form a network.
sections.text:
Connective tissues generally contain cells dispersed within extracellular matrix, unlike the tightly packed cells of epithelia. Matrix consists of ground substance plus fibers; its composition explains why blood is fluid, cartilage firm and flexible, and bone rigid. Most connective tissues develop from mesenchyme, an embryonic tissue with relatively unspecialized cells.

Fibroblasts produce ground substance and fibers. Macrophages phagocytose debris and microbes. Mast cells release mediators including histamine that contribute to inflammation. Adipocytes store lipid; plasma cells produce antibodies; other migrating leukocytes participate in defense. A blast cell typically produces matrix; a mature -cyte maintains it, as in osteoblast/osteocyte and chondroblast/chondrocyte.

Collagen fibers resist tension. Elastic fibers stretch and recoil. Reticular fibers form fine supportive networks. Ground substance permits diffusion and varies from fluid to mineralized material. Vascularity differs: cartilage is avascular, tendons have relatively limited perfusion, and bone is richly vascular. Extracellular fluid includes interstitial fluid, plasma, lymph, and specialized transcellular fluids such as cerebrospinal and synovial fluids. Do not assume every connective tissue has equal healing speed.

sections.title: Loose, dense, and specialized connective tissues
focus: Predict function from fiber arrangement and matrix composition.
Distinguish all three cartilages, compact bone, and blood.
sections.text:
| Type | Key structure | Location and function |
|---|---|---|
| Areolar | Loose fibers, varied cells, hydrated ground substance | Under epithelia; packing and diffusion |
| Adipose | Lipid-filled adipocytes | Hypodermis and around organs; fuel, insulation, cushioning |
| Reticular | Fine branching network | Lymph nodes, spleen, marrow; supportive framework |
| Dense regular | Parallel collagen bundles | Tendons and many ligaments; tension mainly along one axis |
| Dense irregular | Interwoven collagen | Dermis and capsules; stress in several directions |
| Elastic | Abundant elastic fibers | Large arteries and selected ligaments; recoil |
| Hyaline cartilage | Smooth-looking matrix, chondrocytes in lacunae | Articular surfaces, trachea, nose; support/cushioning |
| Elastic cartilage | Elastic fiber-rich cartilage | External ear, epiglottis; flexible support |
| Fibrocartilage | Thick collagen bundles | Intervertebral discs and pubic symphysis; resists compression/tension |
| Bone | Mineralized collagen matrix, osteocytes | Skeleton; support, protection, mineral storage |
| Blood | Cells/fragments in plasma | Transport, defense, hemostasis |

Cartilage heals slowly in part because it lacks blood vessels. Compact bone forms osteons around central canals containing vessels and nerves. Erythrocytes transport gases, leukocytes provide defense, and platelets help stop bleeding. Blood's liquid matrix still makes it a connective tissue. Tendons attach muscle to bone; ligaments generally connect bone to bone.

sections.title: Tissue membranes, muscle, and nervous tissue
focus: Synovial membranes are connective tissue membranes without true epithelium.
Compare skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle by structure, location, and control.
sections.text:
Cutaneous membrane is skin: keratinized epithelium over connective tissue. Mucous membranes line passages opening to the exterior, such as digestive and respiratory tracts, with epithelium supported by lamina propria. Serous membranes line closed ventral body cavities and cover organs with mesothelium over thin connective tissue. Synovial membranes line movable joint capsules and are connective-tissue membranes, lacking a true epithelial layer.

Skeletal muscle has long, cylindrical, striated, multinucleated fibers and normally supports voluntary movement. Cardiac muscle is striated, branched, usually centrally nucleated, involuntary, and joined by intercalated discs; it occurs in the heart. Smooth muscle has spindle-shaped, nonstriated cells with one central nucleus and occurs in walls of hollow organs and vessels. Contractility is the capacity to develop force and shorten under appropriate conditions, although tension can also occur without overall shortening.

Nervous tissue includes neurons and supporting glia in brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves. Neurons receive and transmit signals; glia support, protect, and regulate their environment. Repair depends on the tissue, damage, blood supply, and available progenitor cells; scar connective tissue can replace lost structure without fully restoring original function. Astrocytes support the brain vascular environment; specialized capillary endothelial tight junctions form a principal restrictive seal of the blood-brain barrier.

sections.title: Skin layers and their cell types
focus: Order epidermal strata from basale to corneum; lucidum is specific to thick skin.
Distinguish epidermis, dermis, and hypodermis.
sections.text:
Skin consists of epidermis and dermis; hypodermis lies beneath and is not usually counted as skin proper. Epidermis is avascular keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Dermis is vascular connective tissue supporting the epidermis, sensory structures, follicles, glands, and vessels. Hypodermis contains areolar/adipose tissue that anchors, cushions, stores fuel, and insulates.

From deep to superficial, epidermal strata are basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum in thick skin only, and corneum. Basal division replenishes keratinocytes that move outward, differentiate, accumulate keratin and barrier lipids, lose organelles, and eventually shed. Palms and soles have thick skin and a distinct lucidum, but lack hair follicles. Most other locations have thin skin without a distinct lucidum.

Keratinocytes build the barrier. Melanocytes produce melanin and transfer it to neighboring cells. Epidermal dendritic/Langerhans cells participate in immune surveillance. Tactile/Merkel cells associate with sensory endings. Differences in pigmentation involve melanin production, type, distribution, and persistence rather than a simple difference in melanocyte counts. The epidermal barrier reduces water loss but is not an absolutely impermeable wall.

🖼 Figure — Structure of the skin (image)
Description: The skin is composed of two main layers: the epidermis, made of closely packed epithelial cells, and the dermis, made of dense, irregular connective tissue that houses blood vessels, hair follicles, sweat glands, and other structures. Beneath the dermis lies the hypodermis, which is composed mainly of loose connective and fatty tissues.

🖼 Figure — Epidermal strata in a micrograph (image)
Description: The micrograph labels the superficial stratum corneum and deeper epidermal strata down to stratum basale. Underlying tissue includes a labeled capillary and a remnant of hair follicle. This image illustrates layer arrangement rather than identifying every epidermal cell type individually.

sections.title: Dermal structure, sensation, and skin functions
focus: Papillary dermis is areolar; reticular dermis is dense irregular connective tissue.
Compare superficial tactile receptors with deeper lamellated corpuscles.
sections.text:
Papillary dermis is a superficial areolar layer with dermal papillae, capillary loops, and tactile receptors. Reticular dermis contains interwoven collagen and elastic fibers providing tensile strength and recoil. The hypodermis adds insulation and mobility over deeper structures. Dermal vessels nourish epidermis by diffusion because the epidermis itself lacks vessels.

Tactile/Meissner corpuscles in dermal papillae detect light touch and low-frequency vibration in glabrous skin. Lamellated/Pacinian corpuscles lie deeper in dermis or subcutis and detect vibration and changing deep pressure. Free nerve endings contribute pain and temperature sensation. The onion-like lamellae of a Pacinian corpuscle distinguish it from a superficial tactile corpuscle.

Skin functions include physical/chemical protection, water conservation, immune surveillance, sensation, temperature regulation, a vascular reservoir, and vitamin D precursor synthesis initiated by ultraviolet exposure. Sweat excretion is minor compared with renal waste excretion. Skin immune cells release signals that coordinate defense; skin does not replace bone marrow as the principal blood-cell production site. Barrier disruption can impair fluid balance and infection resistance even when underlying muscle remains intact.

sections.title: Hair, nails, and sebaceous glands
focus: Hair/nails arise from epidermal cells despite follicle structures extending into dermis.
Arrector pili is smooth muscle; sebaceous secretion is holocrine.
sections.text:
Hair and nails are keratinized epidermal derivatives. In hair follicles, dividing matrix cells in the bulb produce the hair; the dermal papilla provides vascular support. The root lies below the surface, while the shaft extends beyond it. The follicle surrounds the root. Pigment contributes hair color; the exposed shaft consists largely of dead keratinized cells.

Arrector pili are smooth muscle bundles associated with hair follicles. Their contraction raises hairs and creates goosebumps during cold or emotional responses. They are not skeletal muscle, and piloerection contributes little insulation in sparsely haired humans. Nails grow from the nail matrix; the nail plate protects digit ends and assists manipulation. The lunula is a visible pale region near the proximal nail, not the only location of all nail growth.

Sebaceous glands usually empty sebum into follicles and use holocrine secretion: whole cells contribute to the product. Sebum lubricates skin and hair. Some sebaceous glands open directly onto the surface, so association with follicles is common rather than universal. Acne involves follicular plugging, sebum, microbial interactions, and inflammation; it is not simply dirt trapped on otherwise normal skin.

sections.title: Eccrine, apocrine, and modified glands
focus: Eccrine glands open to surface and support evaporative cooling.
Apocrine sweat commonly drains into follicles; bacterial metabolism contributes odor.
sections.text:
Eccrine sweat glands are coiled tubular glands whose ducts open onto the skin surface. They release a watery secretion containing salts and small quantities of wastes by merocrine exocytosis. They are widely distributed and important for temperature regulation, especially during heat exposure and activity. Cooling occurs when sweat evaporates, not merely when liquid appears on skin.

Apocrine sweat glands are concentrated in regions such as axillae and groin, commonly drain into follicles, and become more active around puberty. Their secretion contains additional organic components; bacterial metabolism produces much associated odor. The secretion itself is initially relatively odorless. Emotional influences are important. The historical name apocrine does not establish the exact mechanism of every released component in human sweat glands.

Ceruminous glands of the external auditory canal contribute to earwax, and mammary glands produce milk; both are modified cutaneous glands. Contrast sweat with sebum: sebaceous glands release oily material through whole-cell breakdown, whereas eccrine glands release watery sweat without sacrificing whole cells. Predict whether a gland contributes primarily to evaporative cooling, lubrication, or specialized secretion from its structure and outlet.

sections.title: Heat production, transfer, and feedback
focus: Separate hypothalamic control from skin vessel and sweat responses.
Evaporation depends on environmental conditions, including humidity.
sections.text:
Body heat largely comes from metabolism, including active muscle. The hypothalamus integrates temperature signals and coordinates responses. Skin vessels change heat transfer rather than serving as the primary control center. Vasodilation increases cutaneous blood flow and often heat loss when the environment is cooler; vasoconstriction limits this transfer. Shivering increases skeletal muscle heat production.

Radiation transfers infrared energy without direct contact. Conduction transfers heat through contact. Convection carries heat in moving air or water. Evaporation removes heat as liquid becomes vapor. Humidity reduces evaporative effectiveness, and air hotter than skin may add heat by convection. Sweating therefore does not guarantee cooling in every environment.

Hyperthermia reflects heat gain/production exceeding dissipation without a regulated febrile set-point increase. Fever involves altered thermoregulatory signaling and is a different process. Hypothermia reflects abnormally low core temperature. Explain a temperature problem through heat balance, vascular responses, evaporation, and behavior rather than assuming that a single visible sign determines the cause. These principles are for course learning, not a substitute for clinical assessment or treatment protocols.

sections.title: Pigmentation, defense, and skin disorders
focus: Distinguish melanin, carotene, hemoglobin, and bilirubin contributions.
Link pressure/shear to tissue ischemia and UV exposure to DNA damage risk.
sections.text:
Melanin contributes pigmentation and absorbs some ultraviolet radiation; it does not eliminate UV damage. Genetics, ultraviolet exposure, hormones, and selected drugs affect pigmentation. Carotene can contribute a yellow-orange tone. Dermal hemoglobin and perfusion affect redness and pallor. Cyanosis relates to altered oxygenation and hemoglobin state; jaundice reflects bilirubin accumulation. Skin appearance varies with baseline pigmentation and lighting, so color alone is an incomplete assessment.

Pressure injury develops when sustained pressure and shear impair tissue perfusion, often over bony prominences. Inflammation involves vascular and immune signaling and may cause warmth, redness, swelling, and pain; it is not identical to infection. Ultraviolet radiation contributes to many cutaneous cancers. Basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma arise from different cell populations; melanoma can spread aggressively.

Skin aging may reduce elasticity, alter barrier repair, and change glandular function. Vitiligo involves loss of pigment-producing cells in affected areas; albinism involves inherited deficits in melanin production. Avoid conflating pigment changes with vascular changes: increased melanin is not simply increased blood flow, and reduced perfusion is not reduced pigment synthesis.
