sections.title: Wound healing and burns
focus: Compare superficial, partial-thickness, and full-thickness depth and regenerative capacity.
Rule of nines estimates adult surface area, not burn depth.
sections.text:
A superficial epidermal injury may heal through basal epithelial proliferation without substantial scarring. A deeper injury can involve hemostasis, inflammation, migration and proliferation of repair cells, new extracellular matrix, re-epithelialization, and remodeling. Fibroblasts produce collagen; new vessels support repair. Scabs and clot provide temporary protection, while scar tissue may differ from original tissue in strength and function.

Superficial burns, traditionally first degree, affect epidermis. Partial-thickness burns, traditionally second degree, extend into dermis with variable depth and often blistering; surviving epithelial appendages can contribute regeneration. Full-thickness burns, traditionally third degree, destroy the full skin thickness and many regenerative structures; extensive wounds cannot simply regenerate normal skin from their center. Severe burns disrupt fluid balance, protection, and temperature regulation.

The adult rule of nines estimates surface area: each arm 9%, each leg 18%, anterior trunk 18%, posterior trunk 18%, head/neck 9%, and perineum 1%. Children have different proportions and require age-appropriate methods. This surface estimate does not measure depth or replace a clinical severity assessment. Healing depends on injury depth, extent, blood supply, infection, nutrition, and other factors.

chapters.title: The Skeletal System
chapters.intro: Bone structure, bone cells, how bones form and grow, what controls bone remodeling and blood calcium, fractures, the axial and appendicular skeleton, and how bones change with age.

sections.title: The Skeletal System at a Glance
focus: The adult skeleton has 206 bones divided into axial and appendicular portions.
The girdles (pectoral and pelvic) belong to the appendicular skeleton.
sections.text:
The skeletal system is made of bones plus the structures that connect them: ligaments, tendons, and cartilages. The adult skeleton has 206 bones, organized into two divisions:

- The axial skeleton: skull, hyoid bone, vertebral column, and thoracic cage (the body's central axis).
- The appendicular skeleton: the upper and lower limbs plus the pectoral (shoulder) girdle and pelvic (hip) girdle that attach the limbs to the trunk.

Bones are living organs. They contain bone tissue, cartilage, dense connective tissue, blood, nerves, and bone marrow.
sections.markdown:
The skeletal system is made of **bones** plus the structures that connect them: ligaments, tendons, and cartilages. The adult skeleton has **206 bones**, organized into two divisions:

- The **axial skeleton**: skull, hyoid bone, vertebral column, and thoracic cage (the body's central axis).
- The **appendicular skeleton**: the upper and lower limbs plus the **pectoral (shoulder) girdle** and **pelvic (hip) girdle** that attach the limbs to the trunk.

Bones are living organs. They contain bone tissue, cartilage, dense connective tissue, blood, nerves, and bone marrow.

check.question: A student lists the bones of the axial skeleton. Which item does NOT belong on the list?
check.explanation: The scapula is part of the pectoral girdle, which belongs to the appendicular skeleton. The hyoid, sternum (thoracic cage), and sacrum (vertebral column) are all axial.

sections.title: Classification of Bones by Shape
focus: The femur is a long bone; carpals and tarsals (wrists and ankles) are short bones.
The patella is a sesamoid bone (some anatomists call it this because it forms inside the quadriceps tendon).
Vertebrae are irregular bones; skull bones, ribs, sternum, and scapulae are flat bones.
sections.text:
Bones are classified by shape:

| Shape | Description | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Long | A shaft (longer than it is wide) with two expanded ends | Femur (thigh), humerus (arm), radius, ulna, phalanges |
| Short | Cube-like; about as long as they are wide | Carpals (wrist), tarsals (ankle) |
| Flat | Thin, platelike, usually curved | Most skull bones (frontal, parietal), sternum, scapulae, ribs |
| Irregular | Complex shapes that are not long, short, or flat | Vertebrae, auditory ossicles, some facial bones |
| Sesamoid | Small, round bones that develop within a tendon | Patella (kneecap) |
| Sutural (Wormian) | Tiny extra bones in the sutures between skull bones | Found in some skulls along the lambdoid suture |

Study tip (tip)

"Long" refers to shape, not size. The tiny bones of the fingers (phalanges) are long bones because each has a shaft and two ends.

check.question: A small, rounded bone is found embedded inside the tendon of a muscle at the base of the big toe. How would you classify it?
check.explanation: Bones that develop inside a tendon are sesamoid bones. The patella is the classic example; small sesamoid bones are also common near the big toe and thumb.

sections.title: Parts of a Long Bone
focus: The diaphysis is made mostly of compact bone.
The epiphyses are made mainly of spongy bone.
The ends of long bones (articular surfaces) are covered by hyaline cartilage.
The epiphyseal disk (plate) on an X-ray tells you a child's bone is still growing.
sections.text:
🖼 Figure — Figure 7.A. Major parts of a long bone (femur), shown in longitudinal section. (image)
Description: The drawing shows a long bone cut lengthwise. Each end is an expanded epiphysis made mostly of spongy bone, capped with articular cartilage where it forms a joint. The long shaft between the ends is the diaphysis: a thick collar of compact bone around a hollow medullary cavity that holds yellow marrow. A thin epiphyseal line (the remnant of the growth plate) separates each epiphysis from the diaphysis. The periosteum covers the outside of the bone except the articular cartilage, and the endosteum lines the medullary cavity. A nutrient foramen lets blood vessels enter the shaft.

| Part | Description | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Diaphysis | The shaft. A thick collar of compact bone around the medullary cavity | Rigidity and strength |
| Epiphysis (pl. epiphyses) | The expanded ends: mostly spongy bone with a thin outer layer of compact bone; proximal and distal | Hold red marrow (blood cell formation); form joints |
| Articular cartilage | A pad of hyaline cartilage on the epiphysis where the bone joins another bone | Shock absorber; reduces friction in the joint |
| Epiphyseal plate / line | Plate (disk) of hyaline cartilage between epiphysis and diaphysis in a growing bone; becomes the epiphyseal line when growth stops | Site of lengthwise growth |
| Periosteum | Tough, fibrous outer covering (except over articular cartilage); richly supplied with blood vessels, lymph vessels, and nerves; inner osteogenic layer has osteoblasts and osteoclasts | Protection, nourishment, bone formation and repair; attachment for tendons and ligaments |
| Endosteum | Thin inner lining of the medullary cavity with osteoblasts and osteoclasts | Bone remodeling |
| Medullary cavity | Hollow center of the diaphysis, filled with yellow marrow in adults | Fat (energy) storage; makes bone lighter |
| Nutrient foramen | Perforating canal through the compact bone | Lets blood vessels enter and leave the bone |

check.question: A surgeon drills into the middle of a femur shaft and reaches a cavity filled with fatty tissue. Which structures did the drill pass through, in order?
options: Articular cartilage, spongy bone, red marrow
Spongy bone, compact bone, articular cartilage
check.explanation: The shaft (diaphysis) is covered by periosteum, made of a thick collar of compact bone, and surrounds the medullary cavity, which holds fatty yellow marrow.

sections.title: Bone Marrow and Hematopoiesis
focus: Yellow marrow stores fat.
Red marrow forms red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets (hematopoiesis).
In adults, red marrow is found primarily in spongy bone.
sections.text:
Bone marrow is the soft tissue inside the medullary cavities of long bones and the spaces of spongy bone.

| Characteristic | Red bone marrow | Yellow bone marrow |
|---|---|---|
| What it does | Hematopoiesis: forms red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets | Stores fat (an energy reserve) |
| Where in adults | Spongy bone of flat bones (skull, ribs, sternum, clavicles, vertebrae, pelvis) and the proximal epiphyses of the femur and humerus | Medullary cavity of the long bones' shafts |
| Where in infants | Nearly all bones | Little |

As a person ages, much of the red marrow is replaced by yellow marrow. In a flat bone, the arrangement looks like a sandwich: a layer of spongy bone with red marrow (the meat) between two layers of compact bone (the bread).

Clinical connection (clinical)

In an emergency or for a marrow biopsy, red marrow is often sampled from the sternum or the iliac crest of the hip bone because these flat bones keep active red marrow throughout life.

check.question: A patient's bone marrow stops producing platelets and white blood cells. Which tissue is failing?
options: Red bone marrow in spongy bone
Yellow bone marrow in the medullary cavity
check.answer: Red bone marrow in spongy bone
check.explanation: All blood cells, including platelets and white blood cells, are formed by red marrow (hematopoiesis). In adults, red marrow lives in the spongy bone of flat bones and some epiphyses.

sections.title: Bone Matrix and Bone Cells
focus: Osteoclasts break down (resorb) bone tissue.
Osteocytes live inside lacunae.
Most of the bone matrix is made of hydroxyapatite crystals (calcium phosphate).
sections.text:
Bone tissue is a connective tissue: cells surrounded by an extracellular matrix.

Matrix composition - Organic part (about 35%): mostly collagen fibers (called osteoid when newly laid down). Collagen gives bone flexibility and tensile strength so it does not shatter. - Inorganic part (about 65%): mineral salts, mainly calcium phosphate in the form of hydroxyapatite crystals. Hydroxyapatite gives bone its hardness.

Bone cells

| Cell | Where it comes from | Function | Memory trick |
|---|---|---|---|
| Osteoprogenitor cell | Stem cell from mesenchyme | Divides (mitosis) and becomes osteoblasts | "Pro-" = before |
| Osteoblast | From osteoprogenitor cells | Builds bone: secretes collagen and matrix; cannot divide | Blast = Build |
| Osteocyte | A mature osteoblast that became trapped in matrix | Maintains bone; lives inside a lacuna; exchanges nutrients and wastes with blood | Cyte = Caretaker |
| Osteoclast | Large, multinucleated cell (from white blood cell line) | Breaks down (resorbs) bone matrix, releasing calcium and phosphate into the blood | Clast = Cut / Crush |

Osteoclasts secrete acids that dissolve the calcium salts and lysosomal enzymes that digest the collagen.

Description: Study the labeled structures in Bone cells. The accompanying section explains their relationships: Osteoclasts break down (resorb) bone tissue. Osteocytes live inside lacunae. Most of the bone matrix is made of hydroxyapatite crystals (calcium phosphate).
sections.markdown:
Bone tissue is a connective tissue: cells surrounded by an extracellular **matrix**.

**Matrix composition** - **Organic part (about 35%)**: mostly **collagen** fibers (called osteoid when newly laid down). Collagen gives bone **flexibility and tensile strength** so it does not shatter. - **Inorganic part (about 65%)**: mineral salts, mainly calcium phosphate in the form of **hydroxyapatite** crystals. Hydroxyapatite gives bone its **hardness**.

**Bone cells**

| Cell | Where it comes from | Function | Memory trick |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Osteoprogenitor cell** | Stem cell from mesenchyme | Divides (mitosis) and becomes osteoblasts | "Pro-" = before |
| **Osteoblast** | From osteoprogenitor cells | **Builds** bone: secretes collagen and matrix; cannot divide | **B**last = **B**uild |
| **Osteocyte** | A mature osteoblast that became trapped in matrix | Maintains bone; **lives inside a lacuna**; exchanges nutrients and wastes with blood | **C**yte = **C**aretaker |
| **Osteoclast** | Large, multinucleated cell (from white blood cell line) | **Breaks down (resorbs)** bone matrix, releasing calcium and phosphate into the blood | **C**last = **C**ut / **C**rush |

Osteoclasts secrete **acids** that dissolve the calcium salts and **lysosomal enzymes** that digest the collagen.

check.question: A drug blocks the cells that dissolve bone matrix. Which cells are blocked, and what happens to bone density?
options: Osteoclasts; bone density increases or is preserved
check.answer: Osteoclasts; bone density increases or is preserved
check.explanation: Osteoclasts resorb bone. Blocking them shifts the balance toward bone building by osteoblasts, which is how many osteoporosis drugs work.

sections.title: Compact and Spongy Bone
focus: Spongy bone = cancellous bone.
Compact bone forms most of the diaphysis and is built of osteons (concentric circles).
The epiphyses are composed mainly of spongy bone.
sections.text:
🖼 Figure — Figure 7.B. Microscopic structure of compact bone: an osteon (Haversian system). (image)
Description: The illustration enlarges a block of compact bone from the shaft of a long bone. Circular osteons contain concentric lamellae around central canals carrying blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, and nerves. A perforating canal crosses between the central canals and connects them with vessels beneath the periosteum. Circumferential lamellae follow the outer surface, while interstitial lamellae fill spaces between osteons. The right side shows the transition to trabeculae of spongy bone and the medullary cavity. Osteocytes, lacunae, and canaliculi are discussed in the accompanying text but are not individually labeled in this illustration.

| Feature | Compact bone | Spongy bone (also called cancellous bone) |
|---|---|---|
| Appearance | Solid, dense, smooth | Lattice of thin bony plates with open spaces |
| Structural unit | The osteon (Haversian system): concentric circles (lamellae) around a central canal | Trabeculae: needle-like bony plates, no osteons |
| Where | Wall of the diaphysis; thin outer layer over all bones | Epiphyses of long bones; inside flat, short, and irregular bones |
| Nourishment | Blood vessels in central and perforating canals; osteocytes connected by canaliculi | Diffusion from nearby canals and marrow |
| Advantage | Strength and support | Light weight; holds red marrow; trabeculae line up along lines of stress |

Parts of an osteon - Central (Haversian) canal: contains blood vessels and nerves. - Lamellae: concentric layers of matrix. - Lacunae: small chambers holding osteocytes. - Canaliculi: tiny canals that connect lacunae so osteocytes can pass nutrients and wastes. - Perforating (Volkmann's) canals: run at right angles and connect the blood supply of neighboring osteons.

sections.title: How Bones Form: Ossification
focus: The frontal bone (a flat skull bone) forms by intramembranous ossification; the femur, ulna, and radius form by endochondral ossification.
Know the steps of endochondral ossification and recognize the false one (cartilage does not become adipose tissue).
sections.text:
Ossification (osteogenesis) is the formation of bone. It begins at about 6 to 7 weeks of embryonic development. In both patterns, an existing connective tissue is replaced by bone.

1. Intramembranous ossification: bone forms within sheet-like layers of fibrous connective tissue membranes. - Forms the flat bones of the skull (frontal, parietal, occipital, temporal) and the clavicles. - Connective tissue cells become osteoblasts, which deposit spongy bone; the outside becomes compact bone and periosteum.

2. Endochondral ossification: bone forms from a hyaline cartilage model. It forms most bones of the skeleton, including the femur, humerus, radius, ulna, and vertebrae.

Steps of endochondral ossification: 1. Hyaline cartilage develops in the shape of the future bone. 2. The cartilage cells in the center enlarge and the matrix around them calcifies, so the cells die. 3. Periosteum forms from connective tissue on the outside of the developing bone. 4. Blood vessels and osteoblasts invade; the primary ossification center appears in the diaphysis. Osteoblasts deposit bone tissue in place of the disintegrating cartilage. 5. Secondary ossification centers later appear in the epiphyses. 6. Cartilage remains only as articular cartilage and the epiphyseal plates, which allow growth.

Note (note)

Cartilage is replaced by bone, never by adipose (fat) tissue. A statement such as "hyaline cartilage changes to adipose tissue" is not a step of endochondral ossification.

check.question: In a fetus, a bone is developing from a cartilage model, and a collar of periosteum is forming around its middle. Which bone could this be?
check.explanation: A cartilage model means endochondral ossification, which forms most bones, including long bones like the humerus. The flat skull bones form by intramembranous ossification.

sections.title: How Bones Grow in Length and Thickness
focus: All bones are normally ossified by about 25 years of age.
You can tell a child's long bone is growing by looking at the epiphyseal disk on an X-ray.
A bone grows in thickness by deposition of compact bone beneath the periosteum.
sections.text:
Growth in length (longitudinal growth) happens at the epiphyseal plate (epiphyseal disk), a plate of hyaline cartilage between the epiphysis and diaphysis. It has four zones:

1. Zone of resting cartilage: small, scattered chondrocytes anchor the plate to the epiphysis.
2. Zone of proliferating cartilage: chondrocytes divide and stack like coins.
3. Zone of hypertrophic cartilage: large, maturing chondrocytes in columns.
4. Zone of calcified cartilage: a thin layer of dead cells in calcified matrix; osteoclasts break it down and osteoblasts replace it with bone.

New cartilage is made on the epiphyseal side while cartilage is replaced by bone on the diaphyseal side. The plate stays about the same thickness while the bone lengthens.

When growth ends, the plate ossifies and leaves an epiphyseal line. Most epiphyseal plates close between ages 14 and 20, and ossification of all bones is normally complete by about age 25.

Clinical connection (clinical)

On an X-ray of a child, the epiphyseal disk appears as a dark (cartilage) line near the end of the bone. If you can see it, the bone is still growing. In an adult, only a thin epiphyseal line remains.

Growth in thickness (appositional growth) - Osteoblasts beneath the periosteum deposit compact bone on the outer surface. - At the same time, osteoclasts on the endosteal (inner) surface break down bone, enlarging the medullary cavity. - The bone becomes wider without becoming too heavy.

Film 1 shows a fracture; Film 2 is normal

sections.title: Factors That Affect Bone Growth
focus: Vitamin C is required for collagen synthesis.
Excess GH before the epiphyseal plates ossify → pituitary gigantism (after closure → acromegaly).
Excess thyroid hormone can halt bone growth by causing premature ossification of the epiphyseal disks.
Sex hormones stimulate ossification of the epiphyseal disks, with estrogen stronger than androgens.
Increased bone mass from physical stress = bone hypertrophy.
sections.text:
Minerals: calcium and phosphorus (parts of hydroxyapatite); magnesium (osteoblast activity); boron and manganese.

Vitamins

| Vitamin | Role | Deficiency |
|---|---|---|
| Vitamin D | Increases absorption of calcium from the small intestine | Rickets (children), osteomalacia (adults): soft, weak bones |
| Vitamin C | Required for collagen synthesis (maintains bone matrix) | Scurvy: weak, slow-healing bones |
| Vitamin A | Needed for osteoblast and osteoclast activity during development | Retarded bone development |
| Vitamin B12 | May help osteoblast activity |  |

Hormones

| Hormone | Effect on bone |
|---|---|
| Growth hormone (GH) from the pituitary | Stimulates division of cartilage cells in the epiphyseal plates. Too little in childhood causes pituitary dwarfism. Too much before the plates ossify causes pituitary gigantism. Too much in adults (plates already closed) causes acromegaly (bones of hands, feet, and jaw thicken). |
| Thyroid hormones (thyroxine) | Stimulate replacement of cartilage by bone. An excess can halt bone growth by causing premature ossification of the epiphyseal disks. |
| Sex hormones (estrogens and androgens such as testosterone) | Promote osteoblast activity and stimulate ossification of the epiphyseal disks, which ends growth. Estrogen's effect is stronger than androgens', so the plates of females usually close earlier. |
| Parathyroid hormone (PTH) and calcitonin | Control bone remodeling and blood calcium (see Bone Remodeling). |

Physical stress (exercise) - Weight-bearing activity and the pull of muscles stimulate bone growth: the bone becomes thicker and stronger. This increase in bone mass is called bone hypertrophy. - Lack of use causes bone atrophy (bone loss), as in a person on prolonged bed rest or an astronaut in low gravity.

check.question: A 30-year-old notices that his jaw, hands, and feet are slowly getting larger, but he is not getting taller. A tumor is found in his pituitary gland. What explains the pattern?
options: Gigantism, because his epiphyseal plates are still open
Acromegaly, because his epiphyseal plates have already ossified
Rickets, from lack of vitamin D
Dwarfism, from lack of growth hormone
check.answer: Acromegaly, because his epiphyseal plates have already ossified
check.explanation: Excess growth hormone after the epiphyseal plates have closed cannot make bones longer, so bones thicken instead: acromegaly. Before the plates close, the same excess would cause gigantism.

sections.title: Functions of Bones
focus: Production of blood cells, storage of inorganic salts, and protection of organs are all skeletal functions: the answer "all of the above."
sections.text:
1. Support: bones of the legs and pelvis support the trunk; the atlas supports the skull.
2. Protection: the skull protects the brain; the rib cage protects the heart and lungs. Protection is especially important in the head and thorax.
3. Body movement: bones act as levers; skeletal muscles attach to them by tendons.
4. Blood cell formation (hematopoiesis): red marrow produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.
5. Storage of inorganic salts: bone stores calcium and phosphate (and smaller amounts of magnesium, sodium, potassium) and releases them as needed. This is essential for calcium homeostasis.
6. Energy storage: yellow marrow stores fat.

Memory trick (mnemonic)

"SPM-BSE", or think "Some People Move Blood, Salts, and Energy": Support, Protection, Movement, Blood cell formation, Salt storage, Energy storage.

sections.title: Bone Remodeling and Calcium Homeostasis
focus: The thyroid gland releases calcitonin, which causes osteoblasts to deposit calcium in bone.
When the parathyroid glands sense low blood calcium, they release parathyroid hormone.
High blood calcium inhibits osteoclast activity (through calcitonin).
sections.text:
Bone is continuously remodeled throughout life. Osteoclasts remove bone (resorption) and osteoblasts build new bone. The rate varies: part of the distal femur is replaced about every four months, while parts of the diaphysis may never be fully replaced.

Two hormones control remodeling and the calcium level in the blood by negative feedback:

🖼 Figure — Figure 7.C. Negative feedback control of blood calcium by calcitonin and parathyroid hormone. (image)
Description: The diagram is a loop centered on normal blood calcium. On the high side: when blood calcium rises, the thyroid gland releases calcitonin. Calcitonin inhibits osteoclasts, osteoblasts deposit calcium into bone, and the kidneys excrete more calcium, so blood calcium falls back to normal. On the low side: when blood calcium falls, the parathyroid glands release parathyroid hormone. Parathyroid hormone stimulates osteoclasts to resorb bone, the kidneys reabsorb calcium, and the intestine absorbs more calcium (with vitamin D), so blood calcium rises back to normal.

| Characteristic | Calcitonin | PTH (parathyroid hormone) |
|---|---|---|
| Gland | Thyroid gland | Parathyroid glands |
| Stimulus | High blood calcium | Low blood calcium |
| Osteoclasts | Inhibited | Stimulated (bone resorption releases Ca²⁺) |
| Osteoblasts | Stimulated to deposit calcium in bone | — |
| Kidneys | Excrete more Ca²⁺ in urine | Reabsorb Ca²⁺ back into blood |
| Intestine | — | Absorbs more dietary Ca²⁺ (with vitamin D) |
| Result | Blood calcium decreases to normal | Blood calcium increases to normal |

Memory trick (mnemonic)

CalciTONEin tones down blood calcium. PTH Pulls calcium To the Heart (into the blood).

options: The parathyroid glands secrete more PTH, stimulating osteoclasts

sections.title: Fractures and Fracture Repair
focus: A compound fracture: the broken bone is exposed through an opening in the skin.
Fracture repair order: hematoma → granulation tissue → callus (then remodeling).
A spiral fracture is caused by twisting and is often seen in child abuse cases.
sections.text:
A fracture is a break in a bone.

| Fracture type | Description |
|---|---|
| Simple (closed) | Broken bone does not break through the skin |
| Compound (open) | Broken bone is exposed to the outside through an opening in the skin (high infection risk) |
| Greenstick | Incomplete break; the bone bends and breaks on one side only, like a green twig. Common in children, whose bones contain more collagen |
| Fissured | Incomplete longitudinal crack |
| Comminuted | Bone shatters into several fragments |
| Transverse | Complete break straight across the bone |
| Oblique | Break at an angle |
| Spiral | Caused by excessive twisting of a bone; often seen in child abuse cases (a twisting injury of a child's arm or leg) |
| Pathologic | Caused by disease that weakens the bone (for example, osteoporosis or cancer) |

Steps of fracture repair 1. Hematoma: blood vessels break and a blood clot forms at the fracture. 2. Granulation tissue: fibroblasts and new blood vessels invade the clot; phagocytes remove debris. Some cells become cartilage-forming cells. 3. Callus: a cartilaginous callus forms, then osteoblasts replace it with a bony callus of spongy bone that bridges the break. 4. Remodeling: osteoclasts remove excess bone, and compact bone restores the original shape.

Memory trick (mnemonic)

"Happy Grandmas Cook Recipes": Hematoma → Granulation tissue → Callus → Remodeling.

sections.title: The Axial Skeleton
focus: The parietal and temporal bones are joined by a suture (the squamous suture).
Scoliosis causes one hip or shoulder to be lower than the other and is most common in adolescent females.
sections.text:
Skull (22 bones). All skull bones except the mandible are joined by immovable joints called sutures.

- Cranium (8 bones): frontal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid, 2 parietal, 2 temporal.
- Frontal bone: forehead; contains frontal sinuses.
- Parietal bones: bulging sides and top of the skull.
- Occipital bone: back and base of the skull; foramen magnum (spinal cord passes through) and occipital condyles (articulate with the atlas).
- Temporal bones: sides of the skull; external acoustic meatus, mastoid process, styloid process, zygomatic process, mandibular fossa.
- Sphenoid bone: butterfly-shaped "keystone" of the cranial floor; sella turcica holds the pituitary gland.
- Ethmoid bone: cribriform plate, crista galli, perpendicular plate (upper nasal septum), nasal conchae.
- Major sutures: coronal (frontal–parietal), sagittal (between parietals), lambdoid (parietal–occipital), squamous (parietal–temporal).

Vertebral column: 33 vertebrae in an infant; 26 bones in an adult because the sacral and coccygeal vertebrae fuse.

sections.title: The Appendicular Skeleton
focus: The pectoral girdle is made of the clavicle and scapula bones.
sections.text:
Pectoral girdle (shoulder girdle): connects the upper limbs to the trunk. It is made of two clavicles and two scapulae. - Clavicle (collarbone): medial sternal end and lateral acromial end. - Scapula (shoulder blade): flat, triangular; glenoid cavity (holds the head of the humerus), acromion (tip of the shoulder), coracoid process, spine.

Upper limb (30 bones each) - Humerus: head, greater and lesser tubercles, deltoid tuberosity, capitulum (joins radius) and trochlea (joins ulna), olecranon fossa. - Radius (thumb side) and ulna (pinky side). The ulna's olecranon is the point of the elbow. - Carpals (8 wrist bones), metacarpals (5 palm bones), phalanges (14 finger bones; the thumb, or pollex, has 2).

Pelvic girdle: two coxal (hip) bones, each formed by the fusion of the ilium, ischium, and pubis. - The coxal bones join each other anteriorly at the symphysis pubis (a pad of fibrocartilage) and the sacrum posteriorly. - Acetabulum: socket for the head of the femur. Obturator foramen: largest foramen in the skeleton. - The female pelvis is wider and lighter, the ilia flare more, and the pubic arch is wider (an adaptation for childbirth).

Lower limb (30 bones each) - Femur: the longest, largest, and strongest bone. Head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters, linea aspera, condyles. - Patella: sesamoid bone in the quadriceps tendon. - Tibia (shinbone; medial malleolus) and fibula (lateral, thin; lateral malleolus). - Tarsals (7; the talus joins the leg bones, and the calcaneus is the heel), metatarsals (5), phalanges (14).

sections.title: Life-Span Changes and Osteoporosis
focus: A light-skinned woman is most likely to have the lowest bone mass at age 65.
The upper femur commonly breaks in the elderly because trabecular bone weakens sooner than compact bone.
sections.text:
- Height begins to decrease gradually around age 30 to 35, as intervertebral discs compress.
- Bone loss exceeds bone formation with age. After menopause, women lose bone faster because estrogen levels fall. By about age 70, bone loss is similar in both sexes.
- Fractures become more common as bones age.

Osteoporosis is a disease in which bones lose mass and become porous and fragile. Risk factors: - Female sex and menopause (loss of estrogen) - Light-skinned (white or Asian) ancestry: lighter-skinned people start with less peak bone mass - Small, thin body frame - Low calcium or vitamin D intake, inactivity, smoking, heavy alcohol use

Because of these factors, a light-skinned woman is the person most likely to have the lowest bone mass at age 65, compared with a dark-skinned woman or men of similar activity and nutrition.

Why the upper femur breaks in older adults: trabecular (spongy) bone is lost sooner and faster than compact bone. The femoral neck and the vertebral bodies contain a lot of spongy bone, so they weaken first. Hip fractures (fractures of the upper femur), vertebral compression fractures, and wrist fractures are typical.

chapters.title: Joints of the Skeletal System
chapters.intro: How joints are classified, the anatomy of a synovial joint, the six synovial joint types, the movements they allow, the shoulder, elbow, hip and knee, and common joint disorders.

sections.title: What Is a Joint?
sections.text:
A joint (also called an articulation) is a place where two or more bones meet. Joints hold the skeleton together, but they also allow movement.

Joints can be classified in two ways. The two systems describe the same joints from different angles:

- Functional classification: based on how much movement the joint allows.
- Structural classification: based on the material that joins the bones and whether a joint cavity is present.

Study tip (tip)

Think of function as "what does it do?" (movement) and structure as "what is it made of?" (fibrous tissue, cartilage, or a fluid-filled capsule).

check.explanation: Describing how much movement a joint allows is functional. Structural classification describes the tissue that joins the bones.

sections.title: Functional Classification of Joints
focus: Joints with some limited degree of movement are amphiarthrotic.
Synarthrotic = immovable; diarthrotic = freely movable.
sections.text:
| Functional class | Movement | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Synarthrosis (synarthrotic) | Immovable | Sutures of the skull |
| Amphiarthrosis (amphiarthrotic) | Slightly movable (some limited degree of movement) | Intervertebral discs, symphysis pubis, distal tibiofibular joint |
| Diarthrosis (diarthrotic) | Freely movable | Most joints of the limbs (shoulder, elbow, hip, knee) |

Memory trick (mnemonic)

Syn = Stuck (no movement). Amphi = About half (a little movement). Di = Does everything (free movement).

sections.title: Structural Classification: Fibrous Joints
focus: The parietal and temporal bones are joined by a suture.
A suture is a fibrous joint (and functionally synarthrotic).
sections.text:
Structurally, joints are fibrous, cartilaginous, or synovial.

Fibrous joints are held together by dense fibrous connective tissue. They have no joint cavity. There are three types:

| Type | What holds the bones | Example | Movement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Suture | Very short collagen fibers | Between skull bones, such as the parietal and temporal bones (squamous suture) | Synarthrotic (immovable). Found only in the skull |
| Syndesmosis | A longer cord or sheet of fibrous tissue (a ligament) | Distal tibiofibular joint; acromioclavicular joint | Amphiarthrotic (a little "give") |
| Gomphosis | The short periodontal ligament | A tooth in its socket (alveolar process) | Synarthrotic |

Description: Anatomy & Physiology, Connexions Web site. http://cnx.org/content/col11496/1.6/, Jun 19, 2013.

sections.title: Structural Classification: Cartilaginous Joints
focus: The joint between the bodies of the vertebrae and between the two pubic bones is a symphysis.
The symphysis pubis is not a synovial joint and not a fibrous joint.
sections.text:
Cartilaginous joints are joined by cartilage and have no joint cavity. There are two types:

| Type | Cartilage | Examples | Function |
|---|---|---|---|
| Synchondrosis | A plate of hyaline cartilage | Epiphyseal plate; the joint between the first rib and the manubrium | Temporary growth areas; usually synarthrotic. When ossified, the joint becomes a synostosis (a bony fusion) |
| Symphysis | A pad or plate of fibrocartilage | Intervertebral discs (between the bodies of adjacent vertebrae); symphysis pubis (between the two pubic bones) | Compressible shock absorber; amphiarthrotic |

Note (note)

The symphysis pubis is a cartilaginous joint, not a fibrous or synovial joint. So is every intervertebral disc.

Clinical connection (clinical)

Epiphyseal plate versus intervertebral disc. The epiphyseal plate is a synchondrosis of hyaline cartilage that is later replaced by bone. The intervertebral disc is a symphysis of fibrocartilage that stays cartilage for life.

sections.title: Structure of a Synovial Joint
focus: Bones of a synovial joint are held together by a joint capsule (reinforced by ligaments).
The synovial membrane secretes synovial fluid, surrounds the synovial cavity, and reabsorbs fluid.
A meniscus is part of the knee joint.
Bursae are fluid-filled sacs between skin and bony prominences.
The articular ends of long bones are covered with hyaline cartilage.
sections.text:
Synovial joints have a fluid-filled joint cavity and are freely movable (diarthroses). Most joints of the body are synovial, so most types of joints are synovial.

🖼 Figure — Figure 8.A. General structure of a synovial joint, in section. (image)
Description: A cutaway drawing of a synovial joint with one bone above and one below. The rounded end of each bone is covered by a blue-gray layer of articular cartilage. Between the two cartilages is the joint cavity, which contains synovial fluid (shown in pale yellow). Around the cavity is the articular capsule: an outer fibrous layer, and, lining its inside, the synovial membrane (shown in orange-red). Labels: bone (top and bottom), articular cartilage, synovial membrane, articular capsule, and joint cavity containing synovial fluid.

Features common to all synovial joints:

| Feature | Description and function |
|---|---|
| Articular cartilage | Hyaline cartilage covering the ends of the bones. It reduces friction and absorbs shock. It is the tissue that covers the articular ends of long bones. |
| Joint capsule | Double-layered sleeve around the joint. The outer fibrous layer is tough and continuous with the periosteum; it holds the bones together. |
| Synovial membrane | The inner layer of the capsule: loose connective tissue that lines the capsule and all internal surfaces except the articular cartilage. It secretes synovial fluid and reabsorbs fluid; its phagocytes can remove debris and microbes from an infected joint cavity. |
| Synovial cavity | The space between the bones; a "potential space" filled with synovial fluid. |
| Synovial fluid | Clear, viscous lubricant. Reduces friction, nourishes cartilage, and contains phagocytes that clean up debris. |
| Ligaments | Bands of dense connective tissue that connect bone to bone and reinforce the joint capsule. Many are thickened parts of the fibrous capsule. |

Other structures found in some joints:

- Fatty pads (hip and knee): cushion and fill space.
- Menisci (singular meniscus) or articular discs: C-shaped pads of fibrocartilage that divide the cavity into two compartments, absorb shock, and improve fit. A meniscus is part of the knee joint (medial and lateral menisci). Articular discs are also found in the jaw and the sternoclavicular joint.
- Bursae (singular bursa): flat fibrous sacs lined with synovial membrane and filled with synovial fluid, acting as "ball bearings." They lie between skin and bone, and between muscles, tendons, ligaments, and bone, where friction would occur. Fluid-filled sacs between the skin and underlying bony prominences are bursae.

Three factors that influence joint stability: 1. Shape of the articular surfaces (how well the bones fit). 2. Ligaments (number and strength). 3. Muscle tone (tendons and muscles crossing the joint).

Study tip (tip)

Remember the difference: ligaments connect bone to bone. Tendons connect muscle to bone. A joint capsule is reinforced by ligaments, not tendons.

**Synovial joints** have a **fluid-filled joint cavity** and are **freely movable (diarthroses)**. Most joints of the body are synovial, so **most types of joints are synovial**.

> 🖼 **Figure — Figure 8.A. General structure of a synovial joint, in section.** ([image](https://lsc-nh-biol2401-final-study-guide.netlify.app/public/figures/synovial-joint.webp))

Around the cavity is the articular capsule: an outer fibrous layer, and, lining its inside, the synovial membrane (shown in orange-red). Labels: bone (top and bottom), articular cartilage, synovial membrane, articular capsule, and joint cavity containing synovial fluid.

|---|---|

check.question: A runner has pain at the front of the knee where the skin slides over the kneecap. Which structure, when inflamed, would most likely cause this?
check.explanation: Bursae are fluid-filled sacs that reduce friction between skin, tendons, and bone. Inflammation of a bursa is bursitis.

sections.title: Types of Synovial Joints
focus: Rotational movement is possible in the ball-and-socket joint (and pivot joints).
The ball-and-socket joint allows the most movements.
Saddle joint: base of the thumb. Gliding joint: between carpals (and tarsals). Pivot: atlas–axis.
A condyloid joint does not allow rotation, and it is not limited to one plane.
Elbow and knee are primarily hinge joints.
sections.text:
🖼 Figure — Figure 8.B. The six types of synovial joints, with an example of each. (image)
Description: A skeleton in the center with six boxes marking joints, each linked to a simple model that shows the motion. (a) Pivot joint between the C1 and C2 vertebrae: a peg turning inside a ring. (b) Hinge joint at the elbow: a cylinder in a trough, moving in one plane. (c) Saddle joint between the trapezium carpal bone and the first metacarpal at the base of the thumb: two saddle-shaped surfaces. (d) Plane (gliding) joint between tarsal bones: flat surfaces sliding. (e) Condyloid joint between the radius and the carpal bones of the wrist: an oval head in an oval socket. (f) Ball-and-socket joint at the hip: a round head in a cup, moving in all directions.

| Type | Shape | Movements | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ball-and-socket joint | Rounded head in a cup | Most freely movable: all angular movements plus rotation (flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction, rotation) | Shoulder and hip |
| Condyloid joint (ellipsoidal) | Oval head in oval cavity | All angular movements except rotation; can move in two planes | Wrist (radiocarpal), knuckles (metacarpophalangeal) |
| Gliding joint (plane) | Flat or slightly curved surfaces | Sliding or gliding back-and-forth | Between carpals and between tarsals; between vertebral processes; the sternoclavicular joint |
| Hinge joint | Cylinder in trough | Flexion and extension only (one plane) | Elbow (humerus–ulna), knee, interphalangeal joints |
| Pivot joint | Peg rotating in a ring | Rotation around a long axis | Atlas–axis (atlantoaxial joint; "no" movement); proximal radioulnar joint |
| Saddle joint | Two saddle-shaped surfaces | Wide range of movement, including opposition | Base of the thumb (carpometacarpal joint) |

Memory trick (mnemonic)

"Ball and socket: the shoulder and hip rock." "Hinge: like a door at the elbow and knee." "Pivot: shake your head 'no.'" "Saddle: the thumb can touch every finger."

check.question: A dancer swings her leg in a wide circle and rotates it outward. Which joint type allows both?
check.explanation: Only ball-and-socket (and to a lesser extent pivot) joints permit rotation. The hip is a ball-and-socket joint that allows circumduction and rotation.

sections.title: Joint Movements
focus: Dorsiflexion brings the foot closer to the shin.
Adduction means moving a body part closer to the trunk (midline).
sections.text:
Origin and insertion. A muscle's origin is its attachment to the relatively immovable bone. Its insertion is its attachment to the movable bone. When a muscle contracts, the insertion is pulled toward the origin.

There are three general types of movement:

1. Gliding movements. Flat bone surfaces slide over one another (between carpals, between tarsals, between vertebrae).

2. Angular movements change the angle between bones:

| Movement | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Flexion | Decreases the angle between two bones | Bending the elbow, nodding the head toward the chest |
| Extension | Increases the angle | Straightening the elbow |
| Hyperextension | Extension beyond the anatomical position | Tilting the head back |
| Abduction | Movement away from the midline | Raising the arm to the side |
| Adduction | Movement toward the midline | Lowering the arm to the side; bringing the thigh back toward the trunk |
| Circumduction | Moving a limb in a cone-shaped circle | Drawing a circle with your arm |
| Rotation | Turning of a bone around its long axis | Shaking your head "no" |
| Dorsiflexion | Bringing the top of the foot closer to the shin | Standing on your heels |
| Plantar flexion | Pointing the toes (flexion toward the sole) | Standing on tiptoe |

3. Special movements

| Movement | Description |
|---|---|
| Supination and pronation | Rotation of the forearm at the radioulnar joint: palm up (supination, "thumb out") and palm down (pronation) |
| Inversion and eversion | Sole of the foot turned inward (inversion) or outward (eversion) |
| Elevation and depression | Lifting a body part (shoulder shrug) and lowering it (opening the mouth depresses the mandible) |
| Protraction and retraction | Forward (thrust the jaw out) and backward (pull it back) |
| Opposition | Touching the thumb to the fingertips (saddle joint) |

Study tip (tip)

"Adduction" = "add" to the body (toward the trunk). "Abduction" = "abduct" (take away) from the trunk.

sections.title: Shoulder, Elbow, Hip, and Knee
focus: The anatomical term for the shoulder joint is the glenohumeral joint.
The rotator cuff is found at the shoulder.
The radial collateral ligament is associated with the elbow.
The shoulder allows the most range of motion, so it is the most likely to dislocate.
A meniscus is part of the knee.
sections.text:
| Joint | Type and bones | Key features |
|---|---|---|
| Shoulder joint (glenohumeral joint) | Ball-and-socket: head of the humerus in the shallow glenoid cavity of the scapula | Greatest range of motion of any joint, so it is the most likely to dislocate. Stabilized mainly by muscles and tendons: the rotator cuff (four muscles and their tendons) and a fibrous capsule. Many bursae. The acromioclavicular joint is a separate gliding/syndesmosis joint. |
| Elbow joint | Hinge between the trochlea of the humerus and the trochlear notch of the ulna (plus a gliding joint with the radius) | Flexion and extension only. Very stable because of strong ligaments, including the radial collateral ligament (lateral) and ulnar collateral ligament (medial). |
| Hip joint (coxal joint) | Ball-and-socket: head of the femur in the deep acetabulum | Strong and stable: deep socket plus large reinforcing ligaments. Less range of motion than the shoulder because of bony limits. |
| Knee joint | Largest and most complex synovial joint; hinge (with slight rotation), actually three joints: two condyloid (medial and lateral femur–tibia) and one gliding (patella–femur) | Flexion and extension. Menisci (medial and lateral), ACL and PCL (inside the capsule, prevent hyperextension and sliding), tibial (medial) and fibular (lateral) collateral ligaments, patellar ligament, many bursae. |

🖼 Figure — Figure 8.C. The knee joint: sagittal section, superior view of the tibia, and anterior view. (image)
Description: Three views of the right knee. (a) A side section shows the femur above and the tibia below, the patella in front, the synovial cavity, the anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments, the lateral meniscus, the infrapatellar fat pad, and three bursae: suprapatellar, prepatellar, and infrapatellar. (b) A view from above of the tibia shows the C-shaped medial and lateral menisci and the crossing anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments. (c) A view from the front shows the quadriceps muscle and tendon, the patella and patellar ligament, the tibial (medial) and fibular (lateral) collateral ligaments, the tibia, and the fibula.

🖼 Figure — Figure 8.D. The elbow joint: hinge between the humerus and ulna, with its collateral ligaments. (image)
Description: Views of the right elbow showing the distal humerus meeting the ulna and radius. The ulna fits the trochlea of the humerus like a hinge, which allows only flexion and extension. The joint capsule is reinforced by the radial (lateral) collateral ligament and the ulnar (medial) collateral ligament, and the annular ligament holds the head of the radius against the ulna.

Memory trick (mnemonic)

ACL stops the tibia from sliding Anteriorly. PCL stops it from sliding Posteriorly. MCL is Medial and LCL is Lateral.

Note (note)

Hip versus shoulder. The hip allows less freedom of movement than the shoulder, because its deep socket and heavy ligaments make it more stable. The shoulder moves more but dislocates more easily. The knee (not the hip) is the largest and most complex synovial joint.

check.question: A football player is tackled and the front of the knee gives way, so his tibia slides forward under the femur. Which structure is most likely torn?

sections.title: Life-Span Changes
focus: True statement: loss of function of synovial joints often begins in the third decade of life.
sections.text:
- The fontanels of the infant skull harden (ossify) within the first two years.
- Epiphyseal plates harden (close) between about ages 14 and 20.
- With age, fibrocartilage loses water, so intervertebral joints and knees become less flexible.
- Collagen changes cause stiffening beginning around age 30. Loss of function of synovial joints often begins in the third decade of life (in the twenties and thirties).
- Exercise delays the onset of joint stiffening.

check.question: A 55-year-old complains that his knees and back feel stiffer each year, even though he has no injury. Which age-related change most likely contributes?
options: Fibrocartilage losing water and collagen stiffening
Loss of articular cartilage in infancy
check.answer: Fibrocartilage losing water and collagen stiffening
check.explanation: With age, fibrocartilage dries and collagen stiffens, reducing flexibility. Regular exercise helps slow this process.

sections.title: Joint Disorders: Injuries and Arthritis
focus: A dislocation is displacement of the articulating bones, and the joint is clearly deformed.
A sprain is overstretching or tearing of ligaments and tendons in a joint.
RA is autoimmune; OA is caused by the effects of aging (wear and tear).
Lyme arthritis is caused by a tick-borne bacterium.
sections.text:
Joint injuries

| Condition | Description |
|---|---|
| Sprain | Overstretching or tearing of ligaments (and sometimes tendons) in a joint |
| Strain | Overstretching or tearing of a muscle (for example, a hamstring injury) |
| Dislocation (luxation) | The articulating bones are displaced from their normal positions; the joint is clearly deformed. Often damages the capsule and ligaments |
| Bursitis | Inflammation of a bursa |
| Tendinitis | Inflammation of a tendon |
| Ankylosis | Abnormal stiffening or fusion of a joint |

Arthritis means inflammation of the joints (swollen, painful joints). Common forms:

| Type | Cause | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| Osteoarthritis (OA) | Wear-and-tear / effects of aging: articular cartilage softens and degenerates | Most common type; usually affects weight-bearing joints |
| Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) | Autoimmune disease: the immune system attacks the synovial membrane | Inflamed synovial membrane, joint deformity; can occur in younger adults and children (juvenile RA) |
| Gout (gouty arthritis) | Uric acid crystals deposit in the joint | Often affects the big toe |
| Lyme arthritis | A bacterium (Borrelia burgdorferi) transmitted by a tick bite | Joint swelling and pain, especially in the knees |

Study tip (tip)

OA is "Old and Aching" (aging). RA is "Rogue Antibodies" (autoimmune). They do not share the same cause.

chapters.title: The Muscular System
chapters.intro: The three muscle tissues, how a skeletal muscle is built, how it contracts and gets its energy, how muscles respond to stimuli, how muscles work together, and the major muscles of the body.

sections.title: Overview of Muscle Tissues
sections.text:
There are three kinds of muscle tissue. All three have elongated cells called muscle fibers, all depend on two kinds of protein myofilaments (actin and myosin) to contract, and in all three the cell membrane is called the sarcolemma and the cytoplasm is called the sarcoplasm.

| Characteristic | Skeletal | Smooth | Cardiac |
|---|---|---|---|
| Location | Attached to bones | Walls of hollow organs and blood vessels; iris of the eye | Heart only |
| Cell shape | Long, cylindrical, multinucleated | Spindle-shaped, one nucleus | Branched, one nucleus (uninucleate) |
| Striations | Yes | No | Yes |
| Control | Voluntary | Involuntary | Involuntary |
| Contraction | Rapid, forceful, tires easily | Slow and sustained | Rhythmic and steady (pacemaker) |
| Special features | Organized into muscles | Peristalsis | Intercalated discs with gap junctions |

Functions of muscle: movement (walking, facial expression, blood pumping, digestion), posture maintenance, joint stability, and heat generation (almost half the energy released in contraction becomes heat).

Four functional characteristics of muscle tissue

| Characteristic | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Excitability | Ability to receive and respond to a stimulus |
| Contractility | Ability to shorten forcibly |
| Extensibility | Ability to be stretched |
| Elasticity | Ability to recoil to the original length |

Memory trick (mnemonic)

"E.C.E.E.": Excite, Contract, Extend, Elasticity bounce-back.

sections.title: Structure of a Skeletal Muscle
focus: The outermost layer of connective tissue (underneath the fascia) surrounding a skeletal muscle is the epimysium.
A tendon attaches muscle to bone.
The severe pain of compartment syndrome results from excessive fluid pressure within the compartment.
sections.text:
Each skeletal muscle is an organ made of muscle fibers, connective tissue coverings, blood vessels, and nerves.

🖼 Figure — Figure 9.A. Connective tissue coverings of a skeletal muscle. (image)
Description: The illustration shows a skeletal muscle attached to a bone by a tendon. A cutaway exposes bundles called fascicles, and one fascicle is pulled outward to reveal its individual muscle fibers. Epimysium surrounds the whole muscle, perimysium surrounds a fascicle, and endomysium surrounds each muscle fiber. A blood vessel is also labeled. The connective tissue coverings continue into the tendon at the end of the muscle. Deep fascia is discussed in the text but is not labeled in this illustration.

| Layer | What it wraps | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Endomysium | Each individual muscle fiber | Thin and delicate |
| Perimysium | Each fascicle (bundle of fibers) | Collagen; carries blood vessels and nerves |
| Epimysium | The entire muscle: the outermost layer of connective tissue just underneath the fascia | Dense and fibrous |
| Deep fascia | Covers the muscle (and separates muscles) | Very tough outer layer that may extend as a tendon or aponeurosis |

- A tendon is a cord of dense connective tissue that attaches muscle to bone. (A ligament attaches bone to bone.)
- An aponeurosis is a broad, flat sheet of connective tissue that attaches a muscle to another muscle or to bone.
- A raphe is a seam where the fibers of two muscles meet.

Study tip (tip)

Order from inside out: Endomysium (inside the fiber layer) → Perimysium (peri = around the bundle) → Epimysium (epi = on the outside).

Clinical connection (clinical)

Compartment syndrome. Groups of muscles are enclosed by fascia into compartments. After injury, swelling or bleeding inside the compartment raises fluid pressure, which squeezes blood vessels and nerves. The severe pain is caused by this excessive fluid pressure within the compartment, not by torn walls or stretched tendons. Untreated, it can cause permanent tissue damage; surgery (fasciotomy) relieves the pressure.

🖼 Figure — Organization of Muscle Fiber (image)
Description: Version 8.25 from the Textbook OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology Published May 18, 2016

sections.title: Skeletal Muscle Fiber and the Sarcomere
focus: Myofibrils are composed primarily of actin and myosin.
The striated appearance comes from the sarcomere arrangement.
The T tubules transmit muscle impulses into the cell's interior; the SR stores calcium.
The sarcomere is the functional unit of contraction.
The Z line holds the bands of actin together and forms the boundaries of the sarcomere.
sections.text:
A muscle fiber is a long, thin cell packed with myofibrils. Myofibrils are composed primarily of actin and myosin (thin and thick filaments).

🖼 Figure — Figure 9.B. A sarcomere, the functional unit of contraction. (image)
Description: The drawing shows one sarcomere between two Z lines. Thin actin filaments are attached to each Z line and extend toward the center. Thick myosin filaments sit in the middle. The A band is the dark region that spans the full length of the thick filaments. The I band is the light region containing only thin filaments, and it spans across the Z line into the next sarcomere. The H zone is the lighter central region of the A band with only thick filaments, and the M line is the center. When the muscle contracts, the Z lines move closer together, and the I band and H zone shorten while the A band keeps its length.

| Structure | Description |
|---|---|
| Thick filament | Made of the protein myosin: a rod-like tail with two globular heads (cross-bridges) |
| Thin filament | Made of actin (coiled like a twisted strand of pearls), plus tropomyosin (covers the binding sites) and troponin (binds calcium) |
| A band | Dark band: where thick and thin filaments overlap (the whole length of the thick filaments) |
| I band | Light band: thin filaments only |
| Z line | Boundary between sarcomeres: the structure that holds the bands of actin together at each end of the sarcomere |
| Sarcomere | The segment between two Z lines: the functional (contractile) unit of the muscle |

The striations (stripes) of skeletal muscle result from the arrangement of thick and thin filaments in the sarcomeres (alternating A and I bands).

Special membranous organelles - Sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR): network of membranous channels around each myofibril; stores high concentrations of calcium ions (maintained by a calcium pump) and releases them when stimulated. - Transverse tubules (T tubules): inward extensions of the sarcolemma, filled with extracellular fluid, that transmit the muscle impulse (action potential) deep into the cell's interior. One T tubule sits between two enlarged ends of the SR (terminal cisternae), forming a triad.

🖼 Figure — Muscle Fibes (large) (image)
Description: Version 8.25 from the Textbook OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology Published May 18, 2016

check.question: When a muscle contracts, which of the following DOES NOT shorten?
check.explanation: The A band equals the length of the thick filaments, which do not change length. The filaments slide, so the Z lines move closer and the I band and H zone shrink.

sections.title: The Neuromuscular Junction
focus: A motor unit = a motor neuron and the muscle fibers it controls.
Neurotransmitters are stored in vesicles in the motor neuron endings.
Cholinesterase causes acetylcholine to decompose.

A neuromuscular junction is a junction between a motor neuron and a muscle fiber, with a gap (synaptic cleft), where neurotransmitters are released from the neuron: all of these statements are correct.
The functional connection between neuron and fiber is the synapse (neuromuscular junction).
sections.text:
Skeletal muscle fibers contract only when stimulated by a motor neuron.

🖼 Figure — Figure 9.C. The neuromuscular junction. (image)
Description: Three progressively enlarged views show the neuromuscular junction. At the top, a motor neuron's axon branches into terminals contacting a skeletal muscle fiber. The middle view enlarges one terminal and the motor end plate, separated by the synaptic cleft. At the bottom, synaptic vesicles release acetylcholine into the cleft by exocytosis. Acetylcholine binds receptors on the motor end plate, opening channels that allow sodium ions to enter the muscle fiber. Acetylcholinesterase and its role in ending the signal are explained in the text but are not labeled in this illustration.

- Motor neuron: the nerve cell that stimulates the muscle fiber.
- Neuromuscular junction (NMJ): the functional connection (synapse) between a motor neuron's axon ending and a muscle fiber. It includes the synaptic cleft, a small gap, so the neuron and muscle do not touch.
- Motor end plate: the specialized part of the sarcolemma directly beneath the axon terminal, with receptors for acetylcholine.
- Neurotransmitter: chemical messenger released from the axon terminal. At the NMJ it is acetylcholine (ACh). Neurotransmitters are stored in vesicles within the motor neuron endings (axon terminals).
- Motor unit: one motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it controls. Muscles that make fine movements (eye, fingers) have few fibers per neuron; powerful muscles have hundreds.
- Acetylcholinesterase (AChE, also called cholinesterase): enzyme in the synaptic cleft that breaks down (decomposes) acetylcholine, so a single nerve impulse causes only one twitch.

Clinical connection (clinical)

When the NMJ fails. Botulism toxin blocks ACh release (flaccid paralysis). Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune attack on ACh receptors (weakness). Some pesticides and nerve agents inhibit acetylcholinesterase, so ACh stays in the cleft and the muscle stays contracted (spastic paralysis).

sections.title: Steps of Muscle Contraction
focus: The first event in contraction: acetylcholine is released from the end of the motor neuron.
ATP supplies energy for myofilament movement.
Calcium released from the SR binds to troponin.
sections.text:
The sequence (excitation–contraction coupling)

1. A motor impulse from the brain travels down the spinal cord and along a motor neuron to the axon terminals.
2. Acetylcholine is released from the end of the motor neuron (calcium enters the terminal; vesicles release ACh by exocytosis). This is the first event.
3. ACh crosses the synaptic cleft and binds to receptors on the motor end plate, opening ligand-gated channels and depolarizing the sarcolemma.
4. The muscle impulse travels over the surface and deep into the fiber through the T tubules.
5. The impulse reaches the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which releases calcium ions into the sarcoplasm.
6. Calcium binds to troponin, which moves tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin.
7. Cross-bridges form between myosin heads and actin.
8. The myosin heads pivot (power stroke), pulling the thin filaments toward the center of the sarcomere. ATP supplies the energy for this myofilament movement. The fiber shortens.

Cross-bridge cycle. (a) ATP is split to "cock" the myosin head; (b) the cocked head attaches to actin; (c) the head pivots (power stroke) and pulls the actin; (d) a new ATP binds and the head releases from actin. The cycle repeats as long as calcium and ATP are present.

Sliding filament model (Huxley, 1954): thin filaments slide past thick filaments. The filaments themselves do not shorten.

Relaxation 1. Acetylcholinesterase destroys ACh, ending stimulation. 2. Calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum using ATP. 3. Tropomyosin covers the binding sites, cross-bridges break, and the fiber relaxes.

Memory trick (mnemonic)

"A-T-C-C-S": ACh → T tubule → Calcium released → Cross-bridges → Slide.

Clinical connection (clinical)

Rigor mortis. After death, ATP is no longer made. Without ATP, myosin heads cannot detach from actin, so the muscles stay stiff until the proteins break down.

sections.title: Energy for Contraction
focus: Creatine phosphate supplies energy for the synthesis of ATP.
The oxygen needed to convert lactic acid back to glycogen after intense exercise is the oxygen debt.
A muscle cramp is most likely due to a lack of ATP.
sections.text:
Muscle stores only about six seconds of ATP, so ATP must be regenerated continuously. There are three pathways:

| Pathway | How it makes ATP | Duration and notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Creatine phosphate (CP) | CP + ADP → creatine + ATP | About 10 seconds. CP supplies energy for the synthesis of ATP (it is not itself used to break ATP down) |
| 2. Anaerobic respiration (glycolysis) | Glucose → pyruvic acid + 2 ATP in the cytoplasm; no oxygen needed | Fast but low yield; if oxygen is short, pyruvic acid becomes lactic acid |
| 3. Aerobic respiration | Citric acid cycle and electron transport chain in the mitochondria; needs oxygen | About 36 ATP per glucose plus CO₂ and water; sustained, long-term |

Oxygen debt (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption): the amount of oxygen needed after intense exercise to support the conversion of lactic acid back to glucose/glycogen, resynthesize ATP and CP, and restore oxygen levels in blood and tissues. This is why you keep breathing hard after you stop.

Muscle fatigue is the inability to contract, caused by a relative deficit of ATP and/or lactic acid accumulation (which lowers pH).

Muscle cramp. A cramp is most likely due to a lack of ATP: without ATP, calcium cannot be pumped back into the SR and myosin heads cannot detach, so the muscle stays contracted.

Heat. Almost half the energy released in contraction is lost as heat, which helps keep body temperature near 37 °C. Excess heat is lost through negative feedback mechanisms such as sweating and dilation of skin blood vessels.

**Oxygen debt** (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption): the **amount of oxygen needed after intense exercise to support the conversion of lactic acid back to glucose/glycogen**, resynthesize ATP and CP, and restore oxygen levels in blood and tissues. This is why you keep breathing hard after you stop.

**Muscle fatigue** is the inability to contract, caused by a relative deficit of ATP and/or **lactic acid accumulation** (which lowers pH).

**Muscle cramp.** A cramp is most likely due to a **lack of ATP**: without ATP, calcium cannot be pumped back into the SR and myosin heads cannot detach, so the muscle stays contracted.

**Heat.** Almost half the energy released in contraction is lost as heat, which helps keep body temperature near 37 °C. Excess heat is lost through negative feedback mechanisms such as sweating and dilation of skin blood vessels.

> 🖼 **Figure — Muscle Metabolism** ([image](https://lsc-nh-biol2401-final-study-guide.netlify.app/public/figures/1016-muscle-metabolism.webp))
> Description: Version 8.25 from the Textbook OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology Published May 18, 2016

check.question: A sprinter finishes a 200 m race and continues to breathe heavily for several minutes. Which concept explains this?
check.explanation: Oxygen debt is the extra oxygen needed after exercise to convert lactic acid back to glucose, rebuild ATP and creatine phosphate, and restore oxygen stores.

sections.title: Muscle Responses
focus: Latent period = delay between stimulus and response. Refractory period = brief unresponsive moment after stimulation.
Threshold stimulus = the minimal stimulus needed to elicit a contraction.

Matching: isotonic = movement where fibers lengthen or shorten; eccentric = lengthening contraction; concentric = shortening contraction; isometric = tension rises, length unchanged; recruitment = more motor units; twitch = response of one fiber to one impulse; tone = sustained contraction.
Red muscles contract more slowly, have more myoglobin and mitochondria, and fatigue more slowly.
sections.text:
Threshold stimulus: the minimal stimulus needed to elicit a muscular contraction. In a muscle fiber the membrane potential must change from about −100 mV to −70 mV (a +30 mV change) for an impulse to begin.

All-or-none response: a muscle fiber that receives a stimulus at or above threshold contracts completely; a subthreshold stimulus produces no contraction.

Recording a twitch (a myogram)

🖼 Figure — Figure 9.D. A myogram of a single muscle twitch. (image)
Description: The myogram plots muscle tension on the vertical axis against time in milliseconds on the horizontal axis. A single stimulus occurs at time zero. A short latent period precedes the rise in tension. Tension then rises during the contraction period and falls toward baseline during the relaxation period. The three periods have different background shading and are also labeled in words. The refractory period is discussed in the text but is not separately marked on this graph.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Twitch | A single, brief contraction (a fraction of a second) in response to one impulse |
| Latent period | The delay between the stimulus and the start of the response |
| Refractory period | The very brief moment after stimulation when the fiber is unresponsive to another stimulus |
| Staircase effect (treppe) | A rested muscle gives a series of twitches, each slightly stronger than the last |
| Summation | Twitches combine when stimuli arrive faster than the fiber can relax, producing stronger, sustained contraction |
| Tetanus (tetanic contraction) | Sustained contraction with no relaxation between stimuli |
| Recruitment | Increase in the number of activated motor units as stimulus intensity rises |
| Muscle tone | A certain degree of sustained contraction in a resting muscle; maintains posture |

Types of contraction - Isotonic contraction: the muscle changes length (and the load moves). Concentric = shortening contraction; eccentric = lengthening contraction. - Isometric contraction: tension increases but the length does not change (pushing against a wall).

Fast versus slow muscle fibers

| Characteristic | Slow-twitch (red) | Fast-twitch (white) |
|---|---|---|
| Contraction speed | Slower | Faster |
| Myoglobin | More (red color) | Less |
| Mitochondria | More | Fewer |
| Blood supply | Rich | Less |
| Fatigue | Slowly (endurance) | Quickly (lactic acid) |
| Example | Postural muscles, marathon runners | Eye, sprinters; "white meat" |

Note (note)

Watch for the false comparison: red muscles do not have fewer mitochondria than white muscles. They have more.

sections.title: Atrophy, Hypertrophy, and Muscle Disorders
focus: Muscle atrophy from disuse: reduced capillaries, fewer mitochondria, and smaller actin and myosin filaments: all of these.
sections.text:
- Hypertrophy: enlargement of muscle fibers from heavy use (exercise).
- Atrophy: wasting of muscle in response to disuse. Atrophy reduces the capillary networks, the number of mitochondria, and the size of actin and myosin filaments. So all of these are correct.
- Tendinitis: inflammation of a tendon.
- Muscle strain: overstretching or tearing of muscle fibers (a pulled hamstring).
- Compartment syndrome: pressure buildup in a muscle compartment (see Structure).
- Duchenne muscular dystrophy: inherited disease with progressive muscle degeneration.
- Poliomyelitis: virus damages motor neurons.
- Botulism, myasthenia gravis, rigor mortis: see neuromuscular junction and contraction.
- TMJ syndrome: pain in the jaw joint and chewing muscles.
- Parkinson's disease: tremors and rigidity from loss of dopamine neurons.

Life-span changes. ATP, myoglobin, and creatine phosphate supplies start to decline in the forties. By age 80, about half of muscle mass has been replaced by connective and adipose tissue. Exercise is the best way to maintain muscle function.

check.question: A patient's leg is in a cast for eight weeks. After removal, the calf is visibly smaller. Which statement is correct?
options: The muscle fibers increased in number
Disuse caused atrophy: fewer mitochondria, less capillary supply, and smaller myofilaments
The motor units were recruited more

sections.title: Smooth and Cardiac Muscle
sections.text:
Smooth muscle - No striations; lacks organized sarcomeres. No troponin: calmodulin binds calcium instead. Little SR; most calcium enters from extracellular fluid. - Multiunit smooth muscle: fibers act independently; rapid, vigorous contractions. Examples: iris of the eye, walls of large blood vessels. - Visceral (single-unit) smooth muscle: fibers linked by gap junctions, contracting as a sheet; slow and sustained, rhythmic. Found in the walls of hollow organs (stomach, intestine, uterus, bladder). Arranged in an inner circular and outer longitudinal layer. - Peristalsis: wave-like contractions that push substances through tubes (food through the intestine). - Neurotransmitters: acetylcholine and norepinephrine.

Cardiac muscle - Only in the heart. Striated, branched fibers, one nucleus each. - Joined end to end by intercalated discs with gap junctions so the heart works as a syncytium. - Self-exciting (pacemaker), rhythmic, involuntary (about 60–100 beats per minute). - Less developed SR and many mitochondria.

sections.title: How Muscles Produce Movement
focus: A muscle end attached to a relatively immovable part is the origin.
The antagonist opposes the movement of the prime mover (agonist).
sections.text:
Muscles pull on bones by tendons to move them as levers. Every skeletal muscle has two attachments:

- Origin: the attachment to the relatively immovable (stationary) bone.
- Insertion: the attachment to the movable bone. On contraction, the insertion is pulled toward the origin.

How muscles cooperate

| Role | Meaning | Example (elbow flexion) |
|---|---|---|
| Prime mover (agonist) | The muscle mainly responsible for the movement | Biceps brachii |
| Synergist | Assists the prime mover | Brachialis, brachioradialis |
| Antagonist | Opposes the movement; it relaxes or stretches while the prime mover contracts | Triceps brachii |
| Fixator | Stabilizes the origin of the prime mover | Serratus anterior and pectoralis minor hold the scapula |

Another example: in the thigh, the quadriceps (extend the knee) are antagonists of the hamstrings (flex the knee).

Study tip (tip)

The general name for a muscle that opposes a movement is the antagonist. Do not confuse it with agonist (prime mover).
sections.markdown:
Muscles pull on bones by **tendons** to move them as **levers**. Every skeletal muscle has two attachments:

- **Origin**: the attachment to the **relatively immovable** (stationary) bone.
- **Insertion**: the attachment to the **movable** bone. On contraction, the insertion is pulled toward the origin.

**How muscles cooperate**

| Role | Meaning | Example (elbow flexion) |
|---|---|---|
| **Prime mover** (agonist) | The muscle **mainly responsible** for the movement | **Biceps brachii** |
| **Synergist** | Assists the prime mover | **Brachialis**, brachioradialis |
| **Antagonist** | **Opposes** the movement; it relaxes or stretches while the prime mover contracts | **Triceps brachii** |
| **Fixator** | Stabilizes the origin of the prime mover | Serratus anterior and pectoralis minor hold the scapula |

Another example: in the thigh, the **quadriceps** (extend the knee) are antagonists of the **hamstrings** (flex the knee).

> **Study tip** (tip)
>
> The general name for a muscle that **opposes** a movement is the **antagonist**. Do not confuse it with agonist (prime mover).

check.question: When you straighten your elbow, the triceps brachii contracts. What is the biceps brachii called in this movement?
check.explanation: The biceps opposes elbow extension, so it is the antagonist while the triceps is the prime mover.

sections.title: Naming Skeletal Muscles
sections.text:
Muscle names often describe one of these features:

| Naming characteristic | Terms | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Direction of fibers | rectus = straight/parallel; transverse = across; oblique = angled | Rectus abdominis, transversus abdominis, external oblique |
| Location | named for a bone or region | Frontalis (over the frontal bone), tibialis anterior, temporalis |
| Size | maximus (largest), longus (long), brevis (short) | Gluteus maximus, palmaris longus |
| Number of heads | bi- = 2, tri- = 3, quad- = 4 | Biceps brachii, triceps brachii, quadriceps |
| Shape | deltoid = triangle, trapezius = trapezoid, serratus = saw-toothed, orbicularis = circular | Deltoid, trapezius, serratus anterior, orbicularis oris |
| Origin and insertion | uses the attachment sites | Sternocleidomastoid (sternum and clavicle → mastoid process) |
| Action | flexor, extensor, adductor, abductor | Flexor carpi radialis, extensor digitorum, adductor longus |

chapters.title: Nervous System I: Basic Structure and Function
chapters.intro: Trace information through neurons, glia, membrane potentials, and chemical synapses.

sections.title: Nervous-system organization and information flow
focus: CNS is brain/spinal cord; PNS includes peripheral nerves and ganglia.
Afferent arrives, efferent exits; integration links input to output.
sections.text:
The central nervous system (CNS) consists of brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) includes nerves, ganglia, and peripheral receptors outside the CNS. Sensory or afferent pathways carry information toward the CNS; motor or efferent pathways carry commands away. Interneurons connect and integrate within central circuits.

Sensory input detects changes; integration interprets and selects responses; motor output activates effectors. Somatic motor pathways supply skeletal muscle, whereas autonomic motor pathways supply smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands. Visceral describes internal-organ relationships; somatic describes body-wall/limb relationships. Sensory traffic can also be visceral or somatic, so visceral is not simply another word for every motor axon.

A receptor converts a stimulus into a signal. An effector performs a response. For example, skin stimulation activates sensory neurons, spinal circuits process input, and somatic motor neurons activate skeletal muscle. A reflex can be integrated in the spinal cord before conscious awareness. Directional labels are defined relative to the CNS, not whether a particular line in a diagram points left or right.

sections.title: Neuron structure and classification
focus: Locate receptive regions, trigger zone, conducting axon, and secretory terminal.
Distinguish structural neuron classes from sensory/motor/interneuron roles.
sections.text:
A neuron has a cell body or soma, dendrites, and an axon that can give off collaterals and end in axon terminals/synaptic knobs. Dendrites and soma commonly receive input; the axon initial segment commonly initiates action potentials; the axon carries them to terminals. Nissl substance consists of rough ER/ribosomal material in the soma and dendrites, supporting protein synthesis. Mature neurons have limited cell-cycle reentry; simplistic claims that one missing organelle alone explains all inability to divide are incomplete.

Multipolar neurons have one axon and multiple dendrites and are common among CNS interneurons and somatic motor neurons. Bipolar neurons have one main dendritic and one axonal process, as in selected special-sensory pathways. Pseudounipolar sensory neurons have one process that splits into peripheral and central branches, with cell bodies in sensory ganglia.

Functional classification asks where information goes; structural classification asks about processes. They are related but not interchangeable. A damaged axon may regenerate under favorable PNS conditions if its cell body survives; extensive cell-body injury is more likely to destroy the neuron. CNS regeneration is far more restricted. Axonal transport depends on cytoskeletal tracks and moves organelles/materials between soma and terminals.

sections.title: Glia, myelin, gray matter, and white matter
focus: Compare Schwann cells with oligodendrocytes and distinguish the four CNS glial types.
Myelin explains white matter and supports saltatory conduction.
sections.text:
CNS astrocytes regulate extracellular conditions and support the blood-brain barrier; the barrier's restrictive seal primarily depends on specialized endothelial tight junctions. Oligodendrocytes myelinate segments of multiple CNS axons. Microglia provide immune surveillance and phagocytic functions. Ependymal cells line ventricles and the spinal central canal; specialized associated cells participate in cerebrospinal fluid production at choroid plexuses.

In the PNS, Schwann cells support axons and each forms one myelin segment around one axon. Satellite cells surround cell bodies in peripheral ganglia. Small unmyelinated axons can still be supported within Schwann cell grooves without a thick multilayer myelin sheath. Nodes of Ranvier are gaps between myelin segments where ion channels support action potential regeneration.

White matter contains many myelinated axons; gray matter contains neuronal cell bodies, dendrites, synapses, and less-myelinated processes. Location differs: spinal gray matter is central, while cerebral cortical gray matter lies superficially with deeper gray nuclei. Myelin increases electrical insulation and speeds conduction; damage disrupts signaling. Glia are active regulators rather than merely passive packing material.
