sections.title: Resting potential and graded signals
focus: Distinguish maintained ion gradients from moment-to-moment channel currents.
Depolarization approaches zero; hyperpolarization becomes more negative.
sections.text:
Membrane potential is voltage across a cell membrane. A typical resting neuron is about −70 mV inside relative to outside, although values vary. Potassium is relatively concentrated inside and sodium outside. Selective permeability, especially potassium leak conductance, produces much of the resting voltage. The sodium–potassium pump maintains concentration gradients by moving three Na+ outward and two K+ inward per ATP.

Depolarization makes the membrane less negative; hyperpolarization makes it more negative. Local graded potentials vary in size, can decay with distance, and may be excitatory or inhibitory. Excitatory postsynaptic potentials often bring a trigger region closer to threshold; inhibitory effects can oppose firing. A subthreshold depolarization can facilitate a later response without itself becoming an action potential.

Temporal summation combines closely spaced signals from one input; spatial summation combines inputs at different locations. Whether threshold is reached depends on their integrated effect at the trigger region. The pump does not suddenly create each action potential on its own, and a resting neuron is not electrically uncharged. Voltage is a difference in charge distribution across a very thin membrane boundary.

sections.title: Action potentials and conduction
focus: Sodium influx depolarizes; potassium efflux repolarizes.
Predict conduction speed from myelination and diameter.
sections.text:
When a trigger region reaches threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open rapidly and sodium enters, driving depolarization. Sodium channels then inactivate while voltage-gated potassium channels open more slowly; potassium leaves, producing repolarization and often a brief after-hyperpolarization. Channels recover as membrane voltage returns toward resting conditions. Exact threshold and peak values vary among neurons.

An action potential is all-or-none once initiated in a healthy axon segment; greater stimulus strength is usually represented by firing frequency and recruited neurons rather than a taller action potential in the same axon. The absolute refractory period prevents another action potential during sodium-channel unavailability; the relative refractory period requires a stronger stimulus.

Local currents depolarize adjacent membrane, regenerating the signal along an unmyelinated axon. In a myelinated axon, current spreads rapidly beneath myelin and action potentials regenerate at nodes: saltatory conduction. Large diameter reduces internal resistance and generally increases speed; myelination also increases speed. The action potential normally travels from trigger zone to terminals because preceding membrane is refractory, not because sodium ions themselves race the entire axon length.

sections.title: Chemical synapses and neurotransmitter effects
focus: Trace calcium-triggered exocytosis and receptor-dependent postsynaptic response.
Explain transmitter removal and distinguish convergence from divergence.
sections.text:
At a chemical synapse, an arriving action potential opens voltage-gated calcium channels in the presynaptic terminal. Calcium entry triggers vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter exocytosis. Transmitter diffuses across the cleft, binds postsynaptic receptors, and changes channel or signaling activity. It does not cross as an intact action potential. Directionality follows polarized release and receptor machinery.

Acetylcholine acts at neuromuscular junctions and many autonomic synapses. Glutamate is a major excitatory CNS transmitter; GABA is a major inhibitory one. Glycine commonly mediates spinal inhibition. Dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin modulate selected pathways. Effects depend on receptor subtype and target, so a transmitter is not universally excitatory in every tissue. Endorphins and enkephalins are neuropeptides involved in pain modulation.

Signals end through enzymatic breakdown, reuptake, or diffusion. Acetylcholinesterase breaks down acetylcholine; reuptake transporters remove many monoamines. Drugs can alter synthesis, release, breakdown, transporters, or receptors. Disorders can involve transmitter pathways, but statements that one transmitter alone fully explains every case are oversimplifications. Convergence brings several inputs to one neuron; divergence distributes one input to several targets. Neuronal pools integrate information through interconnected circuits.

chapters.title: Nervous System II: Divisions
chapters.intro: Map protective structures, brain regions, spinal pathways, reflexes, peripheral nerves, and autonomic control.

sections.title: Meninges, ventricles, and cerebrospinal fluid
focus: Locate the CSF-filled subarachnoid space and trace ventricular circulation.
Distinguish spinal epidural space from subarachnoid space.
sections.text:
Bone, meninges, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and selective vascular barriers protect the CNS. Dura mater is outermost, arachnoid mater lies beneath, and pia mater closely follows the neural surface. Cranial dura has periosteal and meningeal layers that form dural venous sinuses where separated; spinal dura has a real epidural space outside it containing fat and vessels. An epidural injection is not intended for the CSF-filled subarachnoid space.

The subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia contains CSF. Ventricles and the spinal central canal are lined by ependymal cells. Choroid plexuses produce much CSF. Classical circulation proceeds lateral ventricles → interventricular foramina → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → apertures → subarachnoid spaces. Classical reabsorption involves arachnoid granulations into venous sinuses; additional lymphatic drainage pathways also contribute.

CSF provides buoyancy, cushioning, and a regulated fluid environment. It is not confined to a subdural space. Meningitis is inflammation of meninges and can have different causes. Obstructed circulation can enlarge ventricles. When explaining protection, separate the bony enclosure, meningeal layers, fluid spaces, and endothelial blood-brain barrier rather than calling them one structure.

sections.title: Spinal cord, roots, and tracts
focus: Dorsal root is sensory; ventral root is motor; spinal nerves and rami are mixed.
Differentiate gray horns from white columns and ascending from descending pathways.
sections.text:
The adult spinal cord extends from the medulla through the vertebral canal, usually ending around L1–L2 at the conus medullaris. Roots descending below form the cauda equina; the filum terminale contributes anchoring. Cervical and lumbar enlargements serve limb innervation. There are 31 spinal nerve pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal.

Central H-shaped gray matter forms dorsal and ventral horns, with lateral horns prominent at selected levels. Surrounding white matter forms columns containing tracts. A horn is gray matter; a column is white matter. Dorsal roots carry sensory input, with sensory cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia. Ventral roots carry motor output. Their union forms a mixed spinal nerve, whose dorsal and ventral rami are also mixed.

Ascending tracts carry sensory information toward the brain; descending tracts carry motor-related commands. Tracts have organized origins, destinations, and crossing patterns. Lesion effects depend on level, modality, completeness, and where pathways cross. A complete thoracic cord interruption can affect function below the lesion while sparing pathways entering above it; it does not mean every sensory structure in the body is lost. Central canal contains CSF.

sections.title: Reflex arcs and integrated responses
focus: Trace the five components of a reflex and distinguish monosynaptic from polysynaptic circuits.
A spindle monitors muscle length, not simply tendon tension.
sections.text:
A reflex arc includes receptor → sensory neuron → integration center → motor neuron → effector. A spinal interneuron can relay and modify the signal, but a monosynaptic stretch reflex directly links sensory and motor neurons at its central synapse. Do not require an interneuron in every reflex arc.

Muscle spindle receptors detect stretch in intrafusal fibers. Stretch-related sensory input excites motor neurons to the same muscle and, through inhibitory interneurons, reduces antagonist activity. Withdrawal reflexes use multiple synapses and can recruit several muscles. A crossed extensor response supports the opposite limb while one withdraws. The brain receives information and can modulate reflex activity, even when initiation precedes conscious perception.

Follow each neuron separately: local input reaches a trigger region, an action potential travels along that neuron's axon, and transmitter crosses a chemical synapse to the next cell. At the skeletal neuromuscular junction, the motor neuron activates the muscle fiber through acetylcholine. The sensory axon does not simply become a motor axon midway through the spinal cord. Reflex pathways are useful examples of the nervous system's sensory, integrative, and motor functions working together.

Pathway: Receptor (Detect stimulus) → Sensory neuron (Afferent input) → Spinal integration (Direct or interneuronal) → Motor neuron (Efferent output) → Effector (Produce response)

sections.title: Cerebral cortex, lobes, and association
focus: Associate frontal with planning/motor, parietal with somatic sensation, temporal with hearing, occipital with vision.
Cortex is gray matter; deeper pathways include white matter and gray nuclei.
sections.text:
The cerebrum has two hemispheres connected in part by the corpus callosum. Gyri are ridges, sulci grooves, and fissures deeper divisions. The cerebral cortex is superficial gray matter covering internal white matter and deeper gray nuclei. Major lobes include frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, and insula; the sphenoid is a skull bone, not a cerebral lobe.

The frontal lobe includes primary motor cortex and prefrontal regions contributing planning, judgment, and problem solving. Primary somatosensory cortex lies in the parietal lobe. Occipital regions process vision; temporal regions include auditory processing and important memory functions. Gustatory cortex involves insula and frontal operculum, rather than a simple universal tongue-to-parietal-lobe map. Language networks commonly show left dominance, but lateralization varies and both hemispheres cooperate.

Association regions integrate and interpret information beyond primary input/output. Memory consolidation stabilizes information over time and depends on distributed networks, including medial temporal structures. Basal nuclei help select and regulate movement; they are not the same as peripheral ganglia. An electroencephalogram (EEG) records patterns of electrical activity from scalp electrodes and does not directly photograph thoughts.

sections.title: Diencephalon, brainstem, cerebellum, and networks
focus: Separate thalamic relay from hypothalamic homeostasis.
Identify midbrain, pons, medulla, and cerebellar coordination roles.
sections.text:
The thalamus relays and processes much sensory input to cortex, with olfaction as a classic exception to an obligatory initial thalamic relay. The hypothalamus coordinates temperature, appetite, thirst, autonomic activity, endocrine signaling, and circadian functions. These diencephalic regions differ in role despite their close location.

The brainstem consists of midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata. The midbrain includes visual/auditory orienting circuits and motor pathways. The pons connects regions and contributes to respiratory pattern modulation; older terminology includes the pontine pneumotaxic area. The medulla contains critical cardiovascular and respiratory circuits and continues into the spinal cord near the foramen magnum.

The cerebellum compares intended and actual movement and helps coordinate timing, balance, posture, motor learning, and muscle tone. It does not initiate every conscious decision. The reticular formation contributes arousal, attention, and motor/autonomic regulation. Limbic networks contribute emotion, motivation, and memory, rather than existing as one isolated emotion organ. Predict functional effects by the affected circuit: coordination deficits differ from loss of frontal planning or a primary visual deficit.

sections.title: Cranial nerves and peripheral nerve organization
focus: Know cranial nerve numbers, names, sensory/motor categories, and major actions.
Compare endoneurium, perineurium, epineurium and four major plexuses.
sections.text:
A peripheral nerve contains axons with connective tissue coverings: endoneurium around individual fibers, perineurium around fascicles, and epineurium around the whole nerve. Sensory nerves carry afferent fibers, motor nerves efferent fibers, and mixed nerves both. The 12 cranial nerve pairs have distinct functions:

| Number/name | Category | Major function |
|---|---|---|
| I Olfactory | Sensory | Smell |
| II Optic | Sensory | Vision |
| III Oculomotor | Motor | Most eye movements, pupil constriction |
| IV Trochlear | Motor | Superior oblique eye muscle |
| V Trigeminal | Mixed | Facial sensation and chewing |
| VI Abducens | Motor | Lateral rectus eye muscle |
| VII Facial | Mixed | Facial expression, anterior tongue taste, selected glands |
| VIII Vestibulocochlear | Sensory | Hearing and equilibrium |
| IX Glossopharyngeal | Mixed | Posterior tongue taste/sensation, swallowing contributions |
| X Vagus | Mixed | Visceral sensation and parasympathetic output; pharyngeal/laryngeal functions |
| XI Accessory | Motor | Sternocleidomastoid/trapezius |
| XII Hypoglossal | Motor | Tongue movement |

Spinal ventral rami form cervical, brachial, lumbar, and sacral plexuses; thoracic rami largely remain segmental intercostal nerves. The cervical plexus contributes the phrenic nerve to the diaphragm; brachial serves upper limbs, lumbar and sacral serve lower-body regions. A plexus redistributes fibers, not neuron cell bodies.

sections.title: Somatic and autonomic motor pathways
focus: Somatic output uses one neuron; typical autonomic output uses a two-neuron chain.
Compare thoracolumbar sympathetic with craniosacral parasympathetic origins.
sections.text:
A somatic motor neuron extends from CNS to skeletal muscle, releasing acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. A typical autonomic pathway uses two neurons: a preganglionic neuron with cell body in CNS synapses in a peripheral autonomic ganglion with a postganglionic neuron that supplies smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, or glands.

Sympathetic output is thoracolumbar, approximately T1–L2. Preganglionic fibers commonly are shorter and postganglionic longer; ganglia lie in sympathetic chains or prevertebral locations. Parasympathetic output is craniosacral through selected cranial nerves and sacral segments S2–S4; preganglionic fibers commonly are long and terminal ganglia lie near/in target organs.

Sympathetic activity mobilizes resources during challenge, often increasing heart rate and redirecting circulation. Parasympathetic activity supports functions such as digestion and energy conservation. Both are active in normal regulation and can have complementary as well as opposing effects. Sympathetic fibers entering a chain ganglion may synapse at that level, ascend/descend before synapsing, or pass to prevertebral ganglia. White rami carry preganglionic traffic at thoracolumbar levels; gray rami distribute postganglionic fibers back to spinal nerves.

sections.title: Autonomic transmitters, receptors, and disorders
focus: Trace transmitters and receptor classes at ganglia and targets, including sweat gland exceptions.
Distinguish demyelinating, vascular, degenerative, and neuromuscular mechanisms.
sections.text:
Both sympathetic and parasympathetic preganglionic neurons release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors in autonomic ganglia. Parasympathetic postganglionic neurons generally release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors. Most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine onto adrenergic alpha or beta receptors. An important exception is sympathetic innervation of eccrine sweat glands, which is cholinergic. The adrenal medulla receives preganglionic input and releases catecholamines into blood.

Cholinergic means using acetylcholine; adrenergic means using norepinephrine/epinephrine signaling. Receptor subtype determines response: a transmitter can excite one target and inhibit another. Do not label acetylcholine universally inhibitory or every sympathetic effector adrenergic.

Neurological disorders affect different structures. Multiple sclerosis involves CNS demyelination; Parkinson disease involves loss of dopaminergic neurons in movement circuits; Alzheimer disease is a neurodegenerative disorder affecting cognition; epilepsy involves abnormal network activity; stroke involves disrupted brain perfusion or bleeding. Poliomyelitis can injure motor neurons, myasthenia gravis impairs neuromuscular transmission, meningitis affects meninges, and traumatic cord damage interrupts pathways. These are mechanism distinctions, not diagnostic criteria. The source exam's disease matching requires instructor confirmation where its descriptions or diagrams are incomplete.

sections.title: Comparing neurological disorder mechanisms
focus: Differentiate myelin, vascular, developmental, infectious, degenerative, and CSF-flow mechanisms.
A disorder label alone does not describe all causes or manifestations.
sections.text:
| Condition | Mechanism to distinguish |
|---|---|
| Multiple sclerosis | Immune-mediated CNS myelin damage and other neural injury |
| Parkinson disease | Degeneration involving nigrostriatal dopamine pathways and movement circuits |
| Poliomyelitis | Poliovirus can injure motor neurons, including anterior horn neurons |
| Cerebral palsy | Movement/posture disorders associated with a nonprogressive disturbance of the developing brain; manifestations can change over time |
| Stroke | Brain injury from vascular occlusion or hemorrhage |
| Epilepsy | Predisposition to recurrent unprovoked seizures involving abnormal neural activity |
| Hydrocephalus | Abnormal CSF dynamics associated with ventricular enlargement |
| Meningitis | Inflammation of the meningeal coverings from infectious or other causes |
| Rabies | Viral infection affecting the nervous system and causing encephalitis |

Match disorders to the affected substrate rather than treating all neurological problems as identical transmitter deficiencies. A demyelinating process differs from impaired perfusion, loss of a particular neuron population, or abnormal CSF circulation. Myasthenia gravis affects neuromuscular signaling and is distinct from demyelination. Rabies after symptom onset is nearly always fatal, but absolute claims omit exceptional reports; prevention and urgent management belong to clinical/public-health guidance rather than this practice guide. These descriptions support learning and are not diagnostic or treatment instructions.

chapters.title: Nervous System III: Senses
chapters.intro: Trace somatic and special sensory signals from stimulus transduction to perception.

sections.title: Receptors, sensation, perception, and adaptation
focus: Distinguish detection/transduction from conscious interpretation.
Classify receptors by stimulus and compare adaptation patterns.
sections.text:
A sensory receptor converts stimulus energy into a cellular signal, a process called transduction. Sensation includes detection of a stimulus and its representation in neural pathways; perception is conscious interpretation. Most conscious somatic perception involves cerebral cortex, while many sensory signals support reflexes without becoming conscious.

Mechanoreceptors respond to deformation, thermoreceptors to temperature, chemoreceptors to chemicals, photoreceptors to light, and nociceptors to potentially damaging stimuli. Proprioceptors monitor position and movement. Receptor location can be exteroceptive, interoceptive, or proprioceptive. Classification by stimulus differs from classification by location.

Adaptation is reduced response during sustained stimulation. Rapidly adapting receptors emphasize change; slowly adapting receptors retain information about sustained conditions. Nociceptors generally adapt little or slowly and can sensitize during inflammation; the course shorthand that pain receptors never adapt should not be treated as a universal physiological law. Stimulus intensity can be encoded through firing rate and recruitment, rather than changing every action potential's amplitude. Receptor identity and pathway determine modality, so the same electrical signaling language can represent different experiences depending on where it originates.

sections.title: Somatic sensation, pain, and proprioception
focus: Contrast muscle length sensing by spindles with tension sensing by tendon organs.
Explain referred pain and separate fast/slow fibers from acute/chronic duration.
sections.text:
Somatic senses include touch/pressure, temperature, pain, and position/movement. Free endings detect several modalities including pain and temperature. Tactile corpuscles detect changing light touch; lamellated corpuscles detect vibration and changing deep pressure. Merkel-associated receptors and other endings add sustained touch information. Warm and cold receptor populations respond over different temperature ranges; extreme temperatures can activate nociceptors.

Fast, sharp pain commonly uses myelinated A-delta fibers; slower, diffuse pain commonly uses unmyelinated C fibers. Acute versus chronic pain also describes duration and clinical context, so those categories are not identical to fast versus slow fiber classes. Referred pain is perceived away from its source, in part because visceral and somatic signals converge on shared central circuits. Endogenous opioid systems can modulate pain transmission.

Muscle spindles detect muscle length and stretch, while Golgi tendon organs monitor tension near muscle-tendon junctions. Their information helps coordinate posture and force. A rhizotomy interrupts selected nerve-root input and may reduce selected pain transmission but also risks sensory/motor consequences depending on the target; it is not a general cure or a treatment recommendation here. Always distinguish receptor location, stimulus, and central interpretation.

🖼 Figure — Referred Pain Chart (image)
Description: Conscious perception of visceral sensations map to specific regions of the body, as shown in this chart. Some sensations are felt locally, whereas others are perceived as affecting areas that are quite distant from the involved organ.

sections.title: Olfaction and gustation
focus: Trace smell through receptor cilia, bulb, and tract.
Identify five taste qualities and cranial nerves VII, IX, and X without a rigid tongue map.
sections.text:
Olfaction detects odorants dissolved in mucus around olfactory receptor neuron cilia in the superior nasal region. Axons pass through the cribriform plate to olfactory bulbs, then travel through tracts to primary olfactory and associated limbic/cortical areas. Smell has distinctive early pathways that do not require the usual initial thalamic relay before primary cortex. Adaptation and central habituation reduce awareness of some persistent odors.

Taste receptor cells in taste buds respond to dissolved substances at apical microvilli. Major taste qualities include sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami. Different qualities are not confined to four exclusive tongue zones; the traditional rigid tongue map is inaccurate. Taste buds are associated with selected tongue papillae and other oral/pharyngeal sites.

Taste signals travel mainly through facial nerve VII from anterior tongue, glossopharyngeal IX from posterior tongue, and vagus X from selected epiglottic/pharyngeal regions. Brainstem relays project through thalamus to gustatory cortex in insula/frontal operculum. Trigeminal V carries much oral somatic sensation, including texture and irritation, rather than the principal taste pathway. Flavor combines taste, smell, texture, temperature, and experience. Loss of smell can therefore greatly reduce flavor even with functioning taste receptors.

sections.title: External, middle, and inner ear
focus: Trace auricle → canal → tympanic membrane → ossicles → oval window.
Distinguish middle-ear air space, perilymph, and endolymph.
sections.text:
The external ear includes auricle and auditory canal, directing sound toward the tympanic membrane. The middle ear is an air-filled cavity containing malleus, incus, and stapes. The stapes transmits vibration to the oval window. The auditory/pharyngotympanic tube connects middle ear to nasopharynx and supports pressure equalization. The round window permits pressure displacement within cochlear fluids.

The inner ear includes bony labyrinth surrounding membranous labyrinth. Perilymph occupies spaces outside the membranous labyrinth; endolymph fills it. The cochlea supports hearing, while vestibule and semicircular canals support equilibrium. Utricle and saccule are membranous structures within the vestibule; semicircular ducts lie within bony canals.

Middle-ear muscles reduce ossicular movement during the acoustic/tympanic reflex. This can attenuate selected sustained sounds but has latency and does not reliably protect against all sudden loud impulses. Conductive hearing loss interferes with mechanical transfer; sensorineural loss involves hair cells, neural pathways, or related sensory structures. Age-related hearing decline is often called presbycusis. Keep the fluid-filled inner ear separate from the air-filled middle-ear space.

sections.title: Cochlear transduction and auditory pathways
focus: Locate scalae, basilar membrane, hair cells, and tectorial membrane.
Trace mechanical vibration to CN VIII signaling and temporal cortical processing.
sections.text:
The cochlea contains scala vestibuli and scala tympani with perilymph, and a cochlear duct/scala media containing endolymph. Vestibular membrane separates scala vestibuli from the duct; basilar membrane separates the duct from scala tympani. The spiral organ or organ of Corti rests on the basilar membrane; hair cells interact mechanically with surrounding structures including the tectorial membrane.

Sound vibration moves the oval window, generating fluid pressure waves. Basilar membrane movement bends hair-cell stereocilia, opening mechanically sensitive channels and changing transmitter release onto sensory fibers. Cochlear hair cells are mechanoreceptors, not photoreceptors. High frequencies preferentially excite the stiffer cochlear base; lower frequencies reach maximal displacement nearer the apex.

Signals travel in the cochlear branch of cranial nerve VIII through brainstem auditory relays, midbrain inferior colliculus, thalamic medial geniculate region, and auditory cortex in temporal lobe. Central pathways contain bilateral connections, so a single central lesion does not always cause simple complete deafness in one ear. Distinguish mechanical conduction of sound energy from neural conduction after transduction, and distinguish a cochlear hair cell from an axon in the auditory nerve.

sections.title: Vestibular equilibrium and head movement
focus: Maculae detect gravity/linear acceleration; cristae detect angular acceleration.
Trace vestibular input through CN VIII and central balance/gaze circuits.
sections.text:
The utricle and saccule contain maculae with hair cells embedded in a gelatinous otolithic membrane containing calcium carbonate otoconia. Gravity and linear acceleration shift this mass, bending sensory projections. These structures inform the CNS about head orientation and linear movement, traditionally grouped under static equilibrium.

Each semicircular duct has an enlarged ampulla containing a crista ampullaris. Hair cells project into a gelatinous cupula. Angular acceleration causes relative endolymph movement that deflects the cupula. The three canal orientations support detection of rotation in different planes. At constant prolonged rotation, responses adapt; abrupt stopping can produce a transient opposite sensation.

Vestibular fibers travel through cranial nerve VIII to vestibular nuclei and cerebellar circuits, with connections to eye-movement, postural, and conscious perceptual pathways. The vestibulo-ocular reflex stabilizes gaze during head movement. Balance also relies on vision and proprioception, not inner-ear signals alone. Differentiate macular otolith displacement during linear acceleration from ampullary cupula bending during angular acceleration; both use hair-cell mechanotransduction but are specialized for different stimuli.

sections.title: Eye protection, tunics, and chambers
focus: Identify fibrous, vascular, and neural tunics and their components.
Distinguish aqueous-filled chambers from the vitreous cavity.
sections.text:
Eyebrows, lids, lashes, conjunctiva, extraocular muscles, and the lacrimal apparatus protect and position the eye. Tears lubricate and contain substances including lysozyme, an enzyme that helps disrupt selected bacterial cell walls. Conjunctiva lines eyelids and covers anterior sclera but does not cover the transparent cornea as a separate conjunctival layer.

The fibrous tunic consists of sclera and transparent cornea. The vascular tunic includes choroid, ciliary body, and iris. The neural tunic includes retina. The pupil is an opening in the iris, not a solid lens. Cornea and lens refract light; iris changes the aperture; choroid supports retinal metabolism and absorbs stray light.

The anterior cavity contains aqueous humor, with an anterior chamber between cornea and iris and a posterior chamber between iris and lens. The much larger posterior/vitreous cavity lies behind the lens and contains vitreous humor. Do not confuse posterior chamber with posterior cavity. Aqueous humor circulates from the ciliary region through the pupil and drains at the anterior chamber angle. An ophthalmoscope permits inspection of internal structures such as retina and optic disc.

Description: Study the labeled structures in Eye in The Orbit. The accompanying section explains their relationships: Identify fibrous, vascular, and neural tunics and their components. Distinguish aqueous-filled chambers from the vitreous cavity.

sections.title: Accommodation, photoreceptors, and visual pathways
focus: Near focus: ciliary contraction, reduced zonular tension, rounder lens.
Rods favor dim light; cones favor color/acuity; ganglion axons form CN II.
sections.text:
For near focusing, ciliary muscle contracts, zonular/suspensory tension decreases, and the lens becomes rounder with greater refractive power. For distant focus, ciliary muscle relaxes, zonular tension increases, and the lens flattens. Accommodation changes lens shape rather than moving the retina forward. Cataract is lens clouding; presbyopia is reduced near accommodation with age. They are different processes.

Rods are highly sensitive in dim light and contribute limited color/detail discrimination. Cones support color and high acuity in brighter light and are concentrated in the fovea. The optic disc lacks photoreceptors where retinal axons exit, creating the physiological blind spot. Light passes cornea → aqueous humor → pupil → lens → vitreous → retina. Retinal signaling involves photoreceptors, bipolar cells, and ganglion cells; ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve.

At the optic chiasm, nasal retinal fibers cross while temporal fibers remain ipsilateral. Pathways continue through optic tracts, thalamic lateral geniculate relays, optic radiations, and occipital visual cortex. Pupil reflex pathways branch to other circuits. Explain the difference between the light path through transparent tissues and the neural path after retinal transduction; photons do not travel along the optic nerve as the visual signal.

Description: Study the labeled structures in Rods and Cones. The accompanying section explains their relationships: Near focus: ciliary contraction, reduced zonular tension, rounder lens. Rods favor dim light; cones favor color/acuity; ganglion axons form CN II.

sections.title: Visual pigments, adaptation, and sensory aging
focus: Light hyperpolarizes photoreceptors and changes their transmitter release.
Distinguish presbyopia, cataract, glaucoma, retinal disease, and age-related hearing loss.
sections.text:
In darkness, cGMP-gated channels help maintain a relatively depolarized photoreceptor and ongoing transmitter release. Light changes retinal within an opsin pigment, triggering a signaling cascade that reduces cGMP and closes channels. Photoreceptors hyperpolarize and change glutamate release. This receptor potential affects bipolar and ganglion circuits; the photoreceptor itself does not send a conventional axonal action potential down the optic nerve.

Rhodopsin is the rod pigment. Three cone classes have overlapping sensitivities commonly described as short-, medium-, and long-wavelength sensitive; they do not correspond to rigid single-color detectors. Dark adaptation increases sensitivity over time, while adaptation to bright conditions changes photoreceptor and neural responses. Binocular disparity gives the brain one cue for depth perception; vision uses additional depth cues as well.

Presbyopia reduces near accommodation as lens properties change. Cataract clouds the lens. Glaucoma involves optic nerve damage and is often associated with elevated intraocular pressure, though pressure alone does not define every case. Retinal detachment separates neural retina from its supporting tissues. Macular degeneration affects central retinal function; floaters reflect vitreous-related shadows and have different causes. Hearing changes with age can involve cochlear and neural processes; tinnitus is perceived sound without an equivalent external sound source and is not synonymous with every hearing loss.

Primary-source reading: NIDCD on age-related hearing loss and NIDCD on taste and flavor.
