practice.concept: Structure, function, and levels of organization
practice.question: A lung sample contains epithelium, connective tissue, vessels, and nerves cooperating in gas exchange. What makes the intact lung an organ?
options: Multiple tissue types coordinate a specialized function.
The presence of several organs makes the lung an entire organism.
Only one tissue type defines every organ.
An organ and an organelle are equivalent organizational levels.
practice.answer: Multiple tissue types coordinate a specialized function.
practice.explanation: An organ integrates several tissues; each contributes to the coordinated whole.

practice.question: Absorbed amino acids are joined into a cell's new transport proteins. Which process specifically describes incorporating these building materials?
options: Digestion of dietary protein into smaller units.
practice.explanation: Assimilation incorporates absorbed material into living structures rather than merely moving nutrients across the gut.

practice.question: A breathing model works only when pressure differs between two compartments. Which survival requirement is being illustrated as a physical condition?
practice.explanation: Pressure gradients support ventilation and other physiological flows, even though pressure is not a chemical nutrient.

practice.question: A temperature control loop activates a fan after warming, then reduces fan output as temperature returns toward its target range. What feature identifies negative feedback?
options: The response amplifies the original temperature error.
The response reduces the original error.
The system operates without any sensor input.
The effector acts independently of the regulated variable.
practice.answer: The response reduces the original error.
practice.explanation: Negative feedback counteracts deviations; its components can adjust response strength as the error changes.

practice.question: A learner says homeostasis means every internal measurement remains perfectly constant. Which revision is best?
options: Regulation operates only after every organ has stopped functioning.
All variables are held at exact unchanging values.
Homeostasis concerns external weather but no internal measurements.
Variables fluctuate within regulated ranges while mechanisms counter disturbances.
practice.answer: Variables fluctuate within regulated ranges while mechanisms counter disturbances.
practice.explanation: Homeostasis is dynamic regulation, not a frozen internal state.

practice.question: A teaching instrument enters a fluid space between the heart's covering and its sac lining. Which serous space is modeled?
practice.explanation: The pericardial cavity is the potential space between serous pericardial layers.

practice.question: A model shows a kidney behind the parietal peritoneal lining rather than suspended within its sac. Which location term fits?
practice.explanation: Retroperitoneal structures lie posterior to the peritoneal lining.

practice.question: A student traces metabolic wastes from tissue blood into urine. Which system directly forms the urine?
options: The skeletal system through marrow filtration.
The digestive system through bile secretion.
The reproductive system through gamete ducts.
practice.explanation: Kidneys filter and modify tubular fluid to form urine; ureters, bladder, and urethra transport/store/eliminate it.

practice.question: Two sensors lie on opposite forearms. Which relationship describes their sides?
practice.explanation: Contralateral means opposite sides; ipsilateral means the same side.

practice.question: A section divides a cylindrical limb perpendicular to its long axis. Which description fits the section relative to that limb?
options: A tangential surface view that does not cross the limb.
A section parallel to the limb's long axis.
practice.explanation: A cross-section is perpendicular to the long axis of the object being described.

practice.question: A neutral atom has 11 protons and loses one electron. What changes while elemental identity is preserved?
options: Its mass number must fall by one neutron.
Its atomic number falls by one.
Its charge becomes −1 while proton number stays fixed.
Its charge becomes +1 while atomic number stays 11.
practice.answer: Its charge becomes +1 while atomic number stays 11.
practice.explanation: Ionization changes electrons and charge, while proton number defines the element.

practice.question: Two samples have equal proton numbers but different mass numbers. What difference most directly accounts for the mass numbers?
options: A change only in the number of valence electrons.
A different bonding partner with identical nuclear composition.
A different proton number defining a new element.
practice.explanation: Mass number counts protons plus neutrons; equal protons with different mass numbers imply different neutron counts.

practice.question: A molecule carries separated partial positive and partial negative regions caused by unequal electron sharing. Which description fits?
options: Complete electron transfer producing separated whole ions only.
Perfectly equal electron sharing in every bond.
A change in neutron number without any electron interaction.
practice.explanation: Unequal sharing in polar bonds produces partial charges; molecular geometry determines the overall dipole.

practice.question: Two smaller molecules join and the product-forming process removes water components. How is this relationship described?
options: Dissociation of an ionic salt in water.
practice.explanation: Dehydration synthesis joins subunits with removal of water; hydrolysis reverses many such linkages.

practice.question: A glucose solution dissolves readily yet does not supply ions in the same way as a salt solution. What distinction matters?
options: Dissolution does not always mean ion formation.
Every dissolved substance must separate into ions.
A dissolved glucose molecule necessarily becomes a cation.
practice.answer: Dissolution does not always mean ion formation.
practice.explanation: Some polar nonelectrolytes dissolve without dissociating into mobile ions.

practice.question: A buffer receives a modest acid load. What response helps limit the pH fall?
options: The buffer can absorb an unlimited acid load without changing pH.
The buffer prevents any chemistry from occurring.
The buffer amplifies the hydrogen ion rise.
A buffer component binds some added hydrogen ions.
practice.answer: A buffer component binds some added hydrogen ions.
practice.explanation: Reversible binding of hydrogen ions reduces the immediate free hydrogen change within buffer capacity.

practice.question: A label compares a plant glucose store with a liver glucose store. Which pairing is appropriate?
practice.explanation: Starch and glycogen are storage polysaccharides in plants and animals respectively.

practice.concept: Lipids: stored fuel, membranes, and signaling
practice.question: A membrane diagram includes a four-ring lipid that affects membrane properties and supplies precursors for hormones. Which molecule fits?
options: A phospholipid with two fatty acid tails.
practice.explanation: Cholesterol is a steroid lipid with structural and precursor roles.

practice.question: A protein combines several folded polypeptide subunits. Which structural level describes their association?
options: Tertiary structure of one chain alone.
practice.explanation: Quaternary structure refers to the organization of multiple polypeptide subunits.

practice.question: A molecule contains ribose, adenine, and three phosphates and is consumed during membrane pumping. Which role fits?
options: Long-term storage of inherited sequence in DNA.
practice.explanation: ATP's structure supports rapid energy transfer; it is not the principal long-term fuel store.

practice.concept: The fluid mosaic membrane and cell junctions
practice.question: A small nonpolar gas crosses a lipid bilayer without a carrier. Which property explains the route?
options: All solutes cross the lipid region equally regardless of chemistry.
Its chemistry permits diffusion through the hydrophobic membrane interior.
Its entry necessarily requires ATP-driven uphill transport.
Its charge requires a voltage-gated ion channel for this route.
practice.answer: Its chemistry permits diffusion through the hydrophobic membrane interior.
practice.explanation: Small nonpolar molecules can dissolve in and diffuse across lipid relatively readily.

practice.concept: The fluid mosaic membrane and cell junctions
practice.question: A tissue must prevent material from leaking between neighboring cells. Which junction best supports this requirement?
practice.explanation: Tight junctions form selective seals between adjacent cells rather than communication channels.

practice.concept: Organelles and the protein shipping pathway
practice.question: A cell accumulates undigested worn organelles because acidic digestive compartments malfunction. Which structure is implicated?
options: Golgi sorting vesicle as the main acidic digestive compartment.
practice.explanation: Lysosomal enzymes support breakdown and recycling of cellular material.

practice.question: An absorptive cell has many short actin-supported surface projections. What benefit do they provide?
options: Formation of the mitotic spindle through microtubules.
Movement of mucus along an airway by motile cilia.
practice.explanation: Microvilli amplify surface area for absorption rather than acting as motile cilia.

practice.question: A barrier becomes thicker while area and concentration difference remain unchanged. What happens to simple diffusion across it?
options: Diffusion rate generally increases with a longer path.
A thicker passive barrier automatically converts diffusion into primary active transport.
Thickness cannot affect diffusion under any conditions.
practice.explanation: Longer diffusion distance reduces flux under otherwise similar conditions.

practice.question: A cell swells in a bath and later ruptures. Which interpretation is consistent with a sustained osmotic effect?
options: The bath was effectively hypotonic to the cell.
The cell had lost water continuously to the bath.
The bath was isotonic with no sustained volume change.
practice.answer: The bath was effectively hypotonic to the cell.
practice.explanation: A hypotonic environment promotes net water entry; excessive swelling can cause lysis.

practice.question: A membrane protein uses an existing sodium gradient to drive another solute uphill without hydrolyzing ATP at that carrier. Which category fits?
options: Primary active transport with direct ATP hydrolysis at that carrier.
Osmosis of water without solute coupling.
Facilitated diffusion of both solutes downhill independently.
practice.explanation: The carrier couples downhill ion movement to uphill solute transport; maintaining the gradient ultimately requires energy.

practice.question: A secretory vesicle merges with the cell surface and releases its contents outside. Which process occurred?
practice.explanation: Exocytosis is vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane and release of luminal contents.

practice.question: Two groups of chromosomes arrive at opposite poles and new nuclear envelopes form. Which mitotic stage is being modeled?
practice.explanation: Telophase includes reformation of daughter nuclei after chromosome separation.

practice.concept: Division control, stem cells, and cancer
practice.question: A localized tumor does not invade adjacent tissues or spread, yet compresses a nearby structure. Which statement is sound?
options: Every localized mass has already invaded all nearby tissues.
Benign masses cannot impair any adjacent structure.
A benign growth can still cause harm through location and compression.
A benign mass is defined by distant metastases.
practice.answer: A benign growth can still cause harm through location and compression.
practice.explanation: Benign tumors do not metastasize, but mechanical effects can still be important.

practice.question: Two reactions have the same energy difference with and without an enzyme, but one proceeds faster. What did the enzyme change?
options: The total amount of matter conserved in the reaction.
The equilibrium position of the reaction.
The overall energy difference between reactants and products.
practice.explanation: Catalysts lower the barrier to reaction without changing the overall thermodynamic difference.

practice.question: An inhibitor occupies a substrate-binding region and reduces productive substrate access. Which feature explains why the effect is selective?
options: All pathway enzymes share one identical active site.
Each enzyme binds every substrate equally.
Substrate fit depends only on substrate color.
Active-site interactions depend on molecular compatibility.
practice.answer: Active-site interactions depend on molecular compatibility.
practice.explanation: Enzyme specificity reflects shape and chemical interactions at binding/catalytic sites.

practice.question: A reduced carrier donates electrons to a membrane chain and becomes oxidized. Which description is accurate?
options: Oxidation requires loss of a neutron from the nucleus.
It becomes reduced during electron donation.
practice.explanation: Oxidation is electron loss; reduction is electron gain, whether or not oxygen is directly added.

practice.question: A pathway invests two ATP and later produces four ATP from one glucose. What is its net direct ATP yield?
practice.explanation: Net yield subtracts the ATP invested from the ATP produced.

practice.concept: Pyruvate oxidation, Krebs cycle, and electron transport
practice.question: A labeled acetyl group enters a mitochondrial cycle, while a four-carbon acceptor is regenerated. Which cycle is modeled?
practice.explanation: Acetyl-CoA contributes carbon to the citric acid cycle while oxaloacetate is regenerated.

practice.concept: Pyruvate oxidation, Krebs cycle, and electron transport
practice.question: A membrane becomes leaky to protons so they return without passing through ATP synthase. What is expected?
options: More ATP captured per oxygen without any proton gradient.
Less ATP capture despite possible continued electron transfer.
A growing proton gradient despite unrestricted proton return.
No effect because ATP synthase uses only direct phosphate transfer.
practice.answer: Less ATP capture despite possible continued electron transfer.
practice.explanation: Uncoupling dissipates the proton gradient and reduces its use for ATP synthesis.

practice.question: An amino acid contributes its carbon skeleton to energy pathways after its nitrogen group is removed. Which process is involved?
options: Direct transfer of the intact amino acid into DNA replication.
Phosphorylation of the amino group into ATP.
Conversion of every nitrogen atom directly to glucose carbon.
practice.explanation: Amino-group removal permits selected carbon skeletons to enter shared metabolic pathways while nitrogen requires handling.

practice.question: A model shows discontinuous short DNA segments later joined on one side of a replication fork. What explains the pattern?
options: DNA synthesis proceeds equally in both chemical directions.
The lagging strand is made only after cell division finishes.
Complementary pairing is absent on the lagging strand.
practice.explanation: DNA synthesis proceeds 5′ to 3′; fork geometry leads to discontinuous lagging-strand synthesis.

practice.concept: Transcription, translation, and the genetic code
practice.question: A ribosome reaches an in-frame termination codon. What normally follows?
options: Release of the completed polypeptide through termination machinery.
Addition of a stop amino acid by an ordinary tRNA.
Replication of the mRNA into chromosomal DNA.
Continued elongation through every stop codon.
practice.answer: Release of the completed polypeptide through termination machinery.
practice.explanation: Stop codons recruit termination factors rather than an ordinary aminoacyl-tRNA specifying another amino acid.

practice.concept: Transcription, translation, and the genetic code
practice.question: A DNA alteration changes one codon but leaves the encoded amino acid unchanged. What principle permits this?
options: Several codons can specify the same amino acid.
Every DNA sequence change necessarily changes its amino acid.
The codon is read using amino acid rather than nucleotide triplets.
A change in a codon cannot occur in a coding sequence.
practice.answer: Several codons can specify the same amino acid.
practice.explanation: Degeneracy of the genetic code permits some sequence changes without an amino acid substitution.

practice.concept: Four tissue classes and epithelial organization
practice.question: A stratified tissue has cuboidal basal cells and flattened surface cells. Which shape determines its epithelial name?
options: The shape of the underlying connective tissue cells.
The number of vessels in the underlying dermis.
The shape of the deepest basal cells.
practice.explanation: Stratified epithelia are named by their apical cell shape, so this arrangement is stratified squamous.

practice.question: An airway's cilia fail while mucus production continues. Which consequence follows directly?
options: Conversion of airway epithelium directly into cartilage.
More efficient mucus clearance despite immobile cilia.
Impaired movement of mucus and trapped particles.
Complete cessation of secretion by every goblet cell.
practice.answer: Impaired movement of mucus and trapped particles.
practice.explanation: Cilia move material along the airway surface; goblet-cell secretion alone does not provide clearance.

practice.question: A moist abrasion-prone lining has many layers but lacks a thick dead keratinized surface. Which tissue fits?
practice.explanation: Multiple layers resist abrasion, while nonkeratinized apical cells remain suited to moist surfaces.

practice.question: A gland releases a hormone without a duct into surrounding fluid for transport in blood. Which category fits?
options: A gland defined solely by an unbranched surface duct.
practice.explanation: Endocrine secretion uses interstitial fluid and circulation rather than a duct to a surface/lumen.

practice.concept: Connective tissue cells, fibers, and matrix
practice.question: A fiber stretches and returns toward its original length after unloading. Which matrix component best supplies this property?
options: Collagen fibers specialized mainly for tensile strength.
Reticular fibers as the main source of elastic recoil.
practice.explanation: Elastic fibers support recoil, whereas collagen chiefly provides tensile strength.

practice.concept: Loose, dense, and specialized connective tissues
practice.question: A support tissue must resist multidirectional pulling beneath epidermis. Which arrangement is appropriate?
options: Parallel collagen in dense regular tissue.
Avascular hyaline cartilage replacing all dermis.
Interwoven collagen in dense irregular tissue.
Sparse fibers in areolar tissue as the main tensile framework.
practice.answer: Interwoven collagen in dense irregular tissue.
practice.explanation: Dense irregular collagen networks distribute tensile resistance across multiple directions.

practice.concept: Loose, dense, and specialized connective tissues
practice.question: A tissue framework supports many mobile immune cells through a delicate branching fiber network. Which type fits?
practice.explanation: Reticular fibers provide supporting stroma in lymphoid organs and marrow.

practice.concept: Loose, dense, and specialized connective tissues
practice.question: A specimen contains erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets suspended in extracellular fluid. What explains its connective-tissue classification?
options: All connective tissue must have a mineralized matrix.
Its cells form one continuous tight epithelial sheet.
Its cells and fragments are suspended in a specialized liquid matrix.
practice.answer: Its cells and fragments are suspended in a specialized liquid matrix.
practice.explanation: Blood is a connective tissue with plasma as its liquid matrix.

practice.concept: Tissue membranes, muscle, and nervous tissue
practice.question: A ring of tissue narrows an intestinal lumen through gradual involuntary contractions. Which tissue is best suited to this visceral wall function?
practice.explanation: Smooth muscle is common in hollow-organ walls and lacks the striation pattern of skeletal/cardiac muscle.

practice.concept: Tissue membranes, muscle, and nervous tissue
practice.question: A covering consists of mesothelium over thin connective tissue and reduces friction around a ventral organ. Which membrane fits?
practice.explanation: Serous membranes combine mesothelium with connective tissue and provide lubricated organ surfaces.

practice.concept: Skin layers and their cell types
practice.question: A skin sample contains vascular collagen-rich connective tissue beneath an avascular epithelium. Which layer is collagen-rich and vascular?
practice.explanation: The dermis contains blood vessels and connective matrix; epidermis is avascular epithelium.

practice.concept: Skin layers and their cell types
practice.question: Keratinocytes move from a dividing basal population toward a shedding surface. What maintains normal thickness over time?
options: Permanent retention of every superficial cell.
Balanced production, differentiation, and cell loss.
Division of mature corneocytes as the only renewal source.
practice.answer: Balanced production, differentiation, and cell loss.
practice.explanation: Normal epidermal homeostasis coordinates basal production with surface shedding.

practice.concept: Dermal structure, sensation, and skin functions
practice.question: An instructor compares a superficial tactile corpuscle with a deep lamellated corpuscle. Which distinction is accurate?
options: They differ only in pigment production, not neural function.
They are both pain-specific free endings without encapsulation.
They occur at identical depths and detect exactly the same stimulus dynamics.
They occupy different depths and emphasize different mechanical stimulus features.
practice.answer: They occupy different depths and emphasize different mechanical stimulus features.
practice.explanation: Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles differ in location, encapsulation, and stimulus sensitivity.

practice.question: A hair shaft protrudes above the surface while its growing matrix remains deep in a follicle. What is true about the visible shaft?
options: Living smooth muscle fibers that directly raise the hair.
A layer of cells actively secreting melanin into blood.
It consists largely of dead keratinized cells.
Dividing basal matrix cells throughout the exposed shaft.
practice.answer: It consists largely of dead keratinized cells.
practice.explanation: Hair growth occurs in living follicular regions; the exposed shaft is keratinized material.

practice.question: A sebaceous gland empties oily product into a follicle. How does this differ from ordinary eccrine sweat release?
options: Sebaceous glands are primarily the body's evaporative cooling glands.
Sebaceous product includes whole-cell breakdown; eccrine product is released mainly by exocytosis.
Both release only water through the same duct type.
Eccrine glands use whole-cell breakdown while sebaceous glands use only exocytosis.
practice.answer: Sebaceous product includes whole-cell breakdown; eccrine product is released mainly by exocytosis.
practice.explanation: Holocrine sebaceous secretion differs from merocrine eccrine release.

practice.question: A warm hand is placed against a cooler metal surface and transfers heat by direct contact. Which transfer mode is emphasized?
practice.explanation: Conduction transfers thermal energy through physical contact.

practice.question: A person's skin blood flow increases in a cooler environment while core temperature is high. What is the likely heat-transfer effect?
options: No effect on thermal transfer because only sweating matters.
Reduced outward heat transfer solely because vessel diameter increased.
Greater transfer of heat from blood to the environment.
Guaranteed inward heat transfer regardless of environmental temperature.
practice.answer: Greater transfer of heat from blood to the environment.
practice.explanation: Cutaneous vasodilation commonly increases heat loss when environmental conditions permit outward transfer.

practice.question: A superficial skin color change results from a pigment produced in basal epidermal cells and transferred to keratinocytes. Which pigment fits?
practice.explanation: Melanocytes produce melanin and transfer pigment-containing material to surrounding epidermal cells.

practice.question: A deep wound fills with collagen-producing cells during repair. Which cell type is performing this matrix-building role?
practice.explanation: Fibroblasts produce connective matrix and collagen during repair and scar formation.

practice.question: A burn diagram reports affected surface percentage but omits depth. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The area percentage proves identical tissue depth.
A small area excludes full-thickness injury.
Area alone cannot establish which regenerative structures survived.
Area alone specifies the survival of all hair follicles.
practice.answer: Area alone cannot establish which regenerative structures survived.
practice.explanation: Depth and extent are separate dimensions; both influence physiological consequences and repair.

practice.question: A bone has a shaft with expanded ends and supports a limb lever. Which classification fits?
practice.explanation: Long bones have an elongated shaft and ends; classification is based on shape rather than absolute size alone.

practice.question: A learner labels the long central shaft separately from an end region. Which label belongs on the shaft?
practice.explanation: The diaphysis is the shaft of a long bone; epiphyses are its ends.

practice.question: A microscopic unit contains concentric lamellae around a vessel-bearing passage. Which structure is modeled?
practice.explanation: Compact bone osteons organize lamellae around central canals containing vessels and nerves.

practice.question: A learner describes mature bone cells communicating through small channels in a mineralized matrix. Which pairing is accurate?
options: Osteoblasts and medullary cavity as intercellular channels.
practice.explanation: Osteocytes reside in lacunae and communicate through canaliculi across bone matrix.

practice.concept: How Bones Grow in Length and Thickness
practice.question: A growth plate closes as cartilage is replaced by bone. Which type of growth is most directly limited afterward?
options: Further longitudinal growth at that plate.
practice.answer: Further longitudinal growth at that plate.
practice.explanation: Epiphyseal plates permit lengthening; closure limits additional longitudinal growth at that site.

practice.question: After a fracture callus forms, excess bony material is removed during remodeling. Which cell activity contributes?
options: Fibroblast secretion of only dense regular tendon.
practice.explanation: Osteoclasts resorb bone while osteoblasts form new matrix, reshaping the repair region.

practice.question: A student builds a lumbar-only model with eight movable vertebrae. To represent the usual adult lumbar count, how many pieces should be removed?
practice.explanation: The usual lumbar count is five, so an eight-piece model contains three extra pieces.

practice.question: A side-view skull model marks the junction between temporal and parietal regions. Which joint type characterizes this connection?
practice.explanation: Cranial bones meet at fibrous sutures; named sutures identify particular skull boundaries.

practice.question: A replica has a rounded proximal head fitting the scapular socket and a distal end articulating with radius and ulna. Which bone is represented?
practice.explanation: The humerus is the arm bone; radius and ulna occupy the forearm, and femur the thigh.

practice.question: A skeleton model emphasizes red marrow as well as mineralized support. Which additional function belongs to the skeleton?
options: Hormone storage in an endocrine follicle.
practice.explanation: Red marrow supports hematopoiesis, complementing support, protection, movement, and mineral storage.

practice.question: An articulation has a fluid-filled space, capsule, and articular cartilage. Which structural class fits?
practice.explanation: A synovial cavity and capsule distinguish synovial joints from fibrous and cartilaginous classes.

practice.question: A joint model has dense bands connecting bone to bone around its capsule. Which structures reinforce stability?
options: Articular cartilage replacing every external restraint.
Synovial fluid acting as a tensile band.
practice.explanation: Ligaments generally connect bone to bone and help stabilize joints.

practice.question: A model allows rotation around one longitudinal axis, as in the atlas-axis region. Which joint type best fits?
practice.explanation: Pivot joints permit axial rotation around a central axis.

practice.question: An articulation needs multiaxial motion and circumduction like a shoulder. Which form is suited to this?
practice.explanation: Ball-and-socket geometry allows movement in several planes, including rotation.

practice.question: A person raises the upper limb laterally away from the trunk. Which movement occurs at the shoulder?
practice.explanation: Abduction moves a segment away from the reference midline.

practice.question: With the elbow bent, a person rotates an empty hand into a palm-up position to receive a handful of coins. Which forearm movement is being demonstrated?
practice.explanation: Supination turns the forearm/palm toward the anatomical-position orientation.

practice.question: A foot moves so its dorsal surface approaches the anterior leg. Which movement is being practiced?
practice.explanation: Dorsiflexion brings the top of the foot toward the shin.

practice.question: A knee model includes fibrocartilage pads between femur and tibia. What is one important role of these pads?
options: Serving as the vascular red marrow of the knee.
Distributing load and improving joint congruence.
Replacing cruciate ligaments in limiting every translation.
Producing synovial fluid as their sole role.
practice.answer: Distributing load and improving joint congruence.
practice.explanation: Menisci help spread forces and improve congruence; they are not substitutes for all stabilizing structures.

practice.question: A deep socket and strong supporting structures favor stability in a weight-bearing ball-and-socket joint. Which example fits?
practice.explanation: The hip balances mobility with weight-bearing stability through its deep acetabulum and supporting tissues.

practice.question: An articular surface loses cartilage over time and joint mechanics deteriorate. Which tissue property helps explain limited spontaneous repair?
options: Rapid turnover identical to basal epidermis.
A complete absence of any extracellular matrix.
Extensive vascular canals throughout all articular cartilage.
Articular cartilage has little intrinsic vascular supply.
practice.answer: Articular cartilage has little intrinsic vascular supply.
practice.explanation: Limited vascularity and specialized cartilage biology restrict intrinsic healing.

practice.question: A connective sheath surrounds a whole skeletal muscle, while thinner sheaths separate fascicles and fibers. Which sheath surrounds the whole muscle?
options: Deep fascia only, outside the epimysial sheath.
practice.explanation: Epimysium surrounds the whole muscle; perimysium fascicles and endomysium individual fibers.

practice.concept: Skeletal Muscle Fiber and the Sarcomere
practice.question: A fiber's repeating dark/light pattern follows organized thick and thin filaments. Which structural unit underlies this organization?
options: Myofibril as a single nonrepeating unit.
practice.explanation: Sarcomeres organize actin and myosin into repeating contractile units that produce striation.

practice.question: A motor neuron releases transmitter at a skeletal muscle junction. Which transmitter initiates the usual postsynaptic response?
practice.explanation: Acetylcholine activates nicotinic receptors at the skeletal neuromuscular junction.

practice.question: Calcium binds a thin-filament regulatory complex and moves a blocking protein away from actin sites. Which sequence fits?
options: Calcium binds troponin and shifts tropomyosin.
Troponin removes calcium from the sarcoplasm to start contraction.
Myosin stores calcium in place of the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Calcium binds directly to tropomyosin without a regulatory change.
practice.answer: Calcium binds troponin and shifts tropomyosin.
practice.explanation: Calcium-troponin interaction changes thin-filament regulation, allowing cross-bridge cycling.

practice.question: A myosin head remains tightly attached when ATP becomes unavailable. Which normal ATP role explains the attachment?
options: ATP binding locks the attached head permanently.
ATP is needed only to synthesize actin, not cross-bridge cycling.
ATP release alone moves calcium into the extracellular space.
practice.explanation: ATP binding allows myosin to detach; hydrolysis helps reenergize the head for another cycle.

practice.question: A muscle develops force while its total length remains nearly constant. Which contraction description fits?
practice.explanation: Isometric contraction develops tension without substantial overall length change.

practice.question: A muscle briefly uses phosphocreatine to replenish ATP during rapid demand. What is the immediate advantage?
options: It removes the need for ATP during contraction.
Rapid phosphate transfer helps buffer ATP availability.
It produces oxygen for the electron transport chain.
It supplies the largest long-term fuel reserve for days.
practice.answer: Rapid phosphate transfer helps buffer ATP availability.
practice.explanation: Phosphocreatine provides a rapid limited reserve for ATP regeneration.

practice.question: A laboratory compound reduces involuntary vessel-wall constriction while leaving striated limb muscle fibers directly unaffected. Which tissue is the intended contractile target?
options: A voluntary striated fiber with peripheral nuclei.
practice.explanation: Smooth muscle has a nonstriated spindle-shaped organization suited to many visceral walls.

practice.question: Two muscles produce opposite movements at a joint. How can their relationship be described?
options: They must act as the same agonist in every movement.
They cannot be activated in a coordinated stabilizing pattern.
They are synergists simply because their actions oppose.
practice.explanation: Antagonistic actions permit controlled opposing movements and stabilization.

practice.question: A strong connective structure transmits muscle pull to bone. Which structure provides this linkage?
practice.explanation: Tendons connect muscle with bone and transmit tensile force.

practice.question: A pathway carries stretch information from a limb toward the spinal cord. Which functional direction applies?
options: A descending motor tract by definition.
practice.explanation: Sensory information traveling toward CNS is afferent regardless of where it appears on a drawing.

practice.question: A neuronal cell region contains prominent rough ER supporting protein production. What is the material commonly called?
options: A Golgi stack in an axon terminal.
practice.explanation: Nissl substance corresponds to rough ER and ribosomal material in soma and dendrites.

practice.concept: Glia, myelin, gray matter, and white matter
practice.question: A single peripheral glial cell wraps one segment of one axon in many membrane layers. Which cell fits?
practice.explanation: Schwann cells produce individual PNS myelin segments; oligodendrocytes form CNS myelin.

practice.concept: Glia, myelin, gray matter, and white matter
practice.question: A fluid-filled neural cavity is lined by ciliated glial cells. Which CNS cell class is most relevant?
practice.explanation: Ependymal cells line ventricles and the central canal and contribute to the CSF environment.

practice.question: A graded response shifts from −70 to −80 mV. What effect does this change commonly have relative to a depolarizing threshold?
options: It is depolarization because its magnitude increased.
It moves the membrane closer to a depolarizing threshold.
It moves the membrane farther from that threshold.
It necessarily produces a full sodium spike.
practice.answer: It moves the membrane farther from that threshold.
practice.explanation: Hyperpolarization makes the inside more negative and generally reduces immediate firing likelihood under these conditions.

practice.question: A pump maintains sodium and potassium gradients over repeated signaling. Which direction matches its typical ATP cycle?
options: Two sodium outward and three potassium inward.
Three sodium outward and two potassium inward.
Three potassium outward and two sodium inward.
Three sodium inward and two potassium outward.
practice.answer: Three sodium outward and two potassium inward.
practice.explanation: The sodium–potassium ATPase exports three Na+ and imports two K+ per ATP.

practice.question: A strong stimulus produces more spikes per second but each spike remains similar in amplitude. What coding principle is demonstrated?
options: Frequency coding with all-or-none action potentials.
Loss of all refractory behavior at stronger stimuli.
A decrease in spike frequency as the only intensity code.
Continuous growth of each action potential's amplitude.
practice.answer: Frequency coding with all-or-none action potentials.
practice.explanation: Neural systems can encode intensity through firing rate and recruitment rather than increasing each spike's amplitude.

practice.question: A membrane is repolarizing after its spike peak. Which ion movement commonly contributes strongly?
options: Sodium influx through rapidly opening channels.
Chloride exit as the universal mechanism of all neuronal spikes.
practice.explanation: Delayed potassium conductance supports repolarization and can produce an after-hyperpolarization.

practice.question: A drug slows a transmitter's reuptake without changing release. Which synaptic change is plausible?
options: Shorter transmitter availability because reuptake is slower.
Complete elimination of postsynaptic receptor binding.
A receptor-independent identical response in every target.
A longer period of transmitter availability in the cleft.
practice.answer: A longer period of transmitter availability in the cleft.
practice.explanation: Reduced clearance can prolong transmitter action; the physiological result depends on transmitter and receptors.

practice.question: Several presynaptic neurons deliver signals to one postsynaptic neuron. Which wiring pattern is present?
options: Temporal summation by only one presynaptic input.
practice.explanation: Convergence combines information from multiple inputs onto a common target.

practice.question: A CSF pathway returns fluid from subarachnoid spaces toward a dural venous sinus through classical projections. What structures are involved?
options: Cerebral aqueduct drainage directly into the stomach.
Ependymal production of new blood vessels.
practice.explanation: Arachnoid granulations participate in classical CSF venous drainage, with additional drainage routes also recognized.

practice.question: A central spinal region contains motor cell bodies rather than a long ascending white-matter bundle. Which feature fits?
practice.explanation: Ventral horns contain somatic motor neuron cell bodies; columns are white-matter pathway regions.

practice.question: A lower lumbar canal image shows nerve roots surrounding the filum below the spinal cord tip. Which name describes the root bundle?
practice.explanation: The cauda equina contains descending spinal roots below the conus medullaris.

practice.question: A reflex circuit includes an interneuron contained entirely within spinal gray matter. What role does it provide?
options: Central integration between neural inputs and outputs.
Sensory transduction by the peripheral receptor.
Contraction of the final skeletal effector.
practice.answer: Central integration between neural inputs and outputs.
practice.explanation: Interneurons process and relay signals in central circuits.

practice.question: A visual cortical response is recorded after light reaches a retina. Which cerebral lobe contains the main primary visual region?
practice.explanation: Primary visual cortex lies in occipital cortex, distinct from retinal transduction and optic-nerve conduction.

practice.question: A brainstem section is continuous inferiorly with the spinal cord near the skull opening. Which region fits?
options: Pons as the region immediately continuous with the cord.
practice.explanation: The medulla connects the brainstem with spinal cord and contains critical autonomic circuits.

practice.question: An instructor calls a diencephalic relay a gateway for much incoming sensory information. Which region is intended?
options: Basal nuclei as the universal primary sensory relay.
practice.explanation: The thalamus relays/processes much cortical sensory input; olfaction has a distinctive initial route.

practice.concept: Cranial nerves and peripheral nerve organization
practice.question: A patient scenario centers on impaired lateral eye movement from loss of lateral rectus innervation. Which cranial nerve should a learner identify?
practice.explanation: The abducens nerve supplies lateral rectus; other eye muscles receive III or IV.

practice.question: A craniosacral pathway uses a long preganglionic axon and a ganglion near its target. Which division fits?
options: A sensory afferent pathway entering a dorsal root.
Direct somatic motor output without an autonomic ganglion.
practice.explanation: Parasympathetic ganglia lie near/in targets, supporting the typical long preganglionic, short postganglionic pattern.

practice.question: Both divisions of an autonomic system use the same transmitter at their ganglionic synapses. Which receptor/transmitter pairing fits?
practice.explanation: Autonomic preganglionic neurons release acetylcholine onto nicotinic ganglionic receptors.

practice.question: A sustained harmless pressure becomes less noticeable over time while a new pressure change is easily detected. Which principle helps explain this?
options: A permanent loss of all receptors after any stimulus.
A gradual reduction of each axonal action potential's amplitude.
Sensory adaptation and emphasis on change.
A requirement that every sensory signal stay equally intense forever.
practice.answer: Sensory adaptation and emphasis on change.
practice.explanation: Adaptation can reduce responses to sustained stimuli while preserving sensitivity to change.

practice.question: A receptor in a muscle-tendon junction responds strongly to tension rather than muscle length alone. Which receptor fits?
practice.explanation: Golgi tendon organs monitor tension; muscle spindles emphasize length and stretch.

practice.question: A visceral problem is experienced as discomfort at a separate body-surface location. Which explanation is consistent with referred pain?
options: Visceral sensory signals never enter central processing circuits.
Each visceral pain fiber must terminate directly in the skin.
The pain location always exactly identifies the damaged tissue.
Converging pathways can lead central circuits to attribute signals to a somatic region.
practice.answer: Converging pathways can lead central circuits to attribute signals to a somatic region.
practice.explanation: Shared central processing of visceral and somatic input contributes to referred pain.

practice.question: A person detects basic tastes but food seems less flavorful after loss of smell. Which interpretation fits?
options: Olfactory signals must travel through the optic nerve.
Flavor normally integrates olfaction with taste and other senses.
Flavor depends only on taste buds and never on smell.
Each basic taste is confined to one exclusive tongue zone.
practice.answer: Flavor normally integrates olfaction with taste and other senses.
practice.explanation: Olfactory input contributes substantially to flavor even when gustatory receptors remain functional.

practice.question: An anterior tongue taste signal is contrasted with touch from the same region. Which distinction is appropriate?
options: Taste commonly travels through VII, while much somatic input travels through V.
Anterior tongue taste uses only vagus X and no facial pathway.
Taste uses XII motor axons while touch uses optic II.
Taste and touch from the region both use only VII.
practice.answer: Taste commonly travels through VII, while much somatic input travels through V.
practice.explanation: Cranial nerves have different modalities; trigeminal somatic sensation differs from facial gustatory input.

practice.question: A middle-ear tube opens to help equalize pressure on the tympanic membrane. What region does it connect with the middle ear?
options: External auditory canal directly through the stapes.
practice.explanation: The auditory tube connects middle ear to nasopharynx, not directly to inner-ear endolymph.

practice.question: Basilar membrane motion bends sensory projections and changes transmitter release onto a cranial nerve fiber. What transduction is occurring?
options: Chemical-to-neural signaling by taste receptor cells.
Pressure equalization through the auditory tube without receptor activation.
Mechanical-to-neural signaling by cochlear hair cells.
practice.answer: Mechanical-to-neural signaling by cochlear hair cells.
practice.explanation: Hair-cell mechanotransduction converts cochlear mechanical motion into signaling to auditory fibers.

practice.question: A head begins rotating and fluid motion deflects a cupula in an ampulla. Which sensory structure is responding?
options: Crista ampullaris of a semicircular duct.
practice.answer: Crista ampullaris of a semicircular duct.
practice.explanation: Semicircular duct cristae detect angular acceleration through cupular displacement.

practice.question: A label points to fluid between the iris and lens. Which identification is precise?
options: Aqueous humor in the anterior chamber in front of the iris.
Vitreous humor in the posterior cavity.
Aqueous humor in the posterior chamber.
practice.answer: Aqueous humor in the posterior chamber.
practice.explanation: The posterior chamber is the small aqueous space behind iris and in front of lens, distinct from the large vitreous cavity.

practice.question: A near object is brought into focus after a distant one. Which coordinated change is expected?
options: Ciliary relaxation with reduced zonular tension and a rounder lens.
Ciliary contraction, less zonular tension, and a rounder lens.
Ciliary contraction with greater zonular tension and a flatter lens.
Ciliary relaxation, greater zonular tension, and a flatter lens.
practice.answer: Ciliary contraction, less zonular tension, and a rounder lens.
practice.explanation: Near accommodation relaxes zonular pull through ciliary contraction, allowing a more convex lens.

figures.alt: Figure 7.A. Major parts of a long bone (femur), shown in longitudinal section.
figures.caption: Figure 7.A. Major parts of a long bone (femur), shown in longitudinal section.
figures.description: The drawing shows a long bone cut lengthwise. Each end is an expanded epiphysis made mostly of spongy bone, capped with articular cartilage where it forms a joint. The long shaft between the ends is the diaphysis: a thick collar of compact bone around a hollow medullary cavity that holds yellow marrow. A thin epiphyseal line (the remnant of the growth plate) separates each epiphysis from the diaphysis. The periosteum covers the outside of the bone except the articular cartilage, and the endosteum lines the medullary cavity. A nutrient foramen lets blood vessels enter the shaft.
figures.credit: Image: OpenStax College, 603 Anatomy of Long Bone.jpg, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Resized where needed and converted to WebP; no labels or anatomical artwork changed. Open full-size image.

figures.description: Study the labeled structures in Bone cells. The accompanying section explains their relationships: Osteoclasts break down (resorb) bone tissue. Osteocytes live inside lacunae. Most of the bone matrix is made of hydroxyapatite crystals (calcium phosphate).

figures.alt: Figure 7.B. Microscopic structure of compact bone: an osteon (Haversian system).
figures.caption: Figure 7.B. Microscopic structure of compact bone: an osteon (Haversian system).
figures.description: The illustration enlarges a block of compact bone from the shaft of a long bone. Circular osteons contain concentric lamellae around central canals carrying blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, and nerves. A perforating canal crosses between the central canals and connects them with vessels beneath the periosteum. Circumferential lamellae follow the outer surface, while interstitial lamellae fill spaces between osteons. The right side shows the transition to trabeculae of spongy bone and the medullary cavity. Osteocytes, lacunae, and canaliculi are discussed in the accompanying text but are not individually labeled in this illustration.
figures.credit: Image: OpenStax, 605 Compact Bone.jpg, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Resized where needed and converted to WebP; no labels or anatomical artwork changed. Open full-size image.
figures.author: OpenStax

figures.alt: Figure 7.C. Negative feedback control of blood calcium by calcitonin and parathyroid hormone.
figures.caption: Figure 7.C. Negative feedback control of blood calcium by calcitonin and parathyroid hormone.
figures.description: The diagram is a loop centered on normal blood calcium. On the high side: when blood calcium rises, the thyroid gland releases calcitonin. Calcitonin inhibits osteoclasts, osteoblasts deposit calcium into bone, and the kidneys excrete more calcium, so blood calcium falls back to normal. On the low side: when blood calcium falls, the parathyroid glands release parathyroid hormone. Parathyroid hormone stimulates osteoclasts to resorb bone, the kidneys reabsorb calcium, and the intestine absorbs more calcium (with vitamin D), so blood calcium rises back to normal.
figures.credit: Image: OpenStax College, 625 Calcium Homeostasis.jpg, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Resized where needed and converted to WebP; no labels or anatomical artwork changed. Open full-size image.

figures.alt: Figure 8.A. General structure of a synovial joint, in section.
figures.caption: Figure 8.A. General structure of a synovial joint, in section.
figures.description: A cutaway drawing of a synovial joint with one bone above and one below. The rounded end of each bone is covered by a blue-gray layer of articular cartilage. Between the two cartilages is the joint cavity, which contains synovial fluid (shown in pale yellow). Around the cavity is the articular capsule: an outer fibrous layer, and, lining its inside, the synovial membrane (shown in orange-red). Labels: bone (top and bottom), articular cartilage, synovial membrane, articular capsule, and joint cavity containing synovial fluid.

figures.alt: Figure 8.B. The six types of synovial joints, with an example of each.
figures.caption: Figure 8.B. The six types of synovial joints, with an example of each.
figures.description: A skeleton in the center with six boxes marking joints, each linked to a simple model that shows the motion. (a) Pivot joint between the C1 and C2 vertebrae: a peg turning inside a ring. (b) Hinge joint at the elbow: a cylinder in a trough, moving in one plane. (c) Saddle joint between the trapezium carpal bone and the first metacarpal at the base of the thumb: two saddle-shaped surfaces. (d) Plane (gliding) joint between tarsal bones: flat surfaces sliding. (e) Condyloid joint between the radius and the carpal bones of the wrist: an oval head in an oval socket. (f) Ball-and-socket joint at the hip: a round head in a cup, moving in all directions.
figures.credit: Image: OpenStax College, 909 Types of Synovial Joints.jpg, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Resized and converted to WebP; artwork and labels preserved. Open full-size image.

figures.alt: Figure 8.C. The knee joint: sagittal section, superior view of the tibia, and anterior view.
figures.caption: Figure 8.C. The knee joint: sagittal section, superior view of the tibia, and anterior view.
figures.description: Three views of the right knee. (a) A side section shows the femur above and the tibia below, the patella in front, the synovial cavity, the anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments, the lateral meniscus, the infrapatellar fat pad, and three bursae: suprapatellar, prepatellar, and infrapatellar. (b) A view from above of the tibia shows the C-shaped medial and lateral menisci and the crossing anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments. (c) A view from the front shows the quadriceps muscle and tendon, the patella and patellar ligament, the tibial (medial) and fibular (lateral) collateral ligaments, the tibia, and the fibula.

figures.alt: Figure 9.B. A sarcomere, the functional unit of contraction.
figures.caption: Figure 9.B. A sarcomere, the functional unit of contraction.
figures.description: The drawing shows one sarcomere between two Z lines. Thin actin filaments are attached to each Z line and extend toward the center. Thick myosin filaments sit in the middle. The A band is the dark region that spans the full length of the thick filaments. The I band is the light region containing only thin filaments, and it spans across the Z line into the next sarcomere. The H zone is the lighter central region of the A band with only thick filaments, and the M line is the center. When the muscle contracts, the Z lines move closer together, and the I band and H zone shorten while the A band keeps its length.

figures.caption: Peripheral nerve organization
figures.description: A peripheral nerve contains axons bundled into fascicles. Endoneurium surrounds individual fibers, perineurium surrounds each fascicle, and epineurium surrounds the whole nerve. Vessels travel through connective tissue to supply the nerve. The accompanying micrograph illustrates the bundled organization.
